Cancel \(2cx\) and collect: \(x^2\left(1-\frac{c^2}{a^2}\right)+y^2=a^2-c^2\), that is \(\frac{b^2}{a^2}x^2+y^2=b^2\). Divide by \(b^2>0\): \(\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1\).

Equation \(\Rightarrow\) distances. Suppose \(\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1\). Then \(x^2\le a^2\), so \(\left\lvert\frac cax\right\rvert\le c<a\), and therefore \(a+\frac cax>0\) and \(a-\frac cax>0\). Also \(y^2=b^2-\frac{b^2}{a^2}x^2=a^2-c^2-\left(1-\frac{c^2}{a^2}\right)x^2\). Then

\[u^2=(x+c)^2+y^2=x^2+2cx+c^2+a^2-c^2-x^2+\frac{c^2}{a^2}x^2=a^2+2cx+\frac{c^2}{a^2}x^2=\left(a+\frac cax\right)^2 .\]

Since \(u\ge0\) and \(a+\frac cax>0\), \(u=a+\frac cax\). In the same way \(v^2=\left(a-\frac cax\right)^2\) and \(v=a-\frac cax\). Adding, \(u+v=2a\).

The vertices and minor-axis vertices are the intercepts (\(y=0\) gives \(x=\pm a\); \(x=0\) gives \(y=\pm b\)). The last statement is the first with \(x\) and \(y\) exchanged. ◻ ∎

Example 12.4.8: An ellipse: everything from the equation

Find the vertices, minor-axis vertices, foci, axes, eccentricity and directrices of \(7x^2+16y^2=112\), and sketch it.

Solution. Divide by \(112\): \(\frac{x^2}{16}+\frac{y^2}7=1\). The larger denominator is under \(x^2\), so the foci are on the \(x\)-axis and (Theorem 12.4.7) \(a^2=16\), \(b^2=7\): \(a=4\), \(b=\sqrt7\approx2.65\). Then \(c^2=a^2-b^2=9\), \(c=3\). The vertices are \((\pm4,0)\), the minor-axis vertices \((0,\pm\sqrt7)\) and the foci \((\pm3,0)\). The major axis has length \(2a=8\) and the minor axis \(2b=2\sqrt7\). The eccentricity (Definition 12.4.15 below) is \(e=\frac ca=\frac34\) and the directrices are \(x=\pm\frac ae=\pm\frac{16}3\). Check. The minor-axis vertex \(\left(0,\sqrt7\right)\) is at distance \(\sqrt{3^2+7}=4\) from each focus, and \(4+4=8=2a\), as the definition requires.

The dashed segments join the minor-axis vertex to the foci. Each has length \(a=4\).

Knowledge Check 12.4.2: Parameters of an ellipse

An ellipse centered at the origin with foci on the \(x\)-axis has \(a=10\) and eccentricity \(e=\frac35\). Find \(b\), \(c\) and the directrices.

Pause and think 12.4.2: Squeezing an ellipse

Keep \(a\) fixed in \(\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1\) and let the foci \((\pm c,0)\) move: first \(c\to0\), then \(c\to a\). What does the ellipse look like in each limit, and what happens to \(b\)?

Answer and discussion

Since \(b^2=a^2-c^2\): as \(c\to0\) the foci merge at the center, \(b\to a\) and the ellipse becomes a circle of radius \(a\) (\(e\to0\)). As \(c\to a\) the foci approach the vertices \((\pm a,0)\), \(b\to0\), and the ellipse flattens to the segment from \((-a,0)\) to \((a,0)\) (\(e\to1\)): then \(\lvert PF_1\rvert+\lvert PF_2\rvert=2a\) is the distance \(\lvert F_1F_2\rvert\), which happens only for \(P\) on the segment between the foci.

items.title: The hyperbola
items.text:
Definition 12.4.9: Hyperbola

Let \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) be points at distance \(2c>0\) and let \(0<a<c\). The hyperbola with foci \(F_1,F_2\) is the set of points \(P\) with \(\bigl\lvert\lvert PF_1\rvert-\lvert PF_2\rvert\bigr\rvert=2a\). Its center is the midpoint of \(F_1F_2\) and its vertices are the two points of the hyperbola on the line \(F_1F_2\).

Theorem 12.4.10: Equation of a hyperbola

Let \(c>a>0\) and \(b=\sqrt{c^2-a^2}\), so \(b^2=c^2-a^2\). The hyperbola with foci \((\pm c,0)\) and \(\bigl\lvert\lvert PF_1\rvert-\lvert PF_2\rvert\bigr\rvert=2a\) is the set of points with

\[\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1 .\]

It has two branches (\(x\ge a\) and \(x\le-a\)), vertices \((\pm a,0)\) and no \(y\)-intercept. For every point, \(\lvert PF_1\rvert=\left\lvert a+\frac cax\right\rvert\) and \(\lvert PF_2\rvert=\left\lvert a-\frac cax\right\rvert\). If the foci are \((0,\pm c)\), the equation is \(\frac{y^2}{a^2}-\frac{x^2}{b^2}=1\).

Proof. Let \(u=\lvert PF_1\rvert\) and \(v=\lvert PF_2\rvert\).

Distances \(\Rightarrow\) equation. If \(\lvert u-v\rvert=2a\), then \(u-v=2a\) or \(v-u=2a\). By Theorem K.3(ii) and (iii), in both cases \(u=\pm\left(a+\frac cax\right)\), so \(u^2=\left(a+\frac cax\right)^2\): \(x^2+2cx+c^2+y^2=a^2+2cx+\frac{c^2}{a^2}x^2\). Cancel \(2cx\) and collect: \(x^2\left(1-\frac{c^2}{a^2}\right)+y^2=a^2-c^2\). Now \(1-\frac{c^2}{a^2}=-\frac{b^2}{a^2}\) and \(a^2-c^2=-b^2\), so \(-\frac{b^2}{a^2}x^2+y^2=-b^2\); divide by \(-b^2<0\): \(\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1\).

Equation \(\Rightarrow\) distances. Suppose \(\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1\). Then \(x^2\ge a^2\) and \(y^2=b^2\left(\frac{x^2}{a^2}-1\right)=(c^2-a^2)\frac{x^2}{a^2}-(c^2-a^2)\). Then

\[u^2=x^2+2cx+c^2+y^2=x^2+2cx+c^2+\frac{c^2}{a^2}x^2-x^2-c^2+a^2=a^2+2cx+\frac{c^2}{a^2}x^2=\left(a+\frac cax\right)^2 ,\]

and in the same way \(v^2=\left(a-\frac cax\right)^2\). So \(u=\left\lvert a+\frac cax\right\rvert\) and \(v=\left\lvert a-\frac cax\right\rvert\). If \(x\ge a\), then \(\frac cax\ge c>a\), so \(a+\frac cax>0\) and \(a-\frac cax<0\), whence \(u=a+\frac cax\), \(v=\frac cax-a\) and \(u-v=2a\). If \(x\le-a\), then \(\frac cax\le-c<-a\), so \(a+\frac cax<0\) and \(a-\frac cax>0\), whence \(u=-a-\frac cax\), \(v=a-\frac cax\) and \(v-u=2a\). In both cases \(\lvert u-v\rvert=2a\).

Setting \(y=0\) gives \(x=\pm a\); setting \(x=0\) gives \(y^2=-b^2<0\), impossible. The last statement is the first with \(x\) and \(y\) exchanged. ◻ ∎

Definition 12.4.11: Asymptote

A line \(y=mx+k\) is an asymptote of a curve as \(x\to\infty\) if the curve contains points \((x,y(x))\) for all large \(x\) and \(y(x)-(mx+k)\to0\) as \(x\to\infty\); the definition as \(x\to-\infty\) is the same.

Theorem 12.4.12: Asymptotes of a hyperbola

The hyperbola \(\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1\) has the two asymptotes \(y=\frac bax\) and \(y=-\frac bax\), and no others (and the same two lines are asymptotes in both directions, \(x\to\infty\) and \(x\to-\infty\)). The hyperbola \(\frac{y^2}{a^2}-\frac{x^2}{b^2}=1\) has the asymptotes \(y=\pm\frac abx\).

Proof. On the upper half of the right branch, \(y=\frac ba\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\) for \(x\ge a\). Then

\[\frac bax-y=\frac ba\left(x-\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\right)=\frac ba\cdot\frac{x^2-\left(x^2-a^2\right)}{x+\sqrt{x^2-a^2}}=\frac{ab}{x+\sqrt{x^2-a^2}},\]

(multiplying and dividing by \(x+\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\)), which is positive and tends to \(0\) as \(x\to\infty\), because the denominator exceeds \(x\). So \(y=\frac bax\) is an asymptote. The hyperbola is symmetric about both axes, which gives \(y=-\frac bax\) for the lower half of the right branch, and the left branch as \(x\to-\infty\).

No other line. Suppose \(y-(mx+k)\to0\) along the upper half of the right branch as \(x\to\infty\). Dividing by \(x\), \(\frac yx-m-\frac kx\to0\), so \(m=\lim\frac yx=\lim\frac ba\sqrt{1-\frac{a^2}{x^2}}=\frac ba\). Then \(k=\lim\left(y-\frac bax\right)=0\) by the computation above. The same argument handles the other three pieces, giving \(-\frac ba\) and \(0\). A vertical line cannot be an asymptote of the form \(y=mx+k\) and on the hyperbola \(\lvert y\rvert=\frac ba\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\) stays bounded when \(x\) stays bounded, so \(y\) cannot tend to infinity near a vertical line. The last statement is the first with \(x\) and \(y\) exchanged: \(x=\frac ba y\) means \(y=\frac abx\). ◻ ∎

The rectangle with corners \((\pm a,\pm b)\) is the central rectangle: its diagonals lie on the asymptotes, and its diagonal has length \(2\sqrt{a^2+b^2}=2c\), so the foci lie on the circle through its corners.

Example 12.4.13: A hyperbola with its asymptotes

Find the vertices, foci, asymptotes, eccentricity and directrices of \(9y^2-16x^2=144\) and sketch it. Check a point.

Solution. Divide by \(144\): \(\frac{y^2}{16}-\frac{x^2}9=1\). The \(y^2\)-term is positive, so the vertices are on the \(y\)-axis (Theorem 12.4.10) and \(a^2=16\), \(b^2=9\): \(a=4\), \(b=3\), \(c^2=a^2+b^2=25\), \(c=5\). Vertices \((0,\pm4)\), foci \((0,\pm5)\), asymptotes \(y=\pm\frac abx=\pm\frac43x\) (they pass through the corners \((\pm3,\pm4)\) of the central rectangle), eccentricity \(e=\frac ca=\frac54\) and directrices \(y=\pm\frac ae=\pm\frac{16}5\). Check. The point \(\left(\frac94,5\right)\) satisfies \(\frac{25}{16}-\frac{81/16}9=\frac{25}{16}-\frac9{16}=1\). Its distances to the foci \((0,\pm5)\) are \(\frac94\) and \(\sqrt{\frac{81}{16}+100}=\frac{41}4\), and their difference is \(\frac{41}4-\frac94=8=2a\).

Example 12.4.14: Equations from data: ellipse, hyperbola and a focus–directrix condition

(a) Find the ellipse centered at the origin with foci \((0,\pm3)\) and directrices \(y=\pm\frac{25}3\). (b) Find the hyperbola centered at the origin with vertices \((0,\pm6)\) and eccentricity \(e=\frac53\), and its directrices and asymptotes. (c) Find the set of points \(P=(x,y)\) with \(\lvert PF\rvert=2\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell)\) for \(F=(4,0)\) and \(\ell:\ x=1\).

Solution. (a) The foci are on the \(y\)-axis, so the ellipse is \(\frac{y^2}{a^2}+\frac{x^2}{b^2}=1\) with \(c=3\). The directrices are \(y=\pm\frac ae\) (Theorem 12.4.16 below) and \(e=\frac ca\), so \(\frac ae=\frac{a^2}c=\frac{25}3\), giving \(a^2=c\cdot\frac{25}3=25\) and \(a=5\). Then \(b^2=a^2-c^2=25-9=16\). The ellipse is \(\frac{y^2}{25}+\frac{x^2}{16}=1\), with \(e=\frac35\). Check. The vertex \((0,5)\) is at distance \(5-3=2\) from the focus \((0,3)\) and \(\frac{25}3-5=\frac{10}3\) from the directrix, and \(\frac35\cdot\frac{10}3=2\).

(b) The foci are on the \(y\)-axis (the vertices are), so the hyperbola is \(\frac{y^2}{a^2}-\frac{x^2}{b^2}=1\) with \(a=6\). From \(e=\frac ca\), \(c=ae=6\cdot\frac53=10\), so \(b^2=c^2-a^2=100-36=64\). The hyperbola is \(\frac{y^2}{36}-\frac{x^2}{64}=1\). The directrices are \(y=\pm\frac ae=\pm\frac{18}5\) and the asymptotes are \(y=\pm\frac abx=\pm\frac34x\) (Theorem 12.4.12). Check. The vertex \((0,6)\) is at distance \(10-6=4\) from the focus \((0,10)\) and \(6-\frac{18}5=\frac{12}5\) from the directrix, and \(\frac53\cdot\frac{12}5=4\).

(c) The condition is \(\sqrt{(x-4)^2+y^2}=2\lvert x-1\rvert\). Both sides are nonnegative, so by Theorem K.1 it is equivalent to \((x-4)^2+y^2=4(x-1)^2\). Expand: \(x^2-8x+16+y^2=4x^2-8x+4\); the terms \(-8x\) cancel, leaving \(y^2+12=3x^2\), that is \(3x^2-y^2=12\), or \(\frac{x^2}4-\frac{y^2}{12}=1\). This is a hyperbola with \(a=2\), \(b^2=12\), \(c^2=16\), \(c=4\) and \(e=\frac ca=2\): its focus is \((c,0)=F\) and its directrix is \(x=\frac ae=1=\ell\), as it must be.

items.title: Eccentricity and the directrix
items.text:
Definition 12.4.15: Eccentricity

For an ellipse or a hyperbola with parameters \(a\) and \(c\) (Theorems 12.4.7 and 12.4.10), the eccentricity is \(e=\frac ca\). Thus \(0<e<1\) for an ellipse and \(e>1\) for a hyperbola; a parabola has \(e=1\). (A circle has \(c=0\), so \(e=0\).)

For an ellipse, \(\frac ba=\sqrt{1-e^2}\): if \(e\) is near \(0\) the ellipse is nearly a circle, and if \(e\) is near \(1\) it is long and thin.

Theorem 12.4.16: The directrix property of the ellipse and the hyperbola

Let \(C\) be the ellipse of Theorem 12.4.7 or the hyperbola of Theorem 12.4.10, with \(e=\frac ca\), foci \(F_1=(-c,0)\), \(F_2=(c,0)\) and the two vertical lines \(\ell_1:\ x=-\frac ae\) and \(\ell_2:\ x=\frac ae\) (the directrices). Then for every point \(P\) of \(C\),

\[\lvert PF_1\rvert=e\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell_1)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\lvert PF_2\rvert=e\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell_2).\]

The same holds for foci \((0,\pm c)\) and directrices \(y=\pm\frac ae\).

Proof. By Theorems 12.4.7 and 12.4.10, \(\lvert PF_2\rvert=\left\lvert a-\frac cax\right\rvert=\lvert a-ex\rvert\) (for the ellipse \(a-ex>0\) and the absolute value is not needed). Factor out \(e\): \(\lvert a-ex\rvert=e\left\lvert\frac ae-x\right\rvert=e\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell_2)\), because the distance from \(P=(x,y)\) to the vertical line \(x=\frac ae\) is \(\left\lvert x-\frac ae\right\rvert\). Likewise \(\lvert PF_1\rvert=\lvert a+ex\rvert=e\left\lvert x+\frac ae\right\rvert=e\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell_1)\). The last statement is the same with \(x\) and \(y\) exchanged. ◻ ∎

So every ellipse and hyperbola has two foci and two directrices, and each focus goes with the nearer directrix. The next theorem is the converse: a focus, a line and a number \(e\) determine a conic.

Theorem 12.4.17: The Eccentricity–Directrix Theorem

Let \(F\) be a point, \(\ell\) a line not through \(F\), \(d=\operatorname{dist}(F,\ell)>0\) and \(e>0\). Let \(C\) be the set of points \(P\) with \(\lvert PF\rvert=e\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell)\). Then

(1) if \(e=1\), \(C\) is a parabola with focus \(F\) and directrix \(\ell\);

(2) if \(0<e<1\), \(C\) is an ellipse of eccentricity \(e\), with \(F\) as one focus and \(\ell\) as the directrix nearer to it; here \(a=\frac{ed}{1-e^2}\) and \(c=ae\);

(3) if \(e>1\), \(C\) is a hyperbola of eccentricity \(e\), with \(F\) as one focus and \(\ell\) as the directrix nearer to it; here \(a=\frac{ed}{e^2-1}\) and \(c=ae\).

In particular the value of \(e\) alone decides the type of the conic.

Proof. Every ellipse and hyperbola is such a set. This is Theorem 12.4.16 (with \(e=\frac ca\)), and a parabola is such a set with \(e=1\) by Definition 12.4.1.

Every such set is a conic. By Theorem K.4 we may move the plane so that \(F=(0,0)\) and \(\ell\) is the line \(x=d\). For \(P=(x,y)\) we have \(\lvert PF\rvert=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\ge0\) and \(e\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell)=e\lvert d-x\rvert\ge0\), so by Theorem K.1 the condition is equivalent to \(x^2+y^2=e^2(d-x)^2\), that is

\[(1-e^2)\,x^2+2e^2d\,x+y^2=e^2d^2 .\]

If \(e=1\) this is \(y^2=-2d\left(x-\frac d2\right)\), the parabola of Theorem 12.4.2 with vertex \(\left(\frac d2,0\right)\) and \(p=-\frac d2\); its focus is \(\left(\frac d2+p,0\right)=(0,0)\) and its directrix \(x=\frac d2-p=d\). If \(e<1\) or \(e>1\), the coefficient \(1-e^2\) is positive or negative, and completing the square in \(x\) gives the equation of an ellipse \(\frac{(x+c)^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1\) or of a hyperbola \(\frac{(x-c)^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1\) with \(a,c\) as stated, \(c=ae\) and \(b^2=\pm(a^2-c^2)\); the focus \((0,0)\) and the directrix \(x=d\) are then the right (resp. left) focus and its nearer directrix, and \(\frac ca=e\). This computation, with every step and every reason, is Theorem K.5 in Appendix K, so each of the three cases is proved. The worked computation below shows what it looks like with numbers. ◻ ∎

A worked instance. Take \(F=(0,0)\), \(\ell:\ x=3\) and \(e=2\). Then \(x^2+y^2=4(3-x)^2=4x^2-24x+36\), so \(-3x^2+24x+y^2=36\). Complete the square: \(-3x^2+24x=-3(x-4)^2+48\), so \(-3(x-4)^2+y^2=-12\), that is \(\frac{(x-4)^2}{4}-\frac{y^2}{12}=1\). This is the hyperbola with center \((4,0)\), \(a=2\), \(b^2=12\), \(c=4=ae\), and indeed \(a=\frac{ed}{e^2-1}=\frac63=2\). Its foci are \((4\mp4,0)=(0,0)\) and \((8,0)\), and its directrix nearer to \(F\) is \(x=4-\frac ae=3\).

The three curves of the picture have the same focus \(F\) and the same directrix \(x=2\) (\(d=2\)) and differ only in \(e\): \(r=\frac{1}{1+\frac12\cos\theta}\) (ellipse, vertices \(\left(\frac23,0\right)\) and \((-2,0)\)), \(r=\frac{2}{1+\cos\theta}\) (parabola, vertex \((1,0)\)) and \(r=\frac{4}{1+2\cos\theta}\) (the hyperbola branch around \(F\), vertex \(\left(\frac43,0\right)\)).

items.title: Translated conics and the general equation
items.text:
Theorem 12.4.18: Translating a conic

Let \(C_0\) be a parabola, ellipse or hyperbola with equation \(f(x,y)=0\), and let \(C\) be its image under the translation \((x,y)\mapsto(x+h,y+k)\). Then \(C\) has the equation \(f(x-h,y-k)=0\). The foci, vertices, center, directrices and asymptotes of \(C\) are the images of those of \(C_0\), and \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), \(e\) and \(p\) are unchanged.

Proof. A point \((x,y)\) is in \(C\) if and only if \((x-h,y-k)\) is in \(C_0\), that is, if and only if \(f(x-h,y-k)=0\). A translation preserves distances and carries lines to lines (Theorem K.4), so the conditions that define the focus, directrix and vertex, the distances \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), \(p\) and the ratio \(e\), and the property of being an asymptote (the vertical gap in Definition 12.4.11 is unchanged by a translation) all carry over. ◻ ∎

Standard forms of translated conics

  • Parabola. \((x-h)^2=4p(y-k)\): vertex \((h,k)\), focus \((h,k+p)\), directrix \(y=k-p\). \((y-k)^2=4p(x-h)\): vertex \((h,k)\), focus \((h+p,k)\), directrix \(x=h-p\).

  • Ellipse. \( rac{(x-h)^2}{a^2}+ rac{(y-k)^2}{b^2}=1\) with \(a>b\): center \((h,k)\), vertices \((h\pm a,k)\), foci \((h\pm c,k)\), directrices \(x=h\pm rac ae\). If \(a>b\) is under \((y-k)^2\), exchange the roles: vertices \((h,k\pm a)\), foci \((h,k\pm c)\), directrices \(y=k\pm rac ae\). Always \(c^2=a^2-b^2\).

  • Hyperbola. \( rac{(x-h)^2}{a^2}- rac{(y-k)^2}{b^2}=1\): vertices \((h\pm a,k)\), foci \((h\pm c,k)\), asymptotes \(y-k=\pm rac ba(x-h)\), directrices \(x=h\pm rac ae\). \( rac{(y-k)^2}{a^2}- rac{(x-h)^2}{b^2}=1\): vertices \((h,k\pm a)\), foci \((h,k\pm c)\), asymptotes \(y-k=\pm rac ab(x-h)\), directrices \(y=k\pm rac ae\). Always \(c^2=a^2+b^2\).

A conic with its axes parallel to the coordinate axes is described by an equation \(Ax^2+Cy^2+Dx+Ey+F=0\) with no \(xy\) term. Completing the square puts it into one of the standard forms, or shows that it is a degenerate set.

Theorem 12.4.19: Classification of \(Ax^2+Cy^2+Dx+Ey+F=0\)

Let \(A,C,D,E,F\) be real numbers with \(A\) and \(C\) not both \(0\).

(i) If \(AC>0\), the solution set is an ellipse (a circle if \(A=C\)), a single point, or empty.

(ii) If \(AC<0\), the solution set is a hyperbola or a pair of intersecting lines.

(iii) If \(AC=0\), say \(A=0 e C\) (the case \(C=0 e A\) is the same with \(x\) and \(y\) exchanged), the solution set is a parabola if \(D e0\); if \(D=0\) it is a pair of parallel lines, a single line, or empty.

Proof. (i) and (ii): \(AC e0\). Put \(h=- rac D{2A}\), \(k=- rac E{2C}\). Completing the square, \(A\left(x^2+ rac DAx ight)=A(x-h)^2-Ah^2\) and similarly for \(y\), so the equation is equivalent to

\[A(x-h)^2+C(y-k)^2=K,\qquad K=Ah^2+Ck^2-F .\]

If \(AC>0\) then \(A\) and \(C\) have the same sign; multiplying the whole equation by \(-1\) if necessary, assume \(A,C>0\). If \(K>0\), dividing by \(K\) gives \( rac{(x-h)^2}{K/A}+ rac{(y-k)^2}{K/C}=1\), an ellipse centered at \((h,k)\) (a circle if \(A=C\)). If \(K=0\), a sum of two nonnegative terms is \(0\) only if both vanish: the point \((h,k)\). If \(K<0\), a sum of nonnegative terms cannot be negative: no points. If \(AC<0\) and \(K e0\), dividing by \(K\) gives \( rac{(x-h)^2}{K/A}+ rac{(y-k)^2}{K/C}=1\) in which \( rac KA\) and \( rac KC\) have opposite signs. If \( rac KA>0> rac KC\) this is \( rac{(x-h)^2}{K/A}- rac{(y-k)^2}{-K/C}=1\), a hyperbola with horizontal axis; if \( rac KA<0< rac KC\) it is \( rac{(y-k)^2}{K/C}- rac{(x-h)^2}{-K/A}=1\), a hyperbola with vertical axis. If \(K=0\), then \((y-k)^2=- rac AC(x-h)^2\) with \(- rac AC>0\), that is \(y-k=\pm\sqrt{-A/C}\,(x-h)\): two lines through \((h,k)\).

(iii) \(A=0 e C\). Put \(k=- rac E{2C}\). Then \(Cy^2+Ey=C(y-k)^2-Ck^2\), and the equation is equivalent to \(C(y-k)^2=-Dx+K'\) with \(K'=Ck^2-F\). If \(D e0\), this is \((y-k)^2=- rac DC\left(x- rac{K'}D ight)\), which is \((y-k)^2=4p(x-x_0)\) with \(4p=- rac DC\) and \(x_0= rac{K'}D\): a parabola with vertex \((x_0,k)\) (Theorems 12.4.2 and 12.4.18). If \(D=0\), then \((y-k)^2= rac{K'}C\): two lines \(y=k\pm\sqrt{K'/C}\) if \( rac{K'}C>0\), the line \(y=k\) if \(K'=0\), and no points if \( rac{K'}C<0\). ◻ ∎

Procedure 12.4.20: Identify and sketch a conic \(Ax^2+Cy^2+Dx+Ey+F=0\)

  1. Decide the type from the signs: \(AC>0\) ellipse, \(AC<0\) hyperbola, \(AC=0\) parabola (Theorem 12.4.19); the last depends on step 3.

  2. Group the \(x\)-terms and the \(y\)-terms; factor out the coefficient of the square before completing it: \(A\left(x^2+ rac DAx ight)=A(x-h)^2-Ah^2\).

  3. Collect the constants on the right. If the right side is \(0\) or has the wrong sign, the set is degenerate (a point, two lines, empty), as in Theorem 12.4.19. Otherwise divide to make the right side \(1\).

  4. Read \(h\), \(k\), \(a\), \(b\) (and \(p\)) from the standard forms, then \(c\), \(e\) and the vertices, foci, directrices and asymptotes.

  5. Sketch: center or vertex, axes, the central rectangle, asymptotes, foci. Check one point in the original equation.

Example 12.4.21: A translated ellipse

Identify \(9x^2+16y^2-36x+96y+36=0\) and find its center, vertices, foci, eccentricity and directrices. Sketch it.

Solution. \(AC=144>0\), so it is an ellipse or degenerate. Group: \(9\left(x^2-4x ight)+16\left(y^2+6y ight)=-36\). Complete the squares: \(x^2-4x=(x-2)^2-4\) and \(y^2+6y=(y+3)^2-9\), so \(9(x-2)^2-36+16(y+3)^2-144=-36\), that is \(9(x-2)^2+16(y+3)^2=144\). Divide by \(144\): \( rac{(x-2)^2}{16}+ rac{(y+3)^2}9=1\). The right side is positive, so it is a genuine ellipse with center \((2,-3)\), \(a=4\) (horizontal), \(b=3\), \(c=\sqrt{16-9}=\sqrt7\approx2.65\), \(e= rac{\sqrt7}4\approx0.66\). The vertices are \((2\pm4,-3)=(6,-3),(-2,-3)\); the minor-axis vertices are \((2,-3\pm3)=(2,0),(2,-6)\); the foci are \(\left(2\pm\sqrt7,-3 ight)\approx(4.65,-3),(-0.65,-3)\); the directrices are \(x=2\pm rac ae=2\pm rac{16}{\sqrt7}\approx8.05,\,-4.05\). Check. The vertex \((6,-3)\) satisfies the original equation: \(9\cdot36+16\cdot9-216-288+36=324+144-216-288+36=0\).

Example 12.4.22: A hyperbola and its asymptotes from a general equation

Identify \(x^2-4y^2-6x-16y-11=0\). Find its center, vertices, foci, asymptotes and directrices, and sketch it.

Solution. \(AC=-4<0\), so it is a hyperbola or two lines. Group: \(\left(x^2-6x ight)-4\left(y^2+4y ight)=11\). Complete the squares (the factor \(-4\) must be taken out first, so the \(4\) completing \(y^2+4y\) is multiplied by \(-4\)): \(x^2-6x=(x-3)^2-9\) and \(y^2+4y=(y+2)^2-4\), so \((x-3)^2-9-4(y+2)^2+16=11\), that is \((x-3)^2-4(y+2)^2=4\). Divide by \(4\): \( rac{(x-3)^2}4-(y+2)^2=1\). The right side is \(1 e0\), so it is a hyperbola with center \((3,-2)\), horizontal axis, \(a=2\), \(b=1\), \(c=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}=\sqrt5\), \(e= rac{\sqrt5}2\). The vertices are \((3\pm2,-2)=(1,-2),(5,-2)\); the foci are \(\left(3\pm\sqrt5,-2 ight)\approx(5.24,-2),(0.76,-2)\); the asymptotes are \(y+2=\pm rac ba(x-3)=\pm rac12(x-3)\), that is \(y= rac x2- rac72\) and \(y=- rac x2- rac12\); the directrices are \(x=3\pm rac ae=3\pm rac4{\sqrt5}\approx4.79,\,1.21\). Check. The vertex \((5,-2)\): \(25-16-30+32-11=0\), and the asymptote \(y= rac x2- rac72\) passes through the center \((3,-2)\): \( rac32- rac72=-2\).

Example 12.4.23: A parabola from a general equation

Identify \(y^2-8y-12x+40=0\) and find its vertex, axis, focus, directrix and latus rectum.

Solution. \(A=0\) and \(C=1\), so it is a parabola (the \(x\)-term is of first degree, \(D=-12 e0\); Theorem 12.4.19(iii)). Complete the square in \(y\): \(y^2-8y=(y-4)^2-16\), so \((y-4)^2-16-12x+40=0\), that is \((y-4)^2=12x-24=12(x-2)\). Compare with \((y-k)^2=4p(x-h)\): \(h=2\), \(k=4\), \(4p=12\), \(p=3>0\). The vertex is \((2,4)\), the axis is the line \(y=4\), the parabola opens to the right, the focus is \((h+p,k)=(5,4)\) and the directrix is \(x=h-p=-1\). The latus rectum is the chord \(x=5\): \((y-4)^2=36\), so \(y=10\) or \(y=-2\): its endpoints are \((5,10)\) and \((5,-2)\), and its length is \(12=4p\). Check. The point \((5,10)\) is on the curve: \(100-80-60+40=0\), and its distance to the focus \((5,4)\) is \(6\), the distance to the directrix \(x=-1\) is \(5-(-1)=6\).

items.title: Polar equations of conics
items.text:
Polar coordinates (Section 12.2) describe a conic most simply when a focus is at the pole, because then \(\lvert PF vert\) is just the radial coordinate. Each point has many polar representations, and \(r\) may be negative; “\(P\) is on the curve \(r=g( heta)\)” means that some pair of polar coordinates of \(P\) satisfies the equation.

Theorem 12.4.24: Polar equations of conics

Let \(d>0\) and \(e>0\), and let \(F\) be the pole. The set of points \(P\) with \(\lvert PF vert=e\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell)\) is the curve

\[r= rac{ed}{1+e\cos heta}\quad ext{if }\ell ext{ is the line }x=d,\qquad r= rac{ed}{1-e\cos heta}\quad ext{if }\ell ext{ is }x=-d,\] \[r= rac{ed}{1+e\sin heta}\quad ext{if }\ell ext{ is the line }y=d,\qquad r= rac{ed}{1-e\sin heta}\quad ext{if }\ell ext{ is }y=-d.\]

By Theorem 12.4.17 it is a parabola if \(e=1\), an ellipse if \(0<e<1\) and a hyperbola if \(e>1\). The curve is traced by any interval of \( heta\) of length \(2\pi\) (omitting the angles where the denominator is \(0\)).

Proof. First let \(\ell\) be the line \(x=d\).

The graph lies on the conic. Let \(P\) have polar coordinates \((r, heta)\) with \(r(1+e\cos heta)=ed\). Then \(r=e(d-r\cos heta)\), and since \(r\cos heta=x\) is the \(x\)-coordinate of \(P\), \(r=e(d-x)\). Take absolute values: \(\lvert r vert=e\lvert d-x vert\). Now \(\lvert PF vert=\lvert r vert\) (Section 12.2) and \(\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell)=\lvert d-x vert\), so \(\lvert PF vert=e\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell)\).

The conic lies on the graph. Let \(P\) satisfy \(\lvert PF vert=e\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell)\). Then \(P e F\), because \(F\) gives \(0=e\,d\), which is false. Write \(P=(r, heta)\) with \(r=\lvert PF vert>0\) and \( heta\) the direction of the ray \(FP\), so \(x=r\cos heta\). The condition is \(r=e\lvert d-r\cos heta vert\), so either (1) \(r=e(d-r\cos heta)\) or (2) \(r=-e(d-r\cos heta)\). In case (1), \(r(1+e\cos heta)=ed\) and \(P\) is on the graph. In case (2), \(r(1-e\cos heta)=-ed\). The same point \(P\) has the coordinates \((r', heta')=(-r, heta+\pi)\), and \(\cos heta'=-\cos heta\), so \(r'(1+e\cos heta')=-r(1-e\cos heta)=ed\): again \(P\) is on the graph.

The other three equations. The reflection in the \(y\)-axis preserves distances and sends \(F\) to \(F\), the line \(x=d\) to \(x=-d\), and the point with polar coordinates \((r, heta)\) to \((r,\pi- heta)\). A point \((r, heta)\) is on the new curve if and only if \((r,\pi- heta)\) is on the old one: \(r= rac{ed}{1+e\cos(\pi- heta)}= rac{ed}{1-e\cos heta}\). The rotation through \( rac\pi2\) sends \(x=d\) to \(y=d\) and \((r, heta)\) to \(\left(r, heta+ rac\pi2 ight)\), so the new curve is \(r= rac{ed}{1+e\cos\left( heta- rac\pi2 ight)}= rac{ed}{1+e\sin heta}\). The rotation through \(- rac\pi2\) sends \(x=d\) to \(y=-d\) and gives \(r= rac{ed}{1+e\cos\left( heta+ rac\pi2 ight)}= rac{ed}{1-e\sin heta}\). ◻ ∎

Procedure 12.4.25: Reading a conic from its polar equation

Let the equation be \(r=\dfrac{N}{M\pm K\cos heta}\) or \(r=\dfrac{N}{M\pm K\sin heta}\) with \(M e0\).

  1. Divide the numerator and denominator by \(M\) so that the denominator is \(1\pm e\cos heta\) (or \(1\pm e\sin heta\)): \(e= rac KM\) and \(ed= rac NM\), so \(d= rac{ed}e\).

  2. The type is decided by \(e\): ellipse if \(e<1\), parabola if \(e=1\), hyperbola if \(e>1\). The focus is the pole.

  3. The directrix nearest the pole is \(x=d\) for \(+\cos\), \(x=-d\) for \(-\cos\), \(y=d\) for \(+\sin\), \(y=-d\) for \(-\sin\).

  4. The vertices come from \( heta=0,\pi\) (for \(\cos\)) or \( heta= rac\pi2, rac{3\pi}2\) (for \(\sin\)): compute \(r\) and convert to Cartesian coordinates (a negative \(r\) points in the opposite direction). A parabola has one vertex (the other angle makes the denominator \(0\)).

  5. If \(e e1\): \(a= rac{ed}{\lvert1-e^2 vert}\), \(c=ae\), \(b^2=\lvert a^2-c^2 vert\). The center is the midpoint of the vertices, the other focus is the reflection of the pole in the center, and the other directrix is the reflection of the first directrix in the center.

Example 12.4.26: An ellipse from its polar equation

Find the type, directrices, vertices, foci and axes of \(r=\dfrac{10}{5-3\cos heta}\) and sketch it.

Solution. Divide numerator and denominator by \(5\): \(r=\dfrac{2}{1- rac35\cos heta}\). So \(e= rac35<1\): an ellipse, with a focus at the pole. Also \(ed=2\), so \(d= rac{2}{3/5}= rac{10}3\); the sign in front of \(\cos heta\) is \(-\), so the directrix nearest the pole is \(x=- rac{10}3\). Vertices. \( heta=0\): \(r= rac{10}{5-3}=5\), the point \((5,0)\). \( heta=\pi\): \(r= rac{10}{5+3}= rac54\), the point \(\left( rac54,\pi ight)\), which is \(\left(- rac54,0 ight)\). Axes. The major axis has length \(5+ rac54= rac{25}4\), so \(a= rac{25}8\) (the formula \(a= rac{ed}{1-e^2}= rac{2}{16/25}= rac{25}8\) agrees). The center is the midpoint \(\left( rac{5-5/4}{2},0 ight)=\left( rac{15}8,0 ight)\) and \(c=ae= rac{25}8\cdot rac35= rac{15}8\) is its distance to the pole, as it should be. Then \(b^2=a^2-c^2= rac{625-225}{64}= rac{25}4\), \(b= rac52\). The foci are the pole \((0,0)\) and the reflection of the pole in the center, \(\left( rac{15}4,0 ight)\); the other directrix is the reflection of \(x=- rac{10}3\) in \(x= rac{15}8\): \(x= rac{15}4+ rac{10}3= rac{85}{12}\). Check. At \( heta= rac\pi2\), \(r= rac{10}5=2\), the point \((0,2)\): \(\lvert PF vert=2\), its distance to the directrix \(x=- rac{10}3\) is \( rac{10}3\), and \(e\cdot rac{10}3=2\). It is also on the ellipse \( rac{(x-15/8)^2}{(25/8)^2}+ rac{y^2}{(5/2)^2}=1\): \( rac{(15/8)^2}{(25/8)^2}+ rac{4}{25/4}= rac9{25}+ rac{16}{25}=1\).

Knowledge Check 12.4.3: Which conic?

Without graphing, find the eccentricity, the type and the directrix of \(r=\dfrac{5}{2-\cos heta}\), and the Cartesian coordinates of its vertices.

Example 12.4.27: A hyperbola from its polar equation

Find the type, vertices, center, foci, directrices and asymptotes of \(r=\dfrac{16}{3+5\sin heta}\) and sketch it.

Solution. Divide by \(3\): \(r=\dfrac{16/3}{1+ rac53\sin heta}\), so \(e= rac53>1\): a hyperbola with a focus at the pole, \(ed= rac{16}3\) and \(d= rac{16}5\). The sign is \(+\sin heta\), so the directrix nearest the pole is \(y= rac{16}5\). Vertices. \( heta= rac\pi2\): \(r= rac{16}{3+5}=2\), the point \((0,2)\). \( heta= rac{3\pi}2\): \(r= rac{16}{3-5}=-8\), a negative value: the point is \(8\) units from the pole in the direction opposite to \( rac{3\pi}2\), namely \((0,8)\) (indeed \((r\cos heta,r\sin heta)=(-8\cdot0,-8\cdot(-1))=(0,8)\)). Center and axes. The center is the midpoint \((0,5)\) of the vertices, \(2a=8-2=6\), so \(a=3\) (check: \(a= rac{ed}{e^2-1}= rac{16/3}{16/9}=3\)), \(c=ae=5\) (the distance from the center to the pole), \(b^2=c^2-a^2=16\), \(b=4\). The other focus is the reflection of the pole in the center, \((0,10)\); the other directrix is the reflection of \(y= rac{16}5\) in \(y=5\), that is \(y=10- rac{16}5= rac{34}5\). Asymptotes. The axis is vertical, so they are \(y-5=\pm rac abx=\pm rac34x\). (As a check, \(r o\pm\infty\) when \(3+5\sin heta=0\), \(\sin heta=- rac35\), \(\cos heta=\pm rac45\), \( an heta=\mp rac34\): the curve goes off in directions parallel to the asymptotes.) Check. The vertex \((0,8)\) has \(\lvert PF vert=8\) and distance \(8- rac{16}5= rac{24}5\) to the directrix, and \( rac53\cdot rac{24}5=8\). The vertex \((0,2)\) has \(\lvert PF vert=2\) and distance \( rac{16}5-2= rac65\), and \( rac53\cdot rac65=2\).

Example 12.4.28: Between polar and Cartesian forms

(a) Convert \(r=\dfrac9{5+4\cos heta}\) to Cartesian coordinates and identify the curve. (b) The hyperbola \( rac{x^2}9- rac{y^2}{16}=1\) has a focus at \((5,0)\). Find its polar equation with that focus as the pole and the polar axis along the positive \(x\)-axis.

Solution. (a) Clear the denominator: \(5r+4r\cos heta=9\), so \(5r=9-4x\) (using \(x=r\cos heta\)). Square, using \(r^2=x^2+y^2\): \(25\left(x^2+y^2 ight)=(9-4x)^2=81-72x+16x^2\), so \(9x^2+72x+25y^2=81\). Complete the square: \(9\left(x^2+8x ight)=9(x+4)^2-144\), so \(9(x+4)^2+25y^2=225\), that is \( rac{(x+4)^2}{25}+ rac{y^2}9=1\): an ellipse with center \((-4,0)\), \(a=5\), \(b=3\), \(c=4\), \(e= rac45\). The pole is the focus \((-4+4,0)=(0,0)\). (Squaring adds no points here: if \(25(x^2+y^2)=(9-4x)^2\), the number \(r= rac{9-4x}5\) has \(r^2=x^2+y^2\), so \(\lvert r vert\) is the distance from the pole to \((x,y)\) and the point has polar coordinates \((r, heta)\) for a suitable \( heta\), possibly after adding \(\pi\), with \(5r+4r\cos heta=9\).) Check with the formula: \(r= rac{9/5}{1+ rac45\cos heta}\) has \(e= rac45\) and \(ed= rac95\), so the directrix is \(x= rac94\), which is \(-4+ rac ae=-4+ rac{25}4= rac94\). (b) The center is \((0,0)\), \(a=3\), \(b=4\), \(c=5\), \(e= rac53\). In the pole’s coordinates \(x'=x-5\), the hyperbola is \( rac{(x'+5)^2}9- rac{y^2}{16}=1\). The right directrix is \(x= rac ae= rac95\), which is \(x'= rac95-5=- rac{16}5\): to the left of the pole at distance \(d= rac{16}5\). So the form is \(r= rac{ed}{1-e\cos heta}\) with \(ed= rac53\cdot rac{16}5= rac{16}3\):

\[r= rac{16/3}{1- rac53\cos heta}= rac{16}{3-5\cos heta}.\]

Check. \( heta=\pi\): \(r= rac{16}8=2\), the point \((-2,0)\) in the new coordinates, that is \((3,0)\) in the old: the vertex. \( heta=0\): \(r= rac{16}{-2}=-8\), the point \(-8\) units from the pole opposite to \( heta=0\), namely \(x'=-8\), \(x=-3\), the other vertex.

Pause and think 12.4.3: Two branches from one equation

For \(e>1\) the equation \(r= rac{ed}{1+e\cos heta}\) gives one value of \(r\) for each \( heta\), yet its graph has two branches. Which values of \( heta\) must be omitted, what happens to \(r\) near them, and which branch is traced by the values of \( heta\) for which \(r<0\)?

Answer and discussion

The denominator \(1+e\cos heta\) is \(0\) when \(\cos heta=- rac1e\), which has two solutions \(\pm heta_0\) in \(\left( rac\pi2,\pi ight)\) (since \( rac1e<1\)). Omit them. As \( heta\) approaches either one, \(\lvert r vert o\infty\): the curve goes off to infinity in the direction of an asymptote. For \(- heta_0< heta< heta_0\) the denominator is positive and \(r>0\): this is the branch around the pole (its vertex is at \( heta=0\)). For \( heta_0< heta<2\pi- heta_0\) the denominator is negative, \(r<0\), and each point is plotted in the direction opposite to \( heta\): this is the other branch, on the far side of the directrix (its vertex is the point for \( heta=\pi\), where \(r= rac{ed}{1-e}<0\) puts it at \(x= rac{ed}{e-1}>0\)).

Example 12.4.29: The orbit of a satellite

A satellite orbits the Earth in an ellipse with the center of the Earth at one focus. Its closest distance to the center of the Earth is \(7000\) km and its farthest distance is \(15000\) km. (a) Find the eccentricity and a polar equation of the orbit with the center of the Earth as the pole and the polar axis through the closest point. (b) Use the area formula of Section 12.3 to find the area enclosed by the orbit, and compare it with \(\pi ab\). (c) Find the distance from the center of the Earth at \( heta= rac\pi2\).

Solution. (a) The closest and farthest points are the two vertices, so \(2a=7000+15000=22000\) and \(a=11000\) km. The focus is at distance \(7000\) from the nearer vertex, so \(c=a-7000=4000\) km and \(e= rac ca= rac4{11}\). Also \(b^2=a^2-c^2=121\cdot10^6-16\cdot10^6=105\cdot10^6\). The nearest vertex is at \( heta=0\), so the directrix is \(x=d>0\) and the equation is \(r= rac{ed}{1+e\cos heta}\). We need \(ed\). By Theorem 12.4.24 and Procedure 12.4.25, step 5, \(a= rac{ed}{1-e^2}\), so \(ed=a\left(1-e^2 ight)=11000\cdot rac{105}{121}= rac{105000}{11}\). Therefore

\[r= rac{105000/11}{1+ rac4{11}\cos heta}= rac{105000}{11+4\cos heta}\ ext{km.}\]

Check. \( heta=0\): \(r= rac{105000}{15}=7000\); \( heta=\pi\): \(r= rac{105000}7=15000\). (b) The orbit is a closed curve, \(r=f( heta)>0\) for \(0\le heta\le2\pi\) with \(f(0)=f(2\pi)\), so the region it encloses has area \(A= rac12\int_0^{2\pi}f( heta)^2\,d heta\) (Theorem 12.3.3), the polar area of Section 12.3. Numerically \(A\approx3.5411 imes10^8\) km\(^2\). The area of an ellipse is \(\pi ab\) (Calculus I), with \(b=\sqrt{105\cdot10^6}=1000\sqrt{105}\approx10247\) km: \(\pi\cdot11000\cdot10247\approx3.5411 imes10^8\) km\(^2\). The two agree. (c) At \( heta= rac\pi2\), \(r= rac{105000}{11}\approx9545\) km. This is the semi-latus rectum \(ed\), the distance from the focus to the curve along the line through the focus perpendicular to the axis.

Kepler’s laws of planetary motion are the statements that planets move in ellipses with the sun at a focus, that the line from the sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, and that the square of the period is proportional to the cube of \(a\). The first is the polar equation above; the second is a statement about the integral \( rac12\int r^2\,d heta\) of Section 12.3; for this satellite the part of the orbit between \( heta=0\) and \( heta= rac\pi2\) sweeps about \(13.7\%\) of the area, so it takes about \(13.7\%\) of the period. Proving that orbits are conics from Newton’s law of gravitation is done with vector-valued functions in a later chapter.

items.title: Looking ahead
items.text: Everything in this section describes conics whose axes are parallel to the coordinate axes (a term \(xy\) in the equation would mean a rotated conic, which is treated with a rotation of the axes in a later course). The polar equation \(r=\frac{ed}{1+e\cos\theta}\) is the form in which planetary orbits, comet paths and satellite trajectories are written, and it is the starting point for Kepler’s laws and for the vector-valued functions of a later chapter. In three dimensions, rotating a parabola, an ellipse or a hyperbola about its axis gives a paraboloid, an ellipsoid or a hyperboloid, and the plane sections of a cone that gave the conics their name reappear as the traces of quadric surfaces; both are studied in a later chapter.

items.title: Example bank
items.text:
What’s in this bank. Fourteen further worked examples, grouped by problem type and ordered from easiest to hardest within each group.

  1. Parabolas (Examples 12.4.30–12.4.31): from focus and directrix; from a general equation.

  2. Ellipses (Examples 12.4.32–12.4.33): from foci and the major axis; from a general equation with a vertical major axis.

  3. Hyperbolas (Examples 12.4.34–12.4.35): from vertices and asymptotes; from a general equation.

  4. Eccentricity and the directrix (Examples 12.4.36–12.4.37): the equation from a focus, a directrix and \(e\).

  5. Polar equations (Examples 12.4.38–12.4.39): a parabola to Cartesian form; a polar equation from the data.

  6. Applications (Examples 12.4.40–12.4.41): a satellite dish; the orbit of a comet.

  7. Proofs (Examples 12.4.42–12.4.43).

items.title: Group 1: Parabolas
items.text:
Example 12.4.30: From focus and directrix

Find the equation of the parabola with focus \((1,5)\) and directrix \(y=-1\), and check it.

Solution. The axis is the vertical line through the focus perpendicular to the directrix, \(x=1\), and it meets the directrix at \((1,-1)\). The vertex is the midpoint of the focus and this foot: \(\left(1,\frac{5+(-1)}2\right)=(1,2)\). The distance from the vertex to the focus is \(p=5-2=3>0\), and the focus is above the vertex, so the parabola opens upward: \((x-1)^2=4p(y-2)=12(y-2)\). Check. The point \((7,5)\) is on the curve: \((7-1)^2=36=12\cdot3\). Its distance to the focus is \(\sqrt{6^2+0^2}=6\) and its distance to the directrix is \(5-(-1)=6\). They are equal, so the equation is correct.

Example 12.4.31: From a general equation

Find the vertex, focus, directrix and axis of \(x^2+6x+8y+1=0\).

Solution. Only \(x\) is squared, so it is a parabola with a vertical axis (Theorem 12.4.19(iii)). Complete the square in \(x\): \(x^2+6x=(x+3)^2-9\). Then \((x+3)^2-9+8y+1=0\), so \((x+3)^2=-8y+8=-8(y-1)\). Compare with \((x-h)^2=4p(y-k)\): \(h=-3\), \(k=1\), \(4p=-8\), \(p=-2<0\), so the parabola opens downward. The vertex is \((-3,1)\), the axis is \(x=-3\), the focus is \((h,k+p)=(-3,-1)\) and the directrix is \(y=k-p=3\). Check. The point \((1,-1)\): \(1+6-8+1=0\). Its distance to the focus \((-3,-1)\) is \(4\) and its distance to the directrix \(y=3\) is \(3-(-1)=4\), so it is on the parabola.

items.title: Group 2: Ellipses
items.text:
Example 12.4.32: From the foci and the length of the major axis

Find the equation of the ellipse with foci \((-3,2)\) and \((5,2)\) whose major axis has length \(10\).

Solution. The center is the midpoint of the foci, \((1,2)\), and the major axis is horizontal. The distance from the center to a focus is \(c=5-1=4\), and \(2a=10\) gives \(a=5\). Then \(b^2=a^2-c^2=25-16=9\). The equation is \(\frac{(x-1)^2}{25}+\frac{(y-2)^2}{9}=1\). Check. The point \((1,5)\): \(\frac{0}{25}+\frac99=1\). Its distances to the foci are \(\sqrt{4^2+3^2}=5\) and \(\sqrt{(-4)^2+3^2}=5\), and the sum is \(10=2a\).

Example 12.4.33: An ellipse with a vertical major axis

Find the center, vertices, foci, eccentricity and directrices of \(4x^2+y^2-16x+6y+9=0\).

Solution. \(AC=4>0\): an ellipse or a degenerate set. Group: \(4\left(x^2-4x\right)+\left(y^2+6y\right)=-9\). Complete the squares: \(x^2-4x=(x-2)^2-4\) and \(y^2+6y=(y+3)^2-9\), so \(4(x-2)^2-16+(y+3)^2-9=-9\), that is \(4(x-2)^2+(y+3)^2=16\). Divide by \(16\): \(\frac{(x-2)^2}{4}+\frac{(y+3)^2}{16}=1\). The larger denominator is under \(y\), so the major axis is vertical: \(a=4\), \(b=2\), center \((2,-3)\). Then \(c=\sqrt{16-4}=2\sqrt3\) and \(e=\frac ca=\frac{\sqrt3}2\). The vertices are \((2,-3\pm4)=(2,1),(2,-7)\); the foci are \(\left(2,-3\pm2\sqrt3\right)\); the directrices are \(y=-3\pm\frac ae=-3\pm\frac8{\sqrt3}\). Check. The vertex \((2,1)\): \(16+1-32+6+9=0\).

items.title: Group 3: Hyperbolas
items.text:
Example 12.4.34: From the vertices and the asymptotes

A hyperbola has vertices \((\pm4,0)\) and asymptotes \(y=\pm\frac34x\). Find its equation, foci, eccentricity and directrices.

Solution. The vertices are on the \(x\)-axis, so \(\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1\) with \(a=4\). The asymptotes are \(y=\pm\frac bax\), so \(\frac b4=\frac34\) and \(b=3\). The equation is \(\frac{x^2}{16}-\frac{y^2}9=1\). Then \(c=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}=5\), the foci are \((\pm5,0)\), \(e=\frac54\), and the directrices are \(x=\pm\frac ae=\pm\frac{16}5\). Check. The point \(\left(8,3\sqrt3\right)\): \(\frac{64}{16}-\frac{27}9=4-3=1\). Its distance to the focus \((5,0)\) is \(\sqrt{3^2+27}=6\); its distance to the directrix \(x=\frac{16}5\) is \(8-\frac{16}5=\frac{24}5\); and \(e\cdot\frac{24}5=\frac54\cdot\frac{24}5=6\).

Example 12.4.35: A hyperbola from a general equation

Find the center, vertices, foci and asymptotes of \(4x^2-y^2+8x+4y-4=0\).

Solution. \(AC=-4<0\): a hyperbola or two lines. Group: \(4\left(x^2+2x\right)-\left(y^2-4y\right)=4\); the minus sign in front of the second group stays outside. Complete the squares: \(x^2+2x=(x+1)^2-1\) and \(y^2-4y=(y-2)^2-4\), so \(4(x+1)^2-4-(y-2)^2+4=4\), that is \(4(x+1)^2-(y-2)^2=4\). Divide by \(4\): \((x+1)^2-\frac{(y-2)^2}4=1\). This is a hyperbola with center \((-1,2)\), horizontal axis, \(a=1\), \(b=2\), \(c=\sqrt{1+4}=\sqrt5\). The vertices are \((-1\pm1,2)=(0,2),(-2,2)\), the foci are \(\left(-1\pm\sqrt5,2\right)\), and the asymptotes are \(y-2=\pm\frac ba(x+1)=\pm2(x+1)\). Check. The vertex \((0,2)\): \(0-4+0+8-4=0\).

items.title: Group 4: Eccentricity and the directrix
items.text:
Example 12.4.36: The conic with a given focus, directrix and \(e<1\)

Find the equation of the set of points \(P\) with \(\lvert PF\rvert=\frac12\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell)\), where \(F=(2,0)\) and \(\ell\) is the line \(x=8\).

Solution. Both sides are nonnegative, so square (Theorem K.1): \((x-2)^2+y^2=\frac14(x-8)^2\). Multiply by \(4\): \(4x^2-16x+16+4y^2=x^2-16x+64\), so \(3x^2+4y^2=48\), that is \(\frac{x^2}{16}+\frac{y^2}{12}=1\). Since \(e=\frac12<1\), this is an ellipse (Theorem 12.4.17) with \(a=4\), \(b^2=12\), \(c=\sqrt{16-12}=2\) and \(e=\frac ca=\frac12\), as it should be. The focus \((2,0)=(c,0)\) and the directrix \(x=\frac ae=8\) agree with the data. Check. The point \(\left(0,2\sqrt3\right)\): \(\frac{12}{12}=1\). Its distance to \(F\) is \(\sqrt{4+12}=4\), its distance to \(\ell\) is \(8\), and \(\frac12\cdot8=4\).

Example 12.4.37: The conic with \(e=2\), and its parameters

Find the equation of the set of points \(P\) with \(\lvert PF\rvert=2\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell)\), where \(F=(0,3)\) and \(\ell\) is the line \(y=-1\). Identify the conic and find its center, vertices and foci.

Solution. Square (both sides are nonnegative): \(x^2+(y-3)^2=4(y+1)^2\), so \(x^2+y^2-6y+9=4y^2+8y+4\), that is \(x^2-3y^2-14y+5=0\). Complete the square in \(y\): \(-3y^2-14y=-3\left(y^2+\frac{14}3y\right)=-3\left(y+\frac73\right)^2+\frac{49}3\). So \(x^2-3\left(y+\frac73\right)^2=-5-\frac{49}3=-\frac{64}3\). Multiply by \(-\frac3{64}\): \(\frac{\left(y+7/3\right)^2}{64/9}-\frac{x^2}{64/3}=1\). As \(e=2>1\) this is a hyperbola with vertical axis, center \(\left(0,-\frac73\right)\), \(a^2=\frac{64}9\), \(a=\frac83\), \(b^2=\frac{64}3\), \(c^2=\frac{64}9+\frac{192}9=\frac{256}9\), \(c=\frac{16}3=ae\) (as Theorem 12.4.17 predicts). The vertices are \(\left(0,-\frac73\pm\frac83\right)=\left(0,\frac13\right),(0,-5)\); the foci are \(\left(0,-\frac73\pm\frac{16}3\right)=(0,3),\left(0,-\frac{23}3\right)\), and \((0,3)=F\). Check. The vertex \(\left(0,\frac13\right)\): its distance to \(F\) is \(3-\frac13=\frac83\), its distance to \(\ell\) is \(\frac13+1=\frac43\), and \(2\cdot\frac43=\frac83\).

items.title: Group 5: Polar equations
items.text:
Example 12.4.38: A parabola in polar form

Convert \(r=\dfrac6{2+2\sin\theta}\) to Cartesian form and find the vertex, focus and directrix.

Solution. Divide by \(2\): \(r=\frac3{1+\sin\theta}\), so \(e=1\) and \(ed=3\): a parabola with focus at the pole and directrix \(y=3\) (Theorem 12.4.24). Cartesian form: \(r+r\sin\theta=3\), so \(r=3-y\). Square, with \(r^2=x^2+y^2\): \(x^2+y^2=9-6y+y^2\), so \(x^2=-6\left(y-\frac32\right)\). (If a point satisfies this, then \(r=\pm(3-y)\); the sign \(-\) is the same point with the polar coordinates \((-r,\theta+\pi)\), as in the proof of Theorem 12.4.24.) Compare with \(x^2=4p(y-k)\): \(4p=-6\), \(p=-\frac32\), vertex \(\left(0,\frac32\right)\), focus \(\left(0,\frac32+p\right)=(0,0)\), the pole, and directrix \(y=\frac32-p=3\). Check. At \(\theta=\frac\pi2\), \(r=\frac64=\frac32\): the point \(\left(0,\frac32\right)\), the vertex.

Example 12.4.39: A polar equation from the data

An ellipse has a focus at the pole, the directrix \(y=-4\) and eccentricity \(\frac12\). Find its polar equation, its vertices, its center and its semi-axes.

Solution. The directrix is below the pole, \(y=-d\) with \(d=4\), so \(r=\frac{ed}{1-e\sin\theta}\) (Theorem 12.4.24). With \(ed=\frac12\cdot4=2\): \(r=\frac2{1-\frac12\sin\theta}=\frac4{2-\sin\theta}\). The vertices are at \(\theta=\frac\pi2\): \(r=\frac4{2-1}=4\), the point \((0,4)\); and at \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}2\): \(r=\frac4{2+1}=\frac43\), the point \(\left(0,-\frac43\right)\). The major axis is vertical, \(2a=4+\frac43=\frac{16}3\), so \(a=\frac83\) (also \(a=\frac{ed}{1-e^2}=\frac{2}{3/4}=\frac83\)). The center is the midpoint \(\left(0,\frac{4-4/3}2\right)=\left(0,\frac43\right)\), \(c=ae=\frac43\) is its distance to the pole, and \(b^2=a^2-c^2=\frac{64}9-\frac{16}9=\frac{16}3\). Check. At \(\theta=0\), \(r=\frac42=2\): the point \((2,0)\) has \(\lvert PF\rvert=2\) and distance \(4\) to the directrix, and \(\frac12\cdot4=2\).

items.title: Group 6: Applications
items.text:
Example 12.4.40: A satellite dish

A satellite dish is a paraboloid obtained by rotating a parabola about its axis. It is \(80\) cm across the rim and \(10\) cm deep. How far from the vertex should the receiver be placed?

Solution. Put the vertex at the origin with the axis along the \(y\)-axis, so the dish is the parabola \(x^2=4py\). The rim point is \((40,10)\) (half the width, and the depth). Then \(1600=4p\cdot10\), so \(p=40\). By the reflection property (Theorem 12.4.4) all incoming rays parallel to the axis are reflected through the focus \((0,p)=(0,40)\), so the receiver goes on the axis \(40\) cm from the vertex, which is \(40-10=30\) cm above the plane of the rim.

Example 12.4.41: The orbit of a comet

A comet moves in an ellipse with the sun at a focus. Its closest and farthest distances from the sun are \(2\) and \(8\) (in units of \(10^8\) km). Find a polar equation of the orbit with the sun at the pole and the closest point at \(\theta=0\), the distance at \(\theta=\frac\pi2\), and the area enclosed.

Solution. The distances are those to the vertices, so \(2a=2+8=10\), \(a=5\). The sun is \(2\) from the nearer vertex, so \(c=a-2=3\) and \(e=\frac35\). Then \(b^2=25-9=16\), \(b=4\), and \(ed=a\left(1-e^2\right)=5\cdot\frac{16}{25}=\frac{16}5\). The nearest vertex is at \(\theta=0\), so \(r=\frac{ed}{1+e\cos\theta}=\frac{16/5}{1+\frac35\cos\theta}=\frac{16}{5+3\cos\theta}\). At \(\theta=\frac\pi2\), \(r=\frac{16}5=3.2\). The area is \(\pi ab=20\pi\approx62.8\) (in units of \(10^{16}\) km\(^2\)). Check. \(\theta=0\): \(r=\frac{16}8=2\); \(\theta=\pi\): \(r=\frac{16}2=8\).

items.title: Group 7: Proofs
items.text:
Example 12.4.42: The product of the distances to the asymptotes

Prove that for every point \(P\) on the hyperbola \(\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1\) the product of the distances from \(P\) to the two asymptotes is the constant \(\frac{a^2b^2}{a^2+b^2}\).

Proof. The asymptotes are \(y=\pm\frac bax\), that is \(bx-ay=0\) and \(bx+ay=0\). The distance from \(P=(x_0,y_0)\) to the line \(Ax+By+C=0\) is \(\frac{\lvert Ax_0+By_0+C\rvert}{\sqrt{A^2+B^2}}\), so the two distances are \(\frac{\lvert bx_0-ay_0\rvert}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}\) and \(\frac{\lvert bx_0+ay_0\rvert}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}\). Their product is \(\frac{\lvert b^2x_0^2-a^2y_0^2\rvert}{a^2+b^2}\), because \((bx_0-ay_0)(bx_0+ay_0)=b^2x_0^2-a^2y_0^2\). Now \(P\) is on the hyperbola; multiply \(\frac{x_0^2}{a^2}-\frac{y_0^2}{b^2}=1\) by \(a^2b^2\): \(b^2x_0^2-a^2y_0^2=a^2b^2>0\). Hence the product is \(\frac{a^2b^2}{a^2+b^2}\). Numerical check. For \(a=4\), \(b=3\) and \(P=\left(5,\frac94\right)\) (on the hyperbola: \(\frac{25}{16}-\frac{81/16}{9}=1\)) the distances are \(\frac{\lvert15-9\rvert}5=\frac65\) and \(\frac{\lvert15+9\rvert}5=\frac{24}5\), with product \(\frac{144}{25}=\frac{16\cdot9}{25}\).

Example 12.4.43: The latus rectum of an ellipse

Prove that the chord of the ellipse \(\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1\) through a focus \((c,0)\) perpendicular to the major axis has length \(\frac{2b^2}a\).

Proof. The chord lies on the line \(x=c\). Substitute: \(\frac{c^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1\), so \(y^2=b^2\left(1-\frac{c^2}{a^2}\right)=\frac{b^2\left(a^2-c^2\right)}{a^2}=\frac{b^4}{a^2}\), because \(a^2-c^2=b^2\) (Theorem 12.4.7). Therefore \(y=\pm\frac{b^2}a\); the endpoints are \(\left(c,\frac{b^2}a\right)\) and \(\left(c,-\frac{b^2}a\right)\), and the chord has length \(\frac{2b^2}a\). Numerical check. For \(a=5\), \(b=4\), \(c=3\): \(y^2=16\left(1-\frac9{25}\right)=\frac{256}{25}=\left(\frac{16}5\right)^2\) and \(\frac{2b^2}a=\frac{32}5=2\cdot\frac{16}5\).

items.title: Answers and discussion
items.text:
Knowledge Check 12.4.1. Compare \(x^2=-24y\) with \(x^2=4py\): \(4p=-24\), \(p=-6\). The focus is \((0,p)=(0,-6)\), the directrix is \(y=-p=6\), and since \(p<0\) the parabola opens downward.

Knowledge Check 12.4.2. \(c=ae=10\cdot\frac35=6\), \(b=\sqrt{a^2-c^2}=\sqrt{100-36}=8\), and the directrices are \(x=\pm\frac ae=\pm\frac{10}{3/5}=\pm\frac{50}3\).

Knowledge Check 12.4.3. Divide by \(2\): \(r=\frac{5/2}{1-\frac12\cos\theta}\). So \(e=\frac12<1\): an ellipse. \(ed=\frac52\), so \(d=5\), and the sign is \(-\cos\theta\): the directrix is \(x=-5\). The vertices: \(\theta=0\), \(r=\frac{5}{2-1}=5\), the point \((5,0)\); \(\theta=\pi\), \(r=\frac5{2+1}=\frac53\) at the angle \(\pi\), the point \(\left(-\frac53,0\right)\). Check: \(2a=5+\frac53=\frac{20}3\), and \(a=\frac{ed}{1-e^2}=\frac{5/2}{3/4}=\frac{10}3\).

items.title: 6.1 Velocity and Net Change
items.text:
Download the PDF version

Guiding question

If you know how fast something is changing, can you find out how much it has changed? Differentiation goes from a quantity to its rate; integration goes back. This section uses the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus from Calculus I to turn rates into totals. We start with the case you can feel: an object moving along a line, whose velocity is the rate of change of its position. We separate two questions that sound alike but are not: how far did it end up from where it started (displacement) and how far did it actually travel (distance traveled). We then find the position from the velocity, and the velocity from the acceleration. The same idea works for any quantity with a known rate: the water in a reservoir, a population, the cost of making more books. Each time, accumulating the rate gives the net change, and the net change plus the starting value gives the future value. The idea behind this is slice-and-sum, which is also how the rest of this chapter finds areas, volumes and lengths.

By the end of this section you should be able to:

  • distinguish position, displacement and distance traveled, and compute displacement and distance traveled from a velocity function or from a velocity graph;

  • find the position function from the velocity and the initial position, and the velocity from the acceleration and the initial velocity, by an antiderivative or by an integral from \(0\) to \(t\);

  • compute the net change and the future value of any quantity from its rate of change, with correct units;

  • handle rates that change sign, rates given in pieces, and rates whose total stays bounded for all time;

  • prove each of the theorems of this section.

items.title: Position, displacement and distance traveled
items.text:
An object moves along a line, say a straight road, with a fixed direction called positive. Its position at time \(t\) is a number \(s(t)\): the signed distance from a chosen origin. Its velocity is \(v(t)=s'(t)\) (a number that is positive when it moves in the positive direction and negative when it moves the other way), and its speed is \(\abs{v(t)}\). Throughout this section we assume that \(s\) is differentiable and that \(v=s'\) is continuous.

Definition 6.1.1: Displacement and distance traveled

Let \(a<b\). The displacement of the object over the time interval \([a,b]\) is the signed number \(s(b)-s(a)\): the change in position, positive if it ends up on the positive side of where it started and negative otherwise.

To define the distance traveled, cut \([a,b]\) into \(n\) pieces by times \(a=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_n=b\). During the \(k\)th piece the object moves from \(s(t_{k-1})\) to \(s(t_k)\), so it covers at least the distance \(\abs{s(t_k)-s(t_{k-1})}\), with the direction ignored. The distance traveled is the limit of the sums

\[\sum_{k=1}^n\abs{s(t_k)-s(t_{k-1})}\]

as the longest piece shrinks to \(0\) (Theorem 6.1.3 shows that the limit exists).

The distance traveled is what the odometer of a car reads: it only increases. The displacement is what you get from the position at the end minus the position at the beginning: it can be positive, negative or zero. If you walk \(3\) blocks east and then \(3\) blocks west, your displacement is \(0\) but you have traveled \(6\) blocks.

Theorem 6.1.2: Displacement is the integral of the velocity

If \(s\) is differentiable with a continuous derivative \(v=s'\) on \([a,b]\), then the displacement is

\[s(b)-s(a)=\int_a^bv(t)\,dt .\]

Proof. By definition \(v=s'\), so \(s\) is an antiderivative of the continuous function \(v\) on \([a,b]\). The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Part 2, from Calculus I) says that \(\int_a^bv(t)\,dt=s(b)-s(a)\) for every antiderivative \(s\) of \(v\). ◻ ∎

Geometrically, the displacement is the net area between the graph of \(v\) and the \(t\)-axis: the area above the axis counts \(+\) and the area below counts \(-\). The distance traveled counts all the area as positive.

Theorem 6.1.3: Distance traveled is the integral of the speed

Under the same assumptions, the sums in Definition 6.1.1 converge as the longest piece shrinks to \(0\), and the distance traveled is

\[\int_a^b\abs{v(t)}\,dt .\]

Proof. On the \(k\)th piece \([t_{k-1},t_k]\) the function \(s\) is continuous and differentiable, so the Mean Value Theorem (Calculus I) gives a number \(t_k^*\) in \((t_{k-1},t_k)\) with

\[s(t_k)-s(t_{k-1})=s'(t_k^*)\,(t_k-t_{k-1})=v(t_k^*)\,\Delta t_k,\qquad \Delta t_k=t_k-t_{k-1}.\]

Take absolute values: \(\abs{s(t_k)-s(t_{k-1})}=\abs{v(t_k^*)}\,\Delta t_k\), because \(\Delta t_k>0\). Therefore

\[\sum_{k=1}^n\abs{s(t_k)-s(t_{k-1})}=\sum_{k=1}^n\abs{v(t_k^*)}\,\Delta t_k ,\]

which is a Riemann sum for the function \(\abs{v}\) on \([a,b]\) (with the sample points \(t_k^*\)). The function \(\abs{v}\) is continuous, because \(v\) is, so it is integrable, and its Riemann sums converge to \(\int_a^b\abs{v(t)}\,dt\) as the longest piece shrinks to \(0\), whatever the sample points are. ◻ ∎

How do we compute \(\int_a^b\abs{v}\) when \(v\) changes sign? A continuous function can change sign only where it is zero (the Intermediate Value Theorem), so between two consecutive zeros of \(v\) it is either always positive or always negative. There \(\abs{v}=v\) or \(\abs{v}=-v\), and the integral of \(\abs v\) over the piece equals \(\abs{\text{displacement over that piece}}\).

Procedure 6.1.4: Displacement and distance traveled from a velocity function

Let \(v\) be continuous on \([a,b]\).

  1. Solve \(v(t)=0\) on \([a,b]\). The zeros \(a=c_0<c_1<\dots<c_m=b\) (with \(a\) and \(b\) added) cut the interval into pieces on which \(v\) has one sign. Test one point in each piece to find the sign.

  2. Find an antiderivative \(F\) of \(v\) and check it by differentiating.

  3. The displacement is \(F(b)-F(a)\).

  4. The distance traveled is \(\sum_{j=1}^m\abs{F(c_j)-F(c_{j-1})}\): the absolute value of the displacement over each piece, added.

  5. Check: the distance is at least the absolute value of the displacement (Theorem 6.1.6 below), and the units are units of length.

Example 6.1.5: Displacement and distance for a quadratic velocity

A particle moves along a line with velocity \(v(t)=3t^2-12t+9\) (in m/s) for \(0\le t\le5\) (in s). Find its displacement and the distance it travels, and describe the motion.

Solution. Step 1: the sign of \(v\). Factor, taking out the \(3\) first: \(3t^2-12t+9=3(t^2-4t+3)=3(t-1)(t-3)\). The zeros are \(t=1\) and \(t=3\), both in \([0,5]\), so the pieces are \([0,1]\), \([1,3]\) and \([3,5]\). At \(t=0\): \(v(0)=9>0\). At \(t=2\): \(v(2)=3\cdot4-24+9=-3<0\). At \(t=4\): \(v(4)=48-48+9=9>0\). (Each piece has one sign, since \(v\) can change sign only at a zero.) Step 2: an antiderivative. By the power rule, \(F(t)=t^3-6t^2+9t\) has \(F'(t)=3t^2-12t+9=v(t)\). Step 3: values of \(F\) at the endpoints and zeros. \(F(0)=0\), \(F(1)=1-6+9=4\), \(F(3)=27-54+27=0\), \(F(5)=125-150+45=20\). Step 4: displacement. \(\int_0^5v\,dt=F(5)-F(0)=20-0=20\) m. Step 5: distance traveled. On each piece the distance is the absolute value of the displacement: \(\abs{F(1)-F(0)}=4\), \(\abs{F(3)-F(1)}=\abs{-4}=4\), \(\abs{F(5)-F(3)}=20\). The distance is \(4+4+20=28\) m. Conclusion and check. The particle moves \(4\) m in the positive direction, then \(4\) m back to where it started, then \(20\) m in the positive direction: displacement \(20\) m, distance \(28\) m. As required, \(28\ge\abs{20}\). The figure below shows the net area: the three regions have areas \(4\), \(4\) and \(20\); the middle one counts as \(-4\) in the displacement and \(+4\) in the distance.

Figure. The graph of \(v(t)=3t^2-12t+9\). Displacement \(=4-4+20=20\); distance traveled \(=4+4+20=28\).

Knowledge Check 6.1.1: Out and back

A runner jogs \(3\) km east along a straight road, turns around, and jogs \(5\) km west. Taking east as the positive direction, what are her displacement and the distance she has traveled?

Theorem 6.1.6: The displacement never exceeds the distance

If \(v\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), then

\[\abs{\int_a^bv(t)\,dt}\le\int_a^b\abs{v(t)}\,dt ,\]

with equality if and only if \(v\ge0\) on all of \([a,b]\) or \(v\le0\) on all of \([a,b]\).

Proof. For every \(t\) we have \(-\abs{v(t)}\le v(t)\le\abs{v(t)}\). Integrating (the integral preserves inequalities) gives \(-\int_a^b\abs v\le\int_a^bv\le\int_a^b\abs v\), which is the inequality.

If \(v\ge0\) on \([a,b]\), then \(\abs v=v\) and both sides are equal. If \(v\le0\), then \(\abs v=-v\) and \(\abs{\int v}=\abs{-\int\abs v}=\int\abs v\).

Conversely, suppose equality holds. Then \(\int_a^bv=\int_a^b\abs v\) or \(\int_a^bv=-\int_a^b\abs v\). In the first case let \(g=\abs v-v\). It is continuous, \(g\ge0\), and \(\int_a^bg=0\). If \(g(c)>0\) for some \(c\), then by continuity \(g>g(c)/2\) on a subinterval of length \(\delta>0\), so \(\int_a^bg\ge\delta\,g(c)/2>0\), a contradiction. So \(g\equiv0\), that is \(\abs v=v\) and \(v\ge0\). In the second case apply the first case to \(-v\) (which has \(\abs{-v}=\abs v\)): it gives \(-v\ge0\), that is \(v\le0\). ◻ ∎

Pause and think 6.1.1: Zero displacement

Describe a motion on \([0,4]\) whose displacement is \(0\) but whose distance traveled is \(12\). What does the graph of \(v\) look like? Can the distance be \(0\) if the displacement is \(0\)?

Answer and discussion

For instance the object moves forward at the velocity \(v=3\) for \(2\) s (distance \(6\)) and backward at \(v=-3\) for \(2\) s (distance \(6\)): displacement \(6-6=0\), distance \(6+6=12\). The graph of \(v\) has equal areas above and below the \(t\)-axis. The distance can be \(0\) with displacement \(0\) only if \(\int_0^4\abs v=0\), and by the equality part of Theorem 6.1.6’s proof (\(\abs v\ge0\) continuous with integral \(0\)), \(v\equiv0\): the object never moves.

items.title: Position from velocity
items.text:
The displacement needs only the velocity. To say where the object is at time \(t\), we also need to know where it started.

Theorem 6.1.7: Position from velocity

Let \(v=s'\) be continuous on \([0,\infty)\) (or on an interval starting at \(0\)). Then for every \(t\ge0\),

\[s(t)=s(0)+\int_0^tv(x)\,dx .\]

Proof. Apply Theorem 6.1.2 on the interval \([0,t]\): \(\int_0^tv(x)\,dx=s(t)-s(0)\). Add \(s(0)\) to both sides. ◻ ∎

In words: position at time \(t\) = initial position + displacement over \([0,t]\). The same holds with any starting time \(t_0\) in place of \(0\).

A dummy variable

In \(s(t)=s(0)+\int_0^tv(x)\,dx\) the letter \(t\) is the upper limit, so it cannot also be the variable of integration. Use another letter, here \(x\). The integral \(\int_0^tv(t)\,dt\) is ambiguous and should not be written.

There are two ways to find \(s(t)\): (1) the antiderivative method: \(s(t)=\int v(t)\,dt=V(t)+C\), then use \(s(0)\) to find \(C\); (2) the integral method: Theorem 6.1.7. They always agree. The integral method builds the initial condition into the formula.

Example 6.1.8: Position of an oscillator by two methods

A mass on a spring moves along a line with velocity \(v(t)=3\cos2t\) (in cm/s, \(t\) in s). At \(t=0\) it is at \(s(0)=2\) cm. (a) Find \(s(t)\) by both methods. (b) Find the greatest and least positions and when they are first reached. (c) When does it first return to its starting position, and in which direction is it then moving?

Solution. (a) Method 1 (antiderivative). With \(u=2t\), \(\int3\cos2t\,dt=\frac32\sin2t+C\) (Theorem 8.1.1). Check: \(\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac32\sin2t\right)=\frac32\cdot2\cos2t=3\cos2t\). The initial condition: \(s(0)=\frac32\sin0+C=C=2\). So \(s(t)=\frac32\sin2t+2\).

Method 2 (integral). By Theorem 6.1.7, \(s(t)=2+\int_0^t3\cos2x\,dx=2+\left[\frac32\sin2x\right]_0^t=2+\frac32\sin2t-\frac32\sin0=2+\frac32\sin2t\).

The two answers agree: \(s(t)=2+\frac32\sin2t\).

(b) Because \(-1\le\sin2t\le1\), we get \(2-\frac32\le s\le2+\frac32\), so \(\frac12\le s\le\frac72\). The greatest position \(\frac72\) occurs when \(\sin2t=1\), first at \(2t=\frac\pi2\), that is \(t=\frac\pi4\). The least position \(\frac12\) occurs when \(\sin2t=-1\), first at \(2t=\frac{3\pi}2\), that is \(t=\frac{3\pi}4\). (Check with \(v\): \(v(\pi/4)=3\cos\frac\pi2=0\), and \(v\) changes from \(+\) to \(-\) there.) In particular the mass never reaches \(s=0\).

(c) It is back at \(s=2\) when \(\frac32\sin2t=0\), first when \(2t=\pi\), that is \(t=\frac\pi2\). There \(v(\pi/2)=3\cos\pi=-3<0\): the mass is moving in the negative direction (downward in the picture of a vertical spring if positive is up).

Knowledge Check 6.1.2: Displacement or position?

For the motion in Example 6.1.8, is \(s(t)\) a number or a function? For fixed times \(t=a\) and \(t=b\), is the displacement \(s(b)-s(a)\) a number or a function? What is the displacement over \([0,\pi/2]\)?

Pause and think 6.1.2: Why do we need \(s(0)\)?

Two objects have the same velocity function \(v(t)=3\cos2t\) for all \(t\), but one starts at \(s(0)=2\) and the other at \(s(0)=-5\). Which of the following are the same for both: the displacement over \([0,\pi/2]\), the distance traveled over \([0,\pi/2]\), the position at \(t=\pi/2\), the time of the first maximum?

Answer and discussion

The velocity function is the same, so the displacement and the distance over \([0,\pi/2]\) are the same for both (they depend only on \(v\)): both \(0\) for the displacement, and \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\abs{3\cos2t}\,dt=2\cdot\frac32=3\) for the distance, because \(3\cos2t\) changes sign at \(t=\frac\pi4\) and \(\frac32\sin2t\) goes from \(0\) to \(\frac32\) and back to \(0\). The time of the first maximum of \(s\) is the same too (\(t=\frac\pi4\), where \(v\) changes sign), since \(s\) differs only by a constant. The positions at \(t=\pi/2\) are different: \(2\) for one and \(-5\) for the other. The initial position shifts the whole position curve up or down; it does not change the displacement.

Example 6.1.9: A piecewise velocity: a delivery drone

A drone flies in a straight line. Its velocity (in m/s) is

\[v(t)=\begin{cases}4t&0\le t<5,\\20&5\le t<15,\\80-4t&15\le t\le20.\end{cases}\]

Find (a) the distance it flies, (b) its position at \(t=12\) s, and (c) its average velocity over \([0,20]\). Assume \(s(0)=0\).

Solution. Here \(v\ge0\) everywhere (at \(t=20\), \(v=80-80=0\), and the pieces join: \(4\cdot5=20\) and \(80-4\cdot15=20\)), so the distance equals the displacement, and by Theorem 6.1.2 we integrate each piece separately, over the interval where its formula holds. (a)

\[\int_0^{5}4t\,dt=\left[2t^2\right]_0^5=50,\qquad\int_5^{15}20\,dt=\left[20t\right]_5^{15}=300-100=200,\]

and, with \(\int(80-4t)\,dt=80t-2t^2\),

\[\int_{15}^{20}(80-4t)\,dt=\left[80t-2t^2\right]_{15}^{20}=(1600-800)-(1200-450)=800-750=50.\]

The distance is \(50+200+50=300\) m. Check with geometry: the region under the graph is a trapezoid with parallel sides \(20\) and \(10\) (on the \(t\)-axis) and height \(20\), so its area is \(\frac{20+10}2\cdot20=300\).

(b) Position at \(t=12\): \(s(12)=s(0)+\int_0^{12}v\,dx=0+\int_0^54x\,dx+\int_5^{12}20\,dx=50+20(12-5)=50+140=190\) m.

(c) The average velocity over \([0,20]\) is the displacement divided by the elapsed time: \(\frac{300}{20}=15\) m/s. This is the constant velocity that would cover the same \(300\) m in \(20\) s.

Figure. The velocity of the drone. The area under the graph is the distance, \(50+200+50=300\) m.

items.title: Acceleration
items.text:
Acceleration is to velocity what velocity is to position: \(a(t)=v'(t)\). Everything above applies once \(s\) is replaced by \(v\) and \(v\) by \(a\).

Theorem 6.1.10: Velocity from acceleration

Let \(a=v'\) be continuous on \([0,\infty)\). The change in velocity over \([c,d]\) is \(v(d)-v(c)=\int_c^da(x)\,dx\), and for every \(t\ge0\)

\[v(t)=v(0)+\int_0^ta(x)\,dx .\]

Proof. The function \(v\) is an antiderivative of the continuous function \(a\), so the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus gives \(\int_c^da(x)\,dx=v(d)-v(c)\). Taking \(c=0\) and \(d=t\) and adding \(v(0)\) gives the second formula. ◻ ∎

To find the position from the acceleration, apply this theorem and then Theorem 6.1.7: first \(v\) from \(a\) and \(v(0)\), then \(s\) from \(v\) and \(s(0)\). A very common case is a constant acceleration, such as gravity near the surface of the Earth, \(a=-g\) with \(g\approx9.8\) m/s\(^2\) (taking up as positive).

Theorem 6.1.11: Constant acceleration

If \(a(t)=\alpha\) is constant, then

\[v(t)=v_0+\alpha t,\qquad s(t)=s_0+v_0t+\tfrac12\alpha t^2,\qquad v(t)^2=v_0^2+2\alpha\,(s(t)-s_0),\]

where \(v_0=v(0)\) and \(s_0=s(0)\).

Proof. By Theorem 6.1.10, \(v(t)=v_0+\int_0^t\alpha\,dx=v_0+\alpha t\). By Theorem 6.1.7, \(s(t)=s_0+\int_0^t(v_0+\alpha x)\,dx=s_0+\left[v_0x+\frac12\alpha x^2\right]_0^t=s_0+v_0t+\frac12\alpha t^2\). For the third formula, compute \(v^2-v_0^2=(v_0+\alpha t)^2-v_0^2=2v_0\alpha t+\alpha^2t^2=2\alpha\left(v_0t+\tfrac12\alpha t^2\right)=2\alpha(s-s_0)\). ◻ ∎

Example 6.1.12: A stone thrown from a bridge

A stone is thrown straight up with velocity \(19.6\) m/s from a bridge \(24.5\) m above a river. Measure \(s\) upward from the river, so \(s(0)=24.5\), and take \(a=-9.8\) m/s\(^2\). Find (a) \(v(t)\) and \(s(t)\); (b) the greatest height and when it is reached; (c) when and how fast the stone hits the river; (d) the displacement and the distance traveled from launch to impact.

Solution. (a) By Theorem 6.1.11 with \(\alpha=-9.8\), \(v_0=19.6\), \(s_0=24.5\): \(v(t)=19.6-9.8t\) and \(s(t)=24.5+19.6t-4.9t^2\).

(b) The stone is highest when it stops rising, \(v(t)=0\): \(19.6-9.8t=0\), so \(t=2\) s (and \(v\) changes from positive to negative there). The height is \(s(2)=24.5+39.2-19.6=44.1\) m.

(c) The stone hits the river when \(s(t)=0\), with \(t>0\): \(24.5+19.6t-4.9t^2=0\). Divide by \(-4.9\): \(t^2-4t-5=0\), that is \((t-5)(t+1)=0\). Only \(t=5\) s makes sense. The velocity is \(v(5)=19.6-49=-29.4\) m/s, so the stone is moving downward at \(29.4\) m/s. Check with the third formula of Theorem 6.1.11: \(v^2=19.6^2+2(-9.8)(0-24.5)=384.16+480.2=864.36\), and \(29.4^2=864.36\).

(d) The displacement is \(s(5)-s(0)=0-24.5=-24.5\) m. For the distance, \(v\) changes sign at \(t=2\), so we add the two legs: up, \(s(2)-s(0)=44.1-24.5=19.6\) m; down, \(\abs{s(5)-s(2)}=\abs{0-44.1}=44.1\) m. The distance traveled is \(19.6+44.1=63.7\) m. (As expected, \(63.7\ge24.5\).)

Figure. Height of the stone above the river: \(s(t)=24.5+19.6t-4.9t^2\).

Example 6.1.13: A variable acceleration

An object has acceleration \(a(t)=\dfrac{12}{(t+2)^2}\) (in m/s\(^2\)) for \(t\ge0\), with \(v(0)=3\) m/s and \(s(0)=0\). Find \(v(t)\) and \(s(t)\), the position at \(t=4\), and the limit of the velocity as \(t\to\infty\).

Solution. Velocity. By Theorem 6.1.10, \(v(t)=3+\int_0^t\frac{12}{(x+2)^2}\,dx\). An antiderivative of \(12(x+2)^{-2}\) is \(-12(x+2)^{-1}\) (substitute \(u=x+2\), Theorem 8.1.1); check: \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(-12(x+2)^{-1}\right)=12(x+2)^{-2}\). So

\[v(t)=3+\left[-\frac{12}{x+2}\right]_0^t=3-\frac{12}{t+2}+\frac{12}2=9-\frac{12}{t+2}.\]

Position. By Theorem 6.1.7, \(s(t)=0+\int_0^t\left(9-\frac{12}{x+2}\right)dx=\left[9x-12\ln(x+2)\right]_0^t=9t-12\ln(t+2)+12\ln2\), that is \(s(t)=9t-12\ln\frac{t+2}2\). (We used \(x+2>0\), so no absolute value is needed in the logarithm.) At \(t=4\): \(s(4)=36-12\ln3\approx22.82\) m. Long-term velocity. \(\lim_{t\to\infty}\left(9-\frac{12}{t+2}\right)=9\) m/s. The object speeds up and levels off at \(9\) m/s even though the acceleration is always positive (it tends to \(0\) quickly).

Knowledge Check 6.1.3: Constant acceleration

A car brakes from \(30\) m/s at the constant acceleration \(-6\) m/s\(^2\). How long does it take to stop, and how far does it travel in that time?

items.title: Net change and future value
items.text:
Nothing in the arguments above used the fact that \(s\) was a position. Any quantity \(Q(t)\) that changes with time has a rate of change \(Q'(t)\), and the same theorems hold.

Theorem 6.1.14: Net change and future value

Let \(Q\) be differentiable with a continuous rate of change \(Q'\) on \([a,b]\). The net change in \(Q\) between \(t=a\) and \(t=b\) is

\[Q(b)-Q(a)=\int_a^bQ'(t)\,dt ,\]

and, given the initial value \(Q(0)\), the future value at time \(t\ge0\) is

\[Q(t)=Q(0)+\int_0^tQ'(x)\,dx .\]

Proof. \(Q\) is an antiderivative of the continuous function \(Q'\), so the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus gives the first formula. For \([0,t]\) it says \(\int_0^tQ'(x)\,dx=Q(t)-Q(0)\); add \(Q(0)\). ◻ ∎

Motion on a line Any quantity position \(s(t)\) amount \(Q(t)\) (volume, population, cost) velocity \(s'(t)=v(t)\) rate of change \(Q'(t)\) displacement \(s(b)-s(a)=\int_a^bv\,dt\) net change \(Q(b)-Q(a)=\int_a^bQ'\,dt\) future position \(s(0)+\int_0^tv\,dx\) future value \(Q(0)+\int_0^tQ'\,dx\)

Units

The integrand \(Q'(x)\,dx\) is (units of \(Q\) per unit of time)\(\,\times\,\)(units of time), which is in the units of \(Q\). For instance, a rate in liters per minute integrated over minutes gives liters. Always check that the units of the limits, the rate and the answer are consistent, and write the units in the answer.

Example 6.1.15: A cell culture and its limiting population

A culture has \(250\) cells when nutrient is added at \(t=0\). The population grows at the rate \(P'(t)=60e^{-0.2t}\) cells per hour. (a) Find \(P(t)\). (b) How many cells are added between \(t=2\) and \(t=5\)? (c) What happens to \(P\) as \(t\to\infty\)?

Solution. (a) An antiderivative of \(60e^{-0.2x}\) is \(-300e^{-0.2x}\), because \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(-300e^{-0.2x}\right)=-300(-0.2)e^{-0.2x}=60e^{-0.2x}\). By Theorem 6.1.14,

\[P(t)=250+\int_0^t60e^{-0.2x}\,dx=250+\left[-300e^{-0.2x}\right]_0^t=250-300e^{-0.2t}+300=550-300e^{-0.2t}.\]

Check: \(P(0)=550-300=250\).

(b) The number added between \(t=2\) and \(t=5\) is the net change \(P(5)-P(2)=\left(550-300e^{-1}\right)-\left(550-300e^{-0.4}\right)=300\left(e^{-0.4}-e^{-1}\right)\approx90.7\) cells. (c) As \(t\to\infty\), \(e^{-0.2t}\to0\), so \(P(t)\to550\): the population levels off at \(550\) cells, although the growth rate is positive for every \(t\). Equivalently, the improper integral \(\int_0^\infty60e^{-0.2x}\,dx=\lim_{t\to\infty}\int_0^t60e^{-0.2x}\,dx\) (Definition 8.9.1) converges to \(300\), and \(250+300=550\).

Figure. \(P(t)=550-300e^{-0.2t}\): increasing, but approaching \(550\).

Example 6.1.16: Marginal cost

A publisher estimates the marginal cost of printing a title as \(C'(x)=45-0.003x\) dollars per book, where \(x\) is the number of books printed so far (\(0\le x\le10000\)). Find the cost of printing the \(2001\)st through the \(5000\)th book, and compare it with the cost of the \(5001\)st through the \(8000\)th.

Solution. The cost of the books numbered \(2001\) through \(5000\) is \(C(5000)-C(2000)=\int_{2000}^{5000}C'(x)\,dx\) by Theorem 6.1.14 (we treat \(x\) as continuous). An antiderivative of \(45-0.003x\) is \(45x-0.0015x^2\). So

\[\begin{aligned} \int_{2000}^{5000}(45-0.003x)\,dx&=\Big[45x-0.0015x^2\Big]_{2000}^{5000}=(225000-37500)-(90000-6000)\\ &=187500-84000=103500 \end{aligned}\]

dollars. Similarly, for the books numbered \(5001\) through \(8000\),

\[\Big[45x-0.0015x^2\Big]_{5000}^{8000}=(360000-96000)-(225000-37500)=264000-187500=76500\]

dollars. The cost of the second block of \(3000\) books is smaller, because the marginal cost is decreasing: each additional book costs less than the one before.

Pause and think 6.1.3: A positive rate and a bounded total

In Example 6.1.15 the growth rate \(P'(t)=60e^{-0.2t}\) is positive for every \(t\), yet \(P(t)\) never exceeds \(550\). How can adding a positive amount at every moment not make \(P\) grow without bound? What would you need to know about \(P'\) to be sure that \(P\) stays bounded?

Answer and discussion

The amounts added get smaller and smaller, quickly enough that their sum stays finite: \(\int_0^\infty60e^{-0.2x}\,dx=300\) (Definition 8.9.1). A positive rate does not by itself make the total unbounded; what matters is how fast the rate dies out. For comparison, the rate \(\frac1{x+1}\) is also positive and tends to \(0\), but \(\int_0^t\frac{dx}{x+1}=\ln(t+1)\to\infty\). To be sure \(P\) is bounded, one needs the improper integral \(\int_0^\infty P'\) to converge, for instance by comparison with a convergent integral such as that of an exponential.

items.title: Rates that change sign, and averages
items.text:
A rate of change can be positive for a while and then negative; the quantity then rises and falls. The net change adds the signed areas, exactly as the displacement does. The average rate of change of \(Q\) over \([a,b]\) is \(\dfrac{Q(b)-Q(a)}{b-a}=\dfrac1{b-a}\int_a^bQ'(t)\,dt\), which is the average value of \(Q'\) on \([a,b]\) (Calculus I). It is the constant rate that would produce the same net change in the same time: for a velocity, the average velocity, the constant velocity with the same displacement.

Example 6.1.17: A fish pond whose rate changes sign

The number of fish in a pond changes at the rate \(N'(t)=40-10t\) fish per week (hatching minus harvesting and losses), \(t\) in weeks, and \(N(0)=100\). Find \(N(t)\); when is the population greatest, and what is it then; when does the pond run out of fish? What is the net change over \([0,4]\) and over \([4,10]\)?

Solution. Future value. By Theorem 6.1.14, \(N(t)=100+\int_0^t(40-10x)\,dx=100+\left[40x-5x^2\right]_0^t=100+40t-5t^2\). The maximum. The rate \(40-10t\) is positive for \(t<4\), zero at \(t=4\) and negative for \(t>4\), so \(N\) increases until \(t=4\) and decreases afterwards: the greatest population is \(N(4)=100+160-80=180\) fish at \(t=4\) weeks. When the pond is empty. \(N(t)=0\) means \(5t^2-40t-100=0\). Divide by \(5\): \(t^2-8t-20=0\), that is \((t-10)(t+2)=0\). The positive solution is \(t=10\) weeks. (The model is meaningful only for \(0\le t\le10\), because a population cannot be negative.) Net changes. \(N(4)-N(0)=180-100=80\) fish gained over \([0,4]\). \(N(10)-N(4)=0-180=-180\), a loss of \(180\) over \([4,10]\). Check with the integral: \(\int_4^{10}(40-10t)\,dt=\left[40t-5t^2\right]_4^{10}=(400-500)-(160-80)=-100-80=-180\). The total amount of change in the pond, ignoring direction, is \(80+180=260\) fish (the analogue of the distance traveled: \(\int_0^{10}\abs{N'(t)}\,dt=260\)).

Example 6.1.18: Two cyclists approaching each other

Towns A and B are \(15\) km apart on a straight road. At noon Ana leaves A for B with speed \(v_A(t)=\dfrac{18}{(t+1)^2}\) km/h and Ben leaves B for A with speed \(v_B(t)=\dfrac{12}{(t+1)^2}\) km/h (\(t\) in hours; both slow down as they tire). (a) Find their positions as functions of time. (b) When and where do they meet? (c) Show that they meet only if the towns are less than \(30\) km apart.

Solution. (a) Measure position \(x\) from A toward B. Ana starts at \(x=0\) and moves in the positive direction, so by Theorem 6.1.7

\[x_A(t)=0+\int_0^t\frac{18}{(u+1)^2}\,du=\left[-\frac{18}{u+1}\right]_0^t=18-\frac{18}{t+1}=\frac{18t}{t+1}.\]

Ben starts at \(x=15\) and moves in the negative direction, so his velocity is \(-v_B(t)\) and

\[x_B(t)=15+\int_0^t\left(-\frac{12}{(u+1)^2}\right)du=15-\left(12-\frac{12}{t+1}\right)=3+\frac{12}{t+1}=\frac{3(t+5)}{t+1}.\]

(b) They meet when \(x_A(t)=x_B(t)\): \(\frac{18t}{t+1}=15-\frac{12t}{t+1}\), so \(\frac{30t}{t+1}=15\), so \(30t=15t+15\) and \(t=1\) hour (1:00 p.m.). Then \(x_A(1)=\frac{18}2=9\) km from A, and \(x_B(1)=\frac{3\cdot6}2=9\) km. Ana has ridden \(9\) km and Ben \(6\) km.

(c) Let the towns be \(D\) km apart. Then \(x_A(t)=18p(t)\) and \(x_B(t)=D-12p(t)\) with \(p(t)=\frac t{t+1}\). They meet when \(30p(t)=D\), that is \(p(t)=\frac D{30}\). Now \(p(t)=1-\frac1{t+1}\) increases from \(0\) and stays below \(1\), and takes every value in \([0,1)\). So \(p(t)=\frac D{30}\) has a solution if and only if \(D<30\). (Ana can never ride more than \(18\) km and Ben never more than \(12\) km.)

Figure. Positions of Ana (rising to \(18\)) and Ben (falling to \(3\)): they meet at \((1,9)\).

Example 6.1.19: A depleting resource and an improper integral

A mine extracts ore at the rate \(r(t)=12e^{-kt}\) thousand tonnes per year, \(t\) years from now, where \(k>0\) is a constant (the rate of extraction decays).
