\[\int\frac{\cos^3\theta}{\sin^2\theta}\,d\theta=\int\frac{1-w^2}{w^2}\,dw=\int\big(w^{-2}-1\big)\,dw=-\frac1w-w=-\csc\theta-\sin\theta+C .\]

By Theorem 8.4.2(2) with \(a=2\): \(\sin\theta=\frac x{\sqrt{x^2+4}}\) and \(\csc\theta=\frac{\sqrt{x^2+4}}x\). Therefore

\[\begin{aligned} \int\frac{dx}{x^2(x^2+4)^{3/2}}&=-\frac1{16}\left(\frac{\sqrt{x^2+4}}x+\frac x{\sqrt{x^2+4}}\right)+C\\ &=-\frac1{16}\cdot\frac{(x^2+4)+x^2}{x\sqrt{x^2+4}}+C=-\frac{x^2+2}{8x\sqrt{x^2+4}}+C, \end{aligned}\]

because \(\frac1{16}\cdot(2x^2+4)=\frac{x^2+2}8\). Check by differentiating: with \(F=-\frac{x^2+2}{8x\sqrt{x^2+4}}\), write \(F=-\frac18\big(x^2+2\big)\big(x^2+4\big)^{-1/2}x^{-1}\) and use the product rule. The three terms are \(-\frac18\cdot2x\,(x^2+4)^{-1/2}x^{-1}\), \(+\frac18\big(x^2+2\big)x\,(x^2+4)^{-3/2}x^{-1}\) and \(+\frac18\big(x^2+2\big)(x^2+4)^{-1/2}x^{-2}\). Over the common denominator \(8x^2(x^2+4)^{3/2}\) the numerators are \(-2x^2(x^2+4)\), \(+x^2(x^2+2)\) and \(+(x^2+2)(x^2+4)\), which add to \(-2x^4-8x^2+x^4+2x^2+x^4+6x^2+8=8\). So \(F'=\frac8{8x^2(x^2+4)^{3/2}}\), the integrand.

Knowledge Check 8.4.3: Which method?

For each integral say whether an ordinary substitution is enough or a trigonometric substitution is needed, and name it: (a) \(\int\dfrac{x\,dx}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\); (b) \(\int\dfrac{x^2\,dx}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\); (c) \(\int\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\).

Pause and think 8.4.3: Substitution by \(u\) or by \(\theta\)

For \(\int x\sqrt{x^2+4}\,dx\) the substitution \(u=x^2+4\) works at once, but \(x=2\tan\theta\) also works. Which method gives a simpler integral, and what feature of the integrand told you?

Answer and discussion

The substitution \(u=x^2+4\) is simpler: \(x\,dx=\frac12du\), so \(\int x\sqrt{x^2+4}\,dx=\frac12\int u^{1/2}\,du=\frac13(x^2+4)^{3/2}+C\), in two lines and with no triangle. The feature is the factor \(x\), which is (up to a constant) the derivative of the expression under the root. With \(x=2\tan\theta\) the integral becomes \(8\int\tan\theta\sec^3\theta\,d\theta\), which also gives \(\frac13(x^2+4)^{3/2}\) (substitute \(w=\sec\theta\)), but it takes more steps.

items.title: Looking ahead
items.text: This section completes the toolkit for integrals with square roots of quadratics. Hyperbolic functions give a second family of substitutions, \(x=a\sinh t\) for \(\sqrt{a^2+x^2}\) and \(x=a\cosh t\) for \(\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\), which avoid absolute values and give logarithms directly; we mention them in words only, because the hyperbolic functions are not part of this chapter. The next section combines what we have so far with the method of partial fractions: a rational function with a quadratic denominator is first completed to a square, as in Theorem 8.4.8, and a rational function in several factors is decomposed first. The areas and arc lengths of this section return later in the book for parametric and polar curves, where the circle and the ellipse appear again and the integrals that arise are of the kind treated here, and the Taylor-type estimates of a later chapter will use trigonometric integrals of the form of Section 8.3.

items.title: Example bank
items.text:
What’s in this bank. Fourteen further worked examples, grouped by problem type and ordered from easiest to hardest within each group.

  • Group 1: the sine substitution, \(\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\) and its powers.

  • Group 2: the tangent substitution, \(\sqrt{a^2+x^2}\) and its powers.

  • Group 3: the secant substitution, including \(x\le-a\).

  • Group 4: completing the square first.

  • Group 5: areas and lengths.

  • Group 6: choosing the method; answers that differ by a constant.

  • Group 7: proofs.

items.title: Group 1: The sine substitution
items.text:
Example 8.4.19: The root itself

Find \(\int\sqrt{36-x^2}\,dx\) on \(-6<x<6\).

Solution. \(a=6\): \(x=6\sin\theta\), \(dx=6\cos\theta\,d\theta\), \(\sqrt{36-x^2}=6\cos\theta\). Then \(\int6\cos\theta\cdot6\cos\theta\,d\theta=36\int\cos^2\theta\,d\theta=18\int(1+\cos2\theta)\,d\theta=18\theta+9\sin2\theta+C\) (power-reducing identity, Theorem 8.3.1(3)). Since \(\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta\), this is \(18\theta+18\sin\theta\cos\theta+C\). By Theorem 8.4.2(1), \(\theta=\sin^{-1}\frac x6\), \(\sin\theta=\frac x6\), \(\cos\theta=\frac{\sqrt{36-x^2}}6\), so \(18\sin\theta\cos\theta=\frac{x\sqrt{36-x^2}}2\) and

\[\int\sqrt{36-x^2}\,dx=18\sin^{-1}\frac x6+\frac{x\sqrt{36-x^2}}2+C .\]

Check. \(\frac{d}{dx}\) of the first term is \(\frac{18}{\sqrt{36-x^2}}\); of the second, \(\frac12\left(\sqrt{36-x^2}-\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{36-x^2}}\right)=\frac{36-2x^2}{2\sqrt{36-x^2}}=\frac{18-x^2}{\sqrt{36-x^2}}\). The sum is \(\frac{36-x^2}{\sqrt{36-x^2}}=\sqrt{36-x^2}\).

Example 8.4.20: A power with a negative exponent

Find \(\int\frac{x^2}{(9-x^2)^{3/2}}\,dx\) on \(-3<x<3\).

Solution. \(a=3\): \(x=3\sin\theta\), \(dx=3\cos\theta\,d\theta\), \((9-x^2)^{3/2}=(3\cos\theta)^3=27\cos^3\theta\). Then

\[\int\frac{9\sin^2\theta\cdot3\cos\theta}{27\cos^3\theta}\,d\theta=\int\frac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta}\,d\theta=\int\tan^2\theta\,d\theta=\int\big(\sec^2\theta-1\big)\,d\theta=\tan\theta-\theta+C .\]

By Theorem 8.4.2(1), \(\tan\theta=\frac x{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\), so

\[\int\frac{x^2}{(9-x^2)^{3/2}}\,dx=\frac x{\sqrt{9-x^2}}-\sin^{-1}\frac x3+C .\]

Check. \(\frac{d}{dx}\frac x{\sqrt{9-x^2}}=\frac{\sqrt{9-x^2}+x^2/\sqrt{9-x^2}}{9-x^2}=\frac9{(9-x^2)^{3/2}}\), and \(\frac{d}{dx}\sin^{-1}\frac x3=\frac1{\sqrt{9-x^2}}=\frac{9-x^2}{(9-x^2)^{3/2}}\). The difference is \(\frac{x^2}{(9-x^2)^{3/2}}\).

items.title: Group 2: The tangent substitution
items.text:
Example 8.4.21: A cosecant appears

Find \(\int\frac{dx}{x\sqrt{x^2+25}}\) on \(x\ne0\).

Solution. \(a=5\): \(x=5\tan\theta\), \(dx=5\sec^2\theta\,d\theta\), \(\sqrt{x^2+25}=5\sec\theta\). Then

\[\int\frac{5\sec^2\theta}{5\tan\theta\cdot5\sec\theta}\,d\theta=\frac15\int\frac{\sec\theta}{\tan\theta}\,d\theta=\frac15\int\csc\theta\,d\theta=-\frac15\ln\lvert\csc\theta+\cot\theta\rvert+C,\]

because \(\frac{\sec\theta}{\tan\theta}=\frac1{\sin\theta}\) and \(\int\csc\theta\,d\theta=-\ln\lvert\csc\theta+\cot\theta\rvert\) (Theorem 8.1.7). By Theorem 8.4.2(2), \(\csc\theta=\frac{\sqrt{x^2+25}}x\) and \(\cot\theta=\frac5x\), so

\[\int\frac{dx}{x\sqrt{x^2+25}}=-\frac15\ln\left\lvert\frac{\sqrt{x^2+25}+5}x\right\rvert+C ,\]

valid for \(x>0\) and for \(x<0\) (for \(x<0\) the quotient is negative, which is why the absolute value is needed).

Example 8.4.22: A definite integral with a secant cubed

Evaluate \(\int_0^1\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\,dx\).

Solution. \(a=1\): \(x=\tan\theta\), \(dx=\sec^2\theta\,d\theta\), \(\sqrt{1+x^2}=\sec\theta\). New limits: \(x=0\) gives \(\theta=0\), \(x=1\) gives \(\theta=\frac\pi4\). Then

\[\int_0^1\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\,dx=\int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{\tan^2\theta\sec^2\theta}{\sec\theta}\,d\theta=\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^2\theta\sec\theta\,d\theta=\int_0^{\pi/4}\big(\sec^3\theta-\sec\theta\big)\,d\theta .\]

By Theorem 8.3.8, \(\int\sec^3\theta\,d\theta=\frac12\sec\theta\tan\theta+\frac12\ln\lvert\sec\theta+\tan\theta\rvert\), and \(\int\sec\theta\,d\theta=\ln\lvert\sec\theta+\tan\theta\rvert\), so an antiderivative is \(G(\theta)=\frac12\sec\theta\tan\theta-\frac12\ln\lvert\sec\theta+\tan\theta\rvert\). At \(\theta=\frac\pi4\): \(\sec=\sqrt2\), \(\tan=1\), so \(G=\frac{\sqrt2}2-\frac12\ln\big(\sqrt2+1\big)\); at \(0\), \(G=0\). Hence

\[\int_0^1\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\,dx=\frac{\sqrt2-\ln\big(1+\sqrt2\big)}2\approx0.2664 .\]

Check. The integrand runs from \(0\) to \(\frac1{\sqrt2}\approx0.707\) and is increasing, so the area under it is less than \(0.707\); since it is roughly \(x^2\) for small \(x\), an area near \(\frac13\) to \(\frac14\) is right.

items.title: Group 3: The secant substitution
items.text:
Example 8.4.23: A secant cubed

Find \(\int\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}\,dx\) on \(x>1\).

Solution. \(a=1\): \(x=\sec\theta\), \(0<\theta<\frac\pi2\), \(dx=\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta\), \(\sqrt{x^2-1}=\tan\theta\). Then

\[\int\frac{\sec^2\theta\cdot\sec\theta\tan\theta}{\tan\theta}\,d\theta=\int\sec^3\theta\,d\theta=\frac12\sec\theta\tan\theta+\frac12\ln\lvert\sec\theta+\tan\theta\rvert+C\]

(Theorem 8.3.8). By Theorem 8.4.2(3), \(\sec\theta=x\) and \(\tan\theta=\sqrt{x^2-1}\) for \(x>1\), so

\[\int\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}\,dx=\frac12x\sqrt{x^2-1}+\frac12\ln\big(x+\sqrt{x^2-1}\big)+C .\]

On \(x<-1\) the same formula holds with \(\ln\lvert x+\sqrt{x^2-1}\rvert\) (the steps are those of Example 8.4.7: the root is \(-\tan\theta\), which changes the sign of the integral, and then \(\tan\theta=-\sqrt{x^2-1}\) and \(\ln\lvert x-\sqrt{x^2-1}\rvert=-\ln\lvert x+\sqrt{x^2-1}\rvert\) change it back). A quick check: differentiating gives \(\frac{\sqrt{x^2-1}}2+\frac{x^2}{2\sqrt{x^2-1}}+\frac1{2\sqrt{x^2-1}}=\frac{x^2-1+x^2+1}{2\sqrt{x^2-1}}=\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}\) for either sign of \(x\).

Example 8.4.24: A definite integral on the left branch

Evaluate \(\int_{-6}^{-3\sqrt2}\frac{dx}{x\sqrt{x^2-9}}\).

Solution. The interval lies in \(x\le-3\). Take \(x=3\sec\theta\) with \(\frac\pi2<\theta\le\pi\); then \(dx=3\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta\) and \(\sqrt{x^2-9}=-3\tan\theta\) (since \(\tan\theta<0\)). New limits: \(\cos\theta=\frac3x\); \(x=-6\) gives \(\cos\theta=-\frac12\), \(\theta=\frac{2\pi}3\); \(x=-3\sqrt2\) gives \(\cos\theta=-\frac1{\sqrt2}\), \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}4\). Then

\[\int_{-6}^{-3\sqrt2}\frac{dx}{x\sqrt{x^2-9}}=\int_{2\pi/3}^{3\pi/4}\frac{3\sec\theta\tan\theta}{3\sec\theta\cdot(-3\tan\theta)}\,d\theta=-\frac13\int_{2\pi/3}^{3\pi/4}d\theta=-\frac13\cdot\frac\pi{12}=-\frac\pi{36} .\]

Check. The integrand is negative, so the answer is negative; and formula (13) of Section 8.1 with \(a=3\) gives \(\frac13\left[\sec^{-1}\left\lvert\frac x3\right\rvert\right]_{-6}^{-3\sqrt2}=\frac13\left(\frac\pi4-\frac\pi3\right)=-\frac\pi{36}\).

items.title: Group 4: Completing the square first
items.text:
Example 8.4.25: A numerator with \(x\)

Find \(\int\frac{x\,dx}{(x^2+2x+10)^{3/2}}\).

Solution. \(x^2+2x+10=(x+1)^2+9\). Let \(u=x+1\), so \(x=u-1\), \(dx=du\) and \(x^2+2x+10=u^2+9\):

\[\int\frac{x\,dx}{(x^2+2x+10)^{3/2}}=\int\frac{u-1}{(u^2+9)^{3/2}}\,du=\int\frac{u\,du}{(u^2+9)^{3/2}}-\int\frac{du}{(u^2+9)^{3/2}} .\]

The first integral needs only \(w=u^2+9\), \(dw=2u\,du\): \(\frac12\int w^{-3/2}\,dw=-w^{-1/2}=-\frac1{\sqrt{u^2+9}}\). The second is of tangent type, as in Example 8.4.9 with \(a=3\): \(u=3\tan\theta\) gives \(\frac19\sin\theta=\frac u{9\sqrt{u^2+9}}\). So

\[\int\frac{u-1}{(u^2+9)^{3/2}}\,du=-\frac1{\sqrt{u^2+9}}-\frac u{9\sqrt{u^2+9}}=-\frac{9+u}{9\sqrt{u^2+9}} .\]

Returning to \(x\) (\(9+u=x+10\)):

\[\int\frac{x\,dx}{(x^2+2x+10)^{3/2}}=-\frac{x+10}{9\sqrt{x^2+2x+10}}+C .\]

Check. \(\frac{d}{dx}\left[-\frac{x+10}{9\sqrt{x^2+2x+10}}\right]=-\frac{\sqrt{x^2+2x+10}-(x+10)\frac{x+1}{\sqrt{x^2+2x+10}}}{9\,(x^2+2x+10)}=-\frac{(x^2+2x+10)-(x+10)(x+1)}{9\,(x^2+2x+10)^{3/2}}=\frac{9x}{9\,(x^2+2x+10)^{3/2}}\), because \((x+10)(x+1)=x^2+11x+10\) and so the numerator is \(x^2+2x+10-x^2-11x-10=-9x\).

Example 8.4.26: A shifted secant integral

Find \(\int\frac{\sqrt{x^2-2x-8}}{x-1}\,dx\) on \(x>4\).

Solution. \(x^2-2x-8=(x-1)^2-9\). With \(u=x-1>3\) the integral is \(\int\frac{\sqrt{u^2-9}}u\,du\), of secant type with \(a=3\): \(u=3\sec\theta\), \(0<\theta<\frac\pi2\), \(du=3\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta\), \(\sqrt{u^2-9}=3\tan\theta\). Then

\[\int\frac{3\tan\theta\cdot3\sec\theta\tan\theta}{3\sec\theta}\,d\theta=3\int\tan^2\theta\,d\theta=3\int\big(\sec^2\theta-1\big)\,d\theta=3\tan\theta-3\theta+C .\]

By Theorem 8.4.2(3), \(\tan\theta=\frac{\sqrt{u^2-9}}3\) and \(\theta=\cos^{-1}\frac3u\). So

\[\int\frac{\sqrt{x^2-2x-8}}{x-1}\,dx=\sqrt{x^2-2x-8}-3\cos^{-1}\frac3{x-1}+C .\]

Check (in \(u\)). \(\frac{d}{du}\left[\sqrt{u^2-9}-3\cos^{-1}\frac3u\right]=\frac u{\sqrt{u^2-9}}-\frac{9}{u\sqrt{u^2-9}}=\frac{u^2-9}{u\sqrt{u^2-9}}=\frac{\sqrt{u^2-9}}u\), because \(\frac d{du}\cos^{-1}\frac3u=-\frac1{\sqrt{1-9/u^2}}\cdot\left(-\frac3{u^2}\right)=\frac3{u\sqrt{u^2-9}}\) for \(u>3\).

items.title: Group 5: Areas and lengths
items.text:
Example 8.4.27: The area of a circular segment

A circle of radius \(5\) is cut by the line \(x=3\). Find the area of the segment with \(x\ge3\) (the smaller piece).

Solution. The circle is \(y=\pm\sqrt{25-x^2}\), so the segment is the region between \(y=-\sqrt{25-x^2}\) and \(y=\sqrt{25-x^2}\) for \(3\le x\le5\), and by symmetry its area is \(2\int_3^5\sqrt{25-x^2}\,dx\). Let \(x=5\sin\theta\), \(\sqrt{25-x^2}=5\cos\theta\), \(dx=5\cos\theta\,d\theta\). New limits: \(x=5\) gives \(\theta=\frac\pi2\); \(x=3\) gives \(\sin\theta=\frac35\), \(\theta_0=\sin^{-1}\frac35\), with \(\cos\theta_0=\frac45\). Then

\[2\int_3^5\sqrt{25-x^2}\,dx=2\int_{\theta_0}^{\pi/2}25\cos^2\theta\,d\theta=25\Big[\theta+\sin\theta\cos\theta\Big]_{\theta_0}^{\pi/2}=25\left(\frac\pi2-\theta_0-\frac35\cdot\frac45\right),\]

because \(2\int25\cos^2\theta\,d\theta=25\int(1+\cos2\theta)\,d\theta=25\big(\theta+\frac12\sin2\theta\big)\) and \(\frac12\sin2\theta=\sin\theta\cos\theta\). Since \(\frac\pi2-\sin^{-1}\frac35=\cos^{-1}\frac35\), the area is

\[25\cos^{-1}\frac35-12\approx11.18 .\]

Plausibility. The segment is \(2\) wide and its chord (the line \(x=3\)) has length \(8\). A parabolic segment of that base and height has area \(\frac23\cdot8\cdot2\approx10.7\), close to \(11.18\).

Example 8.4.28: The length of the logarithm curve

Find the length of \(y=\ln x\) from \(x=1\) to \(x=\sqrt3\).

Solution. \(y'=\frac1x\), so \(L=\int_1^{\sqrt3}\sqrt{1+\frac1{x^2}}\,dx=\int_1^{\sqrt3}\frac{\sqrt{x^2+1}}x\,dx\) (for \(x>0\), \(\sqrt{1+\frac1{x^2}}=\frac{\sqrt{x^2+1}}{x}\)). Let \(x=\tan\theta\), \(dx=\sec^2\theta\,d\theta\), \(\sqrt{x^2+1}=\sec\theta\). New limits: \(x=1\) gives \(\theta=\frac\pi4\) and \(x=\sqrt3\) gives \(\theta=\frac\pi3\). Then

\[L=\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/3}\frac{\sec\theta\cdot\sec^2\theta}{\tan\theta}\,d\theta=\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/3}\frac{\sec\theta\big(1+\tan^2\theta\big)}{\tan\theta}\,d\theta=\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/3}\big(\csc\theta+\sec\theta\tan\theta\big)\,d\theta,\]

because \(\frac{\sec\theta}{\tan\theta}=\csc\theta\) and \(\frac{\sec\theta\tan^2\theta}{\tan\theta}=\sec\theta\tan\theta\). An antiderivative is \(-\ln\lvert\csc\theta+\cot\theta\rvert+\sec\theta\). At \(\frac\pi3\): \(\csc=\frac2{\sqrt3}\), \(\cot=\frac1{\sqrt3}\), \(\sec=2\), so the value is \(-\ln\sqrt3+2\). At \(\frac\pi4\): \(\csc=\sqrt2\), \(\cot=1\), \(\sec=\sqrt2\), so it is \(-\ln\big(\sqrt2+1\big)+\sqrt2\). Therefore

\[L=2-\sqrt2-\frac12\ln3+\ln\big(1+\sqrt2\big)\approx0.9179 .\]

Plausibility. The chord from \((1,0)\) to \(\big(\sqrt3,\frac12\ln3\big)\) has length \(\sqrt{\big(\sqrt3-1\big)^2+\big(\frac12\ln3\big)^2}\approx0.915\), slightly shorter than \(0.918\), as it should be.

items.title: Group 6: Choosing the method
items.text:
Example 8.4.29: Three integrals with the same root

Find (a) \(\int\frac{x\,dx}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\), (b) \(\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\), (c) \(\int\frac{x^2\,dx}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\) on \(-3<x<3\), and say which need a trigonometric substitution.

Solution. (a) The numerator is, up to a factor, the derivative of \(9-x^2\): let \(u=9-x^2\), \(du=-2x\,dx\). Then \(\int\frac{x\,dx}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}=-\frac12\int u^{-1/2}\,du=-\sqrt u=-\sqrt{9-x^2}+C\). No trigonometric substitution is needed.

(b) This is formula (12) of Section 8.1 (Theorem 8.1.6) with \(a=3\): \(\sin^{-1}\frac x3+C\).

(c) Neither of the previous methods works, so \(x=3\sin\theta\): \(dx=3\cos\theta\,d\theta\), \(\sqrt{9-x^2}=3\cos\theta\), and

\[\int\frac{9\sin^2\theta\cdot3\cos\theta}{3\cos\theta}\,d\theta=9\int\sin^2\theta\,d\theta=\frac92\int(1-\cos2\theta)\,d\theta=\frac92\theta-\frac92\sin\theta\cos\theta+C .\]

With \(\sin\theta=\frac x3\), \(\cos\theta=\frac{\sqrt{9-x^2}}3\) this is

\[\int\frac{x^2\,dx}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}=\frac92\sin^{-1}\frac x3-\frac{x\sqrt{9-x^2}}2+C .\]

Check of (c). \(\frac{d}{dx}\) gives \(\frac9{2\sqrt{9-x^2}}-\frac{\sqrt{9-x^2}}2+\frac{x^2}{2\sqrt{9-x^2}}=\frac{9-(9-x^2)+x^2}{2\sqrt{9-x^2}}=\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\). Only (c) needs the trigonometric substitution.

Example 8.4.30: Two answers that differ by a constant

Find \(\int\frac{dx}{x\sqrt{x^2-4}}\) on \(x<-2\) in two ways: by \(x=2\sec\theta\) and by formula (13) of Section 8.1.

By substitution. \(x=2\sec\theta\) with \(\frac\pi2<\theta<\pi\), \(dx=2\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta\), \(\sqrt{x^2-4}=-2\tan\theta\). Then

\[\int\frac{2\sec\theta\tan\theta}{2\sec\theta\cdot(-2\tan\theta)}\,d\theta=-\frac12\int d\theta=-\frac\theta2+C=-\frac12\cos^{-1}\frac2x+C .\]

By the formula. \(\frac12\sec^{-1}\left\lvert\frac x2\right\rvert+C=\frac12\cos^{-1}\frac2{\lvert x\rvert}+C=\frac12\cos^{-1}\left(-\frac2x\right)+C\), because \(\lvert x\rvert=-x\) for \(x<0\).

Comparison. Since \(\cos^{-1}(-w)=\pi-\cos^{-1}w\), the formula gives \(\frac12\left(\pi-\cos^{-1}\frac2x\right)=\frac\pi2-\frac12\cos^{-1}\frac2x\). The two answers differ by \(\frac\pi2\):

\[\frac12\sec^{-1}\left\lvert\frac x2\right\rvert-\left(-\frac12\cos^{-1}\frac2x\right)=\frac12\Big(\cos^{-1}\Big(-\frac2x\Big)+\cos^{-1}\frac2x\Big)=\frac\pi2 .\]

Both are antiderivatives of the same function on an interval, so they differ by a constant, and they do.

items.title: Group 7: Proofs
items.text:
Example 8.4.31: The antiderivative of \(\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\)

Let \(a>0\). Prove that for \(\lvert x vert>a\),

\[\int\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\,dx= rac x2\sqrt{x^2-a^2}- rac{a^2}2\ln ig\lvert x+\sqrt{x^2-a^2} ig vert+C ,\]

on both \(x>a\) and \(x<-a\).

Proof. We differentiate the right side \(F(x)\). Write \(s=\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\), so \(s'= rac xs\). By the product rule, \( rac{d}{dx}\left( rac x2s ight)= rac s2+ rac{x^2}{2s}\). For the logarithm, \(x+s e0\) when \(\lvert x vert>a\) (since \((x+s)(x-s)=x^2-s^2=a^2 e0\)), and \( rac{d}{dx}\ln\lvert w vert= rac{w'}w\) for \(w e0\) of either sign (Section 8.1). So

\[ rac{d}{dx}\ln\lvert x+s vert= rac{1+ rac xs}{x+s}= rac{ rac{s+x}s}{x+s}= rac1s .\]

Hence \(F'(x)= rac s2+ rac{x^2}{2s}- rac{a^2}2\cdot rac1s= rac{s^2+x^2-a^2}{2s}= rac{2s^2}{2s}=s\), because \(s^2=x^2-a^2\). This holds for every \(x\) with \(\lvert x vert>a\), positive or negative, which proves the claim on both branches. \( lacksquare\)

Example 8.4.32: A reduction formula for \(\int(x^2+a^2)^{-n}\,dx\)

Let \(a>0\) and \(I_n=\int rac{dx}{(x^2+a^2)^n}\). Prove that for every integer \(n\ge1\),

\[I_{n+1}= rac{x}{2na^2\,(x^2+a^2)^n}+ rac{2n-1}{2na^2}\,I_n .\]

Proof. Use \(x=a an heta\), \(dx=a\sec^2 heta\,d heta\), \((x^2+a^2)^n=a^{2n}\sec^{2n} heta\) (Theorem 8.4.1(2)). For every \(m\ge1\),

\[I_m=\int rac{a\sec^2 heta}{a^{2m}\sec^{2m} heta}\,d heta=a^{1-2m}\int\cos^{2m-2} heta\,d heta .\]

Taking \(m=n+1\) and then using the reduction formula for cosine (Theorem 8.2.11) with the exponent \(2n\),

\[I_{n+1}=a^{-1-2n}\int\cos^{2n} heta\,d heta=a^{-1-2n}\left[ rac{\cos^{2n-1} heta\sin heta}{2n}+ rac{2n-1}{2n}\int\cos^{2n-2} heta\,d heta ight] .\]

By the first display with \(m=n\), \(\int\cos^{2n-2} heta\,d heta=a^{2n-1}I_n\), so the second term is \(a^{-1-2n}\cdot rac{2n-1}{2n}\cdot a^{2n-1}I_n= rac{2n-1}{2na^2}I_n\). For the first term, Theorem 8.4.2(2) gives \(\cos heta= rac a{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}\) and \(\sin heta= rac x{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}\), so \(\cos^{2n-1} heta\sin heta= rac{a^{2n-1}x}{(x^2+a^2)^{n}}\) and the first term is \(a^{-1-2n}\cdot rac{a^{2n-1}x}{2n\,(x^2+a^2)^n}= rac{x}{2na^2(x^2+a^2)^n}\). \( lacksquare\)

Check for \(a=3\), \(n=1\). Here \(I_1= rac13 an^{-1} rac x3\) (Theorem 8.1.6), and the formula says \(I_2= rac x{18(x^2+9)}+ rac1{18}I_1= rac x{18(x^2+9)}+ rac1{54} an^{-1} rac x3\). Differentiating, \( rac{d}{dx} rac x{18(x^2+9)}= rac{(x^2+9)-2x^2}{18(x^2+9)^2}= rac{9-x^2}{18(x^2+9)^2}\) and \( rac{d}{dx} rac1{54} an^{-1} rac x3= rac1{54}\cdot rac3{x^2+9}= rac{x^2+9}{18(x^2+9)^2}\). The sum is \( rac{18}{18(x^2+9)^2}= rac1{(x^2+9)^2}\), as it must be.

items.title: Answers and discussion
items.text:
Knowledge Check 8.4.1. (a) \(\sqrt{x^2+49}=\sqrt{x^2+7^2}\) is of tangent type: \(x=7\tan\theta\) with \(-\frac\pi2<\theta<\frac\pi2\), and the root becomes \(7\sec\theta\). (b) \(1-9x^2=9\big(\frac19-x^2\big)\), or \(\sqrt{1-9x^2}=\sqrt{1^2-(3x)^2}\), is of sine type with \(a=\frac13\): \(x=\frac13\sin\theta\) with \(-\frac\pi2\le\theta\le\frac\pi2\), and the root becomes \(\cos\theta\) (alternatively set \(u=3x\) first and then \(u=\sin\theta\)). (c) On \(x>6\), \(x^2-36=x^2-6^2\) is of secant type: \(x=6\sec\theta\) with \(0<\theta<\frac\pi2\), and \((x^2-36)^{3/2}=(6\tan\theta)^3=216\tan^3\theta\).

Knowledge Check 8.4.2. Let \(x=\tan\theta\), \(dx=\sec^2\theta\,d\theta\), \((1+x^2)^{3/2}=\sec^3\theta\). New limits: \(x=0\) gives \(\theta=0\) and \(x=\sqrt3\) gives \(\theta=\frac\pi3\) (since \(\tan\frac\pi3=\sqrt3\)), in the range \(\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)\). Then \(\int_0^{\sqrt3}\frac{dx}{(1+x^2)^{3/2}}=\int_0^{\pi/3}\frac{\sec^2\theta}{\sec^3\theta}\,d\theta=\int_0^{\pi/3}\cos\theta\,d\theta=\sin\frac\pi3=\frac{\sqrt3}2\). With the antiderivative \(\frac x{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\): at \(\sqrt3\) it is \(\frac{\sqrt3}2\), at \(0\) it is \(0\). The two agree.

Knowledge Check 8.4.3. (a) An ordinary substitution is enough: \(u=9-x^2\), \(du=-2x\,dx\) gives \(-\sqrt{9-x^2}+C\). (b) A trigonometric substitution is needed: \(x=3\sin\theta\) gives \(\frac92\sin^{-1}\frac x3-\frac{x\sqrt{9-x^2}}2+C\) (Example 8.4.29). (c) No substitution is needed: it is formula (12) of Section 8.1, \(\sin^{-1}\frac x3+C\).

items.title: 8.5 Partial Fractions
items.text:
Download the PDF version

Guiding question

A rational function is a quotient of two polynomials. The integral \(\int\frac{7x+5}{(x-1)(x+2)}\,dx\) cannot be found by a substitution or by parts, yet it is easy once we notice that \(\frac{7x+5}{(x-1)(x+2)}=\frac4{x-1}+\frac3{x+2}\): each piece is a logarithm. The method of partial fractions undoes the addition of fractions that you learned in algebra. This section answers three questions. Can it always be done? Yes (Theorem 8.5.5), and the decomposition is unique; the proof uses only the division of polynomials, and one fact about real polynomials, proved in Appendix L (Theorem L.2). How do we find the numerators? By equating coefficients, by substituting numbers, and by the cover-up shortcut (Theorem 8.5.6). How do we integrate the pieces? The linear pieces give powers and logarithms; the quadratic pieces give a logarithm and an inverse tangent, and repeated quadratic factors need the reduction formula of Section 8.4 (Theorem 8.5.9). The last part of the section shows when a substitution turns an integral that is not rational into one that is.

By the end of this section you should be able to:

  • divide first when the numerator has degree at least that of the denominator, and say why (Theorem 8.5.2);

  • write the form of the partial fraction decomposition for each of the four kinds of factor (distinct linear, repeated linear, irreducible quadratic, repeated irreducible quadratic) and say why that form always works and is unique;

  • find the unknown numerators by equating coefficients, by substituting values, by the cover-up method and by the derivative trick, and know when each is quicker;

  • integrate \(\frac A{(x-r)^n}\) and \(\frac{Bx+C}{(x^2+bx+c)^n}\), separating the logarithm from the inverse tangent, and use the reduction formula for \(n\ge2\);

  • evaluate definite integrals of rational functions and check the sign and size of the answer;

  • recognize when partial fractions are not needed, and when a substitution such as \(u=e^x\) makes an integrand rational;

  • check every antiderivative by differentiating it.

items.title: The idea
items.text:
In algebra, \(\frac4{x-1}+\frac3{x+2}=\frac{4(x+2)+3(x-1)}{(x-1)(x+2)}=\frac{7x+5}{(x-1)(x+2)}\). To integrate the right side we must run this backward. Each term on the left is a case of \(\int\frac{dx}{x-r}=\ln\lvert x-r\rvert+C\) (the table of Section 8.1), so the whole integral is immediate. Figure 1 shows what the decomposition means: the graph of the rational function is the sum of the graphs of its pieces.

Example 8.5.1: The idea: undoing the addition of fractions

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{7x+5}{(x-1)(x+2)}\,dx\).

Solution. Look for numbers \(A\) and \(B\) with

\[\frac{7x+5}{(x-1)(x+2)}=\frac A{x-1}+\frac B{x+2}.\]

Multiply both sides by \((x-1)(x+2)\) (allowed for \(x\ne1,-2\)): \(7x+5=A(x+2)+B(x-1)\). This is true for all \(x\ne1,-2\), and both sides are polynomials, so it is true for every \(x\) (both sides have degree at most \(1\), and two such polynomials that agree at more than one point are the same polynomial). Put \(x=1\): \(12=3A\), so \(A=4\). Put \(x=-2\): \(-9=-3B\), so \(B=3\). Check by adding back: \(4(x+2)+3(x-1)=7x+5\). Then

\[\int\frac{7x+5}{(x-1)(x+2)}\,dx=4\int\frac{dx}{x-1}+3\int\frac{dx}{x+2}=4\ln\lvert x-1\rvert+3\ln\lvert x+2\rvert+C .\]

Check. \(\frac d{dx}\left(4\ln\lvert x-1\rvert+3\ln\lvert x+2\rvert\right)=\frac4{x-1}+\frac3{x+2}=\frac{7x+5}{(x-1)(x+2)}\).

Figure 1. (a) The function \(f(x)=\frac{7x+5}{(x-1)(x+2)}\) (blue) with its vertical asymptotes \(x=-2\) and \(x=1\) (dashed); the graph is cut off at \(y=\pm5\). (b) For \(x>1\), the graph of \(f\) (blue) is the sum of the graphs of its partial fractions \(\frac4{x-1}\) (red) and \(\frac3{x+2}\) (green); at \(x=3\) the heights are \(2\) and \(\frac35\), and \(\frac42+\frac35=\frac{13}5\). Near \(x=1\) the red piece blows up and the green one stays small; near \(x=-2\) the roles are reversed. That is why each numerator can be found by looking at one asymptote at a time.

items.title: Step 0: divide when the numerator is too large
items.text:
A proper rational function \( rac PD\) has \(\deg P<\deg D\); otherwise it is improper. Adding fractions never produces an improper term out of proper ones, so an improper function must first be split into a polynomial plus a proper function. That is the division of polynomials.

Theorem 8.5.2: Division of polynomials

Let \(N\) and \(D\) be polynomials with \(D e0\). There are polynomials \(Q\) and \(R\), with \(\deg R<\deg D\) (or \(R=0\)), such that \(N=QD+R\). They are unique. In particular, if \(\deg N\ge\deg D\) then \(\deg Q=\deg N-\deg D\), and

\[ rac ND=Q+ rac RD .\]

Proof. Existence, by induction on \(\deg N\). If \(N=0\) or \(\deg N<\deg D\), take \(Q=0\) and \(R=N\). Suppose \(\deg N=n\ge d=\deg D\) and that the claim holds for all numerators of smaller degree. Let \(\alpha x^n\) and \(\delta x^d\) be the leading terms of \(N\) and \(D\) (\(\delta e0\)). The polynomial \(N_1=N- rac\alpha\delta x^{n-d}D\) has no \(x^n\) term (the two leading terms cancel), so \(\deg N_1<n\). By the induction hypothesis \(N_1=Q_1D+R\) with \(\deg R<d\). Then \(N=\left(Q_1+ rac\alpha\delta x^{n-d} ight)D+R\).

Uniqueness. If \(N=QD+R=Q'D+R'\) with \(\deg R,\deg R'<d\), then \((Q-Q')D=R'-R\). The right side has degree less than \(d\). If \(Q e Q'\) the left side has degree \(\deg(Q-Q')+d\ge d\), which is impossible. So \(Q=Q'\), and then \(R=R'\). The degree of \(Q\) follows from the construction (each step lowers the degree of the numerator, and the first step contributes the term \( rac\alpha\delta x^{n-d}\) of highest degree). Dividing \(N=QD+R\) by \(D\) gives \( rac ND=Q+ rac RD\). ◻ ∎

The algorithm in the proof is long division: at each step remove the leading term. A quotient polynomial integrates term by term, so only \( rac RD\) needs partial fractions.

Example 8.5.3: Division first

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int rac{x^3+2x^2-6}{x^2-x-2}\,dx\).

Solution. The numerator has degree \(3\ge2\), so divide. First term: \(x^3\div x^2=x\), and \(x\,(x^2-x-2)=x^3-x^2-2x\). Subtract: \((x^3+2x^2-6)-(x^3-x^2-2x)=3x^2+2x-6\). Next term: \(3x^2\div x^2=3\), and \(3(x^2-x-2)=3x^2-3x-6\). Subtract: \((3x^2+2x-6)-(3x^2-3x-6)=5x\). The degree of \(5x\) is less than \(2\), so we stop:

\[ rac{x^3+2x^2-6}{x^2-x-2}=x+3+ rac{5x}{x^2-x-2}.\]

Factor \(x^2-x-2=(x-2)(x+1)\) and write \( rac{5x}{(x-2)(x+1)}= rac A{x-2}+ rac B{x+1}\), so \(5x=A(x+1)+B(x-2)\). At \(x=2\): \(10=3A\), \(A= rac{10}3\). At \(x=-1\): \(-5=-3B\), \(B= rac53\). Therefore

\[\int rac{x^3+2x^2-6}{x^2-x-2}\,dx=\int\left(x+3+ rac{10/3}{x-2}+ rac{5/3}{x+1} ight)dx= rac{x^2}2+3x+ rac{10}3\ln\lvert x-2 vert+ rac53\ln\lvert x+1 vert+C .\]

Check. The derivative of the right side is \(x+3+ rac{10/3}{x-2}+ rac{5/3}{x+1}\), which is \(x+3+ rac{5x}{x^2-x-2}\) by the partial fractions above, and that equals the integrand by the division.

Knowledge Check 8.5.1: Is division needed?

For each integrand say whether to divide first, and if so find the quotient and remainder: (a) \(\dfrac{x^2+1}{x^2-4}\); (b) \(\dfrac{3x+2}{x^2-4}\); (c) \(\dfrac{x^3}{x^2+1}\).

items.title: The decomposition theorem
items.text:
Which fractions do we add up? The denominator tells us. By Theorem L.2 every real polynomial is a constant times a product of real linear factors and real quadratic factors with no real root; collecting equal factors, a monic denominator is

\[D(x)=(x-r_1)^{m_1}\cdots(x-r_s)^{m_s}\,\left(x^2+b_1x+c_1 ight)^{n_1}\cdots\left(x^2+b_tx+c_t ight)^{n_t},\]

with the \(r_i\) distinct, the quadratics distinct, and \(b_j^2-4c_j<0\). The linear factors are of two kinds: appearing once (\(m=1\)) or repeated. The same is true of the quadratic factors. Each prime factor \(p\) of power \(m\) contributes \(m\) fractions, with denominators \(p,p^2,\dots,p^m\), and the numerators have degree less than that of \(p\): a constant over a linear factor, and \(Bx+C\) over a quadratic one.

The proof of the next theorem needs one property of irreducible factors: they behave like prime numbers. Call a nonconstant polynomial \(p\) irreducible if its only divisors are constants and constant multiples of \(p\). A linear polynomial is irreducible (a divisor has degree \(0\) or \(1\)). A quadratic \(x^2+bx+c\) with \(b^2-4c<0\) is irreducible, since a divisor of degree \(1\) would give a real root.

Theorem 8.5.4: Euclid’s lemma for polynomials

Let \(p\) be an irreducible polynomial and \(A,B\) polynomials. If \(p\) divides \(AB\), then \(p\) divides \(A\) or \(p\) divides \(B\).

Proof. Suppose \(p\) does not divide \(A\); we show that \(p\) divides \(B\). Among all nonzero polynomials of the form \(Up+VA\) (\(U,V\) polynomials) choose one, \(g\), of least degree. Divide \(p\) by \(g\) (Theorem 8.5.2): \(p=Qg+R\) with \(\deg R<\deg g\). Then \(R=p-Qg=p-Q(Up+VA)=(1-QU)p+(-QV)A\) is of the same form, and has smaller degree than \(g\), so \(R=0\) by the choice of \(g\). Thus \(g\) divides \(p\). In the same way \(g\) divides \(A\). Since \(p\) is irreducible, \(g\) is a constant or a constant multiple of \(p\); the second would make \(p\) divide \(A\), which is excluded. So \(g\) is a nonzero constant, and, dividing by it, \(1=U_1p+V_1A\) for some polynomials \(U_1,V_1\). Multiply by \(B\): \(B=U_1pB+V_1AB\). Both terms on the right are divisible by \(p\) (the second because \(p\) divides \(AB\)). Hence \(p\) divides \(B\). ◻ ∎

Theorem 8.5.5: The partial fraction decomposition

Let \(D\) be as above and let \(P\) be a polynomial with \(\deg P<\deg D\). Then there are real numbers \(A_{ik}\) \((1\le i\le s,\ 1\le k\le m_i)\) and \(B_{jk},C_{jk}\) \((1\le j\le t,\ 1\le k\le n_j)\) such that

\[ rac{P(x)}{D(x)}=\sum_{i=1}^s\sum_{k=1}^{m_i} rac{A_{ik}}{(x-r_i)^k}+\sum_{j=1}^t\sum_{k=1}^{n_j} rac{B_{jk}x+C_{jk}}{\left(x^2+b_jx+c_j ight)^k}\]

for all \(x\) where \(D(x) e0\), and these numbers are unique. The number of unknowns is \(\sum m_i+2\sum n_j=\deg D\).

Proof. Let \(\mathcal V\) be the set of all lists of real coefficients as in the theorem; it is a vector space of dimension \(\sum m_i+2\sum n_j=\deg D\) (each linear factor power \(m_i\) contributes \(m_i\) numbers, each quadratic \(2n_j\)). Let \(\mathcal W\) be the vector space of polynomials of degree less than \(\deg D\) (together with \(0\)); its dimension is also \(\deg D\) (the coefficients of \(1,x,\dots,x^{\deg D-1}\)). Given a list \(c\in\mathcal V\), multiply the right side of the decomposition by \(D\). A term \( rac{N}{p^k}\) with \(\deg N<\deg p\) becomes \(N\cdot rac D{p^k}\), a polynomial (because \(p^k\) divides \(D\) for \(k\le\) the power of \(p\) in \(D\)) of degree less than \(\deg p+\deg D-k\deg p\le\deg D\). So \(c\mapsto\Phi(c)=\) (sum of these polynomials) is a linear map \(\Phi:\mathcal V o\mathcal W\). The theorem says: for every \(P\in\mathcal W\) there is exactly one \(c\) with \(\Phi(c)=P\). Since \(\dim\mathcal V=\dim\mathcal W\), it is enough to show that \(\Phi\) is one-to-one, that is, that \(\Phi(c)=0\) forces \(c=0\) (a one-to-one linear map between spaces of the same finite dimension is onto, by the rank–nullity theorem of linear algebra).

Suppose \(\Phi(c)=0\), so \(\sum_p\sum_k rac{N_{p,k}}{p^k}=0\) for all \(x\) with \(D(x) e0\), where \(p\) runs through the distinct irreducible factors of \(D\) and \(N_{p,k}\) is the numerator over \(p^k\) (\(\deg N_{p,k}<\deg p\)). Assume not all \(N_{p,k}\) are \(0\). Choose a factor \(p\) and the largest \(k_0\) with \(N_{p,k_0} e0\) (and, for the other factors, nothing is claimed). Let \(E\) be the product of all the other prime powers \(q^{n_q}\) in \(D\). Multiply the identity by \(p^{k_0}E\):

\[0=\sum_{k\le k_0}p^{k_0-k}E\,N_{p,k}+\sum_{q e p}\sum_k p^{k_0}\, rac{E}{q^k}\,N_{q,k}.\]

(Terms with \(k>k_0\) have \(N_{p,k}=0\).) Every term of the first sum with \(k<k_0\) contains the factor \(p\) because \(k_0-k\ge1\); every term of the second sum contains \(p^{k_0}\) and \(k_0\ge1\), and \( rac E{q^k}\) is a polynomial. The only term without an evident factor \(p\) is \(EN_{p,k_0}\). Hence \(p\) divides \(EN_{p,k_0}\). By Theorem 8.5.4, \(p\) divides \(N_{p,k_0}\) or \(p\) divides \(E\). The first is impossible: \(N_{p,k_0} e0\) has degree less than \(\deg p\). For the second, \(E\) is a product of irreducible polynomials \(q e p\); applying Theorem 8.5.4 again and again, \(p\) would divide one of them, say \(q\); then \(q\) is a constant multiple of \(p\) (the divisors of the irreducible \(q\) are only constants and its own multiples), and since both are monic, \(q=p\), contradicting \(q e p\). This contradiction shows that all \(N_{p,k}\) vanish, so \(c=0\) and \(\Phi\) is one-to-one. ◻ ∎

Factor of \(D\) Terms to include Example \(x-r\) \(\dfrac A{x-r}\) \(\dfrac{A}{x-3}\) \((x-r)^m\) \(\dfrac A{x-r}+\dfrac B{(x-r)^2}+\cdots+\dfrac Z{(x-r)^m}\) \((x+1)^3\): \(\dfrac A{x+1}+\dfrac B{(x+1)^2}+\dfrac C{(x+1)^3}\) \(x^2+bx+c\), \(b^2-4c<0\) \(\dfrac{Bx+C}{x^2+bx+c}\) \(\dfrac{Bx+C}{x^2+4}\) \((x^2+bx+c)^n\) \(\dfrac{B_1x+C_1}{x^2+bx+c}+\cdots+\dfrac{B_nx+C_n}{(x^2+bx+c)^n}\) \((x^2+1)^2\): \(\dfrac{Bx+C}{x^2+1}+\dfrac{Dx+E}{(x^2+1)^2}\)

Knowledge Check 8.5.2: The form of the decomposition

Write the form of the partial fraction decomposition (do not find the numbers) of (a) \(\dfrac{x+2}{x(x-3)(x+5)}\); (b) \(\dfrac{3x-1}{x^2(x^2+1)}\); (c) \(\dfrac{x^2}{(x-1)^3(x^2+x+1)^2}\).

Pause and think 8.5.1: Why \(Bx+C\) over a quadratic?

A student writes \( rac{1}{x(x^2+1)}= rac Ax+ rac B{x^2+1}\) with constant numerators, and cannot find \(A\) and \(B\). Why does this fail? How many unknowns does Theorem 8.5.5 give, and how many does the student’s form have?

Answer and discussion

With constant numerators \(1=A(x^2+1)+Bx\). At \(x=0\) this gives \(A=1\); comparing the coefficients of \(x^2\) gives \(A=0\), a contradiction. The denominator \(x(x^2+1)\) has degree \(3\), so Theorem 8.5.5 gives three unknowns (\( rac Ax+ rac{Bx+C}{x^2+1}\)), and the numerators \(1\cdot\) (any polynomial of degree \(<3\)) form a space of dimension \(3\); the student’s form has only two unknowns and cannot reach every such polynomial. The correct decomposition is \( rac1x- rac x{x^2+1}\).

items.title: Finding the numerators
items.text:
Once the form is chosen, multiply by \(D\) to get a polynomial identity, and find the unknowns in one of three ways. Equating coefficients compares the coefficients of each power of \(x\) and gives a linear system. Substituting values puts convenient numbers (the roots of \(D\) first) into the identity. The cover-up method is substituting a root of \(D\) in a smart way; the theorem below says exactly what it computes.

Theorem 8.5.6: Cover-up and the derivative trick

Let \(\frac PD\) be proper, let \(D=(x-r)^m E\) with \(E(r)\ne0\), and put \(G(x)=\dfrac{P(x)}{E(x)}\). In the decomposition of Theorem 8.5.5, the numerators over the powers of \(x-r\) are

\[A_m=G(r),\qquad A_{m-j}=\frac{G^{(j)}(r)}{j!}\quad(j=1,\dots,m-1).\]

In particular, for a simple root (\(m=1\)), \(A_1=\dfrac{P(r)}{E(r)}=\dfrac{P(r)}{D'(r)}\): cover up the factor \(x-r\) in \(D\) and evaluate the rest of the fraction at \(r\).

Proof. Multiply the decomposition by \((x-r)^m\). The terms over powers of \(x-r\) become \(A_m+A_{m-1}(x-r)+\dots+A_1(x-r)^{m-1}\). Every other term of the decomposition has a denominator that is a power of a different irreducible factor, so after multiplication it has the form \((x-r)^m\times\) (a fraction whose denominator does not vanish at \(r\)). Collecting these terms into one fraction \(H\), whose denominator does not vanish at \(r\) (so \(H\) has derivatives of all orders near \(r\)), we get, for \(x\) near \(r\) and \(x\ne r\),

\[G(x)=\frac{P(x)}{E(x)}=A_m+A_{m-1}(x-r)+\dots+A_1(x-r)^{m-1}+(x-r)^mH(x).\]

Differentiate \(j\) times, \(0\le j\le m-1\), and put \(x=r\). The polynomial part gives \(j!\,A_{m-j}\). By the product rule every term of the \(j\)-th derivative of \((x-r)^mH(x)\) contains a factor \((x-r)^{m-i}\) with \(i\le j<m\), so it is \(0\) at \(r\). Hence \(G^{(j)}(r)=j!\,A_{m-j}\). For \(m=1\): \(D=(x-r)E\) gives \(D'=E+(x-r)E'\), so \(D'(r)=E(r)\). ◻ ∎

Example 8.5.7: Three distinct linear factors, the cover-up method, and a definite integral

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^2\frac{5x+7}{(x+1)(x+2)(x+3)}\,dx\) and check the sign and size of the answer.

Solution. The degree \(1\) of the numerator is less than \(3\), so no division is needed. Write

\[\frac{5x+7}{(x+1)(x+2)(x+3)}=\frac A{x+1}+\frac B{x+2}+\frac C{x+3}.\]

Cover-up (Theorem 8.5.6, \(m=1\)): \(A\) is the fraction with \(x+1\) covered up, evaluated at \(x=-1\): \(A=\frac{5(-1)+7}{(1)(2)}=1\). For \(B\) cover up \(x+2\) and put \(x=-2\): \(B=\frac{5(-2)+7}{(-1)(1)}=3\). For \(C\) cover up \(x+3\) and put \(x=-3\): \(C=\frac{5(-3)+7}{(-2)(-1)}=-4\). Check at \(x=0\): the left side is \(\frac76\), the right side is \(1+\frac32-\frac43=\frac{6+9-8}6=\frac76\). An antiderivative is \(\ln\lvert x+1\rvert+3\ln\lvert x+2\rvert-4\ln\lvert x+3\rvert\), and on \([0,2]\) all three arguments are positive, so

\[\int_0^2\ldots\,dx=\Big[\ln(x+1)+3\ln(x+2)-4\ln(x+3)\Big]_0^2=\big(\ln3+3\ln4-4\ln5\big)-\big(0+3\ln2-4\ln3\big).\]

With \(3\ln4=6\ln2\) this is \(5\ln3+3\ln2-4\ln5=\ln\dfrac{3^5\cdot2^3}{5^4}=\ln\dfrac{1944}{625}\approx1.1348\). Sign and size. The integrand is positive on \([0,2]\) (every factor is positive), so the integral must be positive. At \(x=0\) it equals \(\frac76\approx1.17\) and at \(x=2\) it equals \(\frac{17}{60}\approx0.28\), and it decreases between them, so the area is between \(2\cdot0.28=0.57\) and \(2\cdot1.17=2.33\); the value \(1.13\) is in that range (the trapezoid with these end heights has area \(1.45\), and the curve is bowed below its chord). Figure 2 shows the region.

Figure 2. The region under \(y=\frac{5x+7}{(x+1)(x+2)(x+3)}\) for \(0\le x\le2\). It has area \(\ln\frac{1944}{625}\approx1.135\). The dashed line \(x=-1\) is a vertical asymptote of the graph, where the factor \(x+1\) vanishes; the region stays to its right.

Example 8.5.8: A repeated linear factor and the derivative trick

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2+7x+1}{(x-1)^2(x+2)}\,dx\).

Solution. The form is

\[\frac{x^2+7x+1}{(x-1)^2(x+2)}=\frac A{x-1}+\frac B{(x-1)^2}+\frac C{x+2}.\]

Use Theorem 8.5.6. For the simple root \(-2\) cover up \(x+2\): \(C=\frac{4-14+1}{(-3)^2}=\frac{-9}9=-1\). For the double root \(1\), \(E=x+2\) and \(G(x)=\frac{x^2+7x+1}{x+2}\). Then \(B=G(1)=\frac93=3\), and \(A=G'(1)\) with

\[G'(x)=\frac{(2x+7)(x+2)-(x^2+7x+1)\cdot1}{(x+2)^2},\qquad G'(1)=\frac{9\cdot3-9}{9}=2 .\]

So \(A=2\), \(B=3\), \(C=-1\). Check at \(x=0\): left \(\frac1{(1)(2)}=\frac12\); right \(\frac2{-1}+\frac3{1}+\frac{-1}2=-2+3-\frac12=\frac12\). Integrate each piece (Theorem 8.5.9(1)):

\[\int\left(\frac2{x-1}+\frac3{(x-1)^2}-\frac1{x+2}\right)dx=2\ln\lvert x-1\rvert-\frac3{x-1}-\ln\lvert x+2\rvert+C .\]

Check. \(\frac d{dx}\left(-\frac3{x-1}\right)=\frac3{(x-1)^2}\), and the other two terms differentiate to \(\frac2{x-1}\) and \(-\frac1{x+2}\), which are the pieces.

Knowledge Check 8.5.3: Cover-up

Use the cover-up method to find \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) in \(\dfrac{3x^2+x+2}{x(x-1)(x+2)}=\dfrac Ax+\dfrac B{x-1}+\dfrac C{x+2}\), and check at \(x=2\).

items.title: Integrating the pieces
items.text:
Theorem 8.5.5 reduces every rational integral to two kinds of integrals: \(\int\frac{dx}{(x-r)^n}\) and \(\int\frac{Bx+C}{(x^2+bx+c)^n}\,dx\). The first is a power or a logarithm. For the second, complete the square as in Section 8.4 (Theorem 8.4.8): with \(u=x+\frac b2\) and \(a^2=c-\frac{b^2}4>0\) we have \(x^2+bx+c=u^2+a^2\), and \(Bx+C=Bu+K\) with \(K=C-\frac{Bb}2\). Split into the part with \(u\) (a logarithm or a power) and the part with \(K\) (an inverse tangent or its reduction).

Theorem 8.5.9: Integrals of the pieces

(1) \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x-r}=\ln\lvert x-r\rvert+C\), and for \(n\ge2\), \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{(x-r)^n}=-\frac1{(n-1)(x-r)^{n-1}}+C\), on each interval not containing \(r\).

(2) Let \(b^2-4c<0\), \(a=\sqrt{c-b^2/4}\), \(u=x+\frac b2\), \(K=C-\frac{Bb}2\). Then for all \(x\)

\[\int\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+bx+c}\,dx=\frac B2\ln\left(x^2+bx+c\right)+\frac Ka\tan^{-1}\frac ua+C_0 .\]

(3) With the same notation, for \(n\ge2\),

\[\int\frac{Bx+C}{(x^2+bx+c)^n}\,dx=-\frac{B}{2(n-1)\left(x^2+bx+c\right)^{n-1}}+K\,I_n(u)+C_0,\]

where \(I_n(u)=\displaystyle\int\frac{du}{(u^2+a^2)^n}\) satisfies \(I_1(u)=\frac1a\tan^{-1}\frac ua\) and

\[I_{n+1}(u)=\frac{u}{2na^2\,(u^2+a^2)^n}+\frac{2n-1}{2na^2}\,I_n(u)\qquad(n\ge1).\]

Proof. (1) The first formula is in the table of Section 8.1; the second is the power rule, since \(\frac d{dx}\left[-\frac1{(n-1)(x-r)^{n-1}}\right]=(x-r)^{-n}\).

(2) With \(u=x+\frac b2\), \(du=dx\), \(x^2+bx+c=u^2+a^2\) and \(Bx+C=Bu+K\) (indeed \(Bu+K=Bx+\frac{Bb}2+C-\frac{Bb}2\)):

\[\int\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+bx+c}\,dx=B\int\frac{u\,du}{u^2+a^2}+K\int\frac{du}{u^2+a^2}.\]

For the first integral put \(w=u^2+a^2\), \(dw=2u\,du\): \(\int\frac{u\,du}{u^2+a^2}=\frac12\ln(u^2+a^2)\), with no absolute value because \(u^2+a^2>0\). The second is \(\frac1a\tan^{-1}\frac ua\) (Theorem 8.1.6, or Theorem 8.1.13(i)).

(3) In the same way the first integral is, for \(n\ge2\), \(\int\frac{u\,du}{(u^2+a^2)^n}=\frac12\int w^{-n}\,dw=-\frac{1}{2(n-1)\,w^{n-1}}\). The reduction formula for \(I_n\) is Example 8.4.32 (proved there by the tangent substitution and the reduction formula for \(\cos^{2n}\theta\) of Theorem 8.2.11), applied with the variable \(u\) in place of \(x\). ◻ ∎

Example 8.5.10: An irreducible quadratic factor

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{5x^2+5x+6}{(x-1)(x^2+2x+5)}\,dx\).

Solution. The quadratic has \(b^2-4c=4-20=-16<0\), so it is irreducible. The form is \(\dfrac A{x-1}+\dfrac{Bx+C}{x^2+2x+5}\). Cover up \(x-1\) and put \(x=1\): \(A=\frac{5+5+6}{1+2+5}=\frac{16}8=2\). Multiply out: \(5x^2+5x+6=2(x^2+2x+5)+(Bx+C)(x-1)\). Compare the coefficients of \(x^2\): \(5=2+B\), so \(B=3\). Compare the constants: \(6=10-C\), so \(C=4\). Check with the coefficients of \(x\): \(5=4+(C-B)=4+1\). So

\[\frac{5x^2+5x+6}{(x-1)(x^2+2x+5)}=\frac2{x-1}+\frac{3x+4}{x^2+2x+5}.\]

For the second term, \(u=x+1\), \(a^2=5-1=4\), \(a=2\), and \(3x+4=3u+1\), so \(K=C-\frac{Bb}2=4-3=1\). By Theorem 8.5.9(2),

\[\int\frac{3x+4}{x^2+2x+5}\,dx=\frac32\ln\left(x^2+2x+5\right)+\frac12\tan^{-1}\frac{x+1}2+C_0 .\]

Altogether

\[\int\frac{5x^2+5x+6}{(x-1)(x^2+2x+5)}\,dx=2\ln\lvert x-1\rvert+\frac32\ln\left(x^2+2x+5\right)+\frac12\tan^{-1}\frac{x+1}2+C .\]

Check. Differentiate: \(\frac2{x-1}+\frac32\cdot\frac{2x+2}{x^2+2x+5}+\frac12\cdot\frac{1/2}{1+\left(\frac{x+1}2\right)^2}=\frac2{x-1}+\frac{3x+3}{x^2+2x+5}+\frac{1}{x^2+2x+5}\), because \(\frac14\cdot\frac{1}{1+(x+1)^2/4}=\frac1{4+(x+1)^2}=\frac1{x^2+2x+5}\). The last two terms add to \(\frac{3x+4}{x^2+2x+5}\).

Pause and think 8.5.2: Why every power?

Why does the decomposition of \(\frac P{(x-1)^2}\) need both \(\frac A{x-1}\) and \(\frac B{(x-1)^2}\)? What goes wrong if we use only \(\frac B{(x-1)^2}\) with \(P(x)=x\)? Count unknowns.

Answer and discussion

Using only \(\frac B{(x-1)^2}\) gives \(\frac{x}{(x-1)^2}=\frac B{(x-1)^2}\), so \(x=B\): a constant cannot equal \(x\) for all \(x\). The denominator has degree \(2\), so there are \(2\) unknowns, and the polynomials of degree \(<2\) (such as \(x\)) form a space of dimension \(2\); one unknown cannot reach all of them. With both terms, \(x=A(x-1)+B\) gives \(A=1\), \(B=1\): \(\frac x{(x-1)^2}=\frac1{x-1}+\frac1{(x-1)^2}\).

Example 8.5.11: A repeated irreducible quadratic factor

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{2x^3+4x^2+3x+1}{x\,(x^2+1)^2}\,dx\).

Solution. The degree \(3\) is less than \(5\). The form (Theorem 8.5.5; the quadratic \(x^2+1\) is repeated, so both powers appear) is

\[\frac{2x^3+4x^2+3x+1}{x(x^2+1)^2}=\frac Ax+\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+1}+\frac{Dx+E}{(x^2+1)^2}.\]

Multiply by \(x(x^2+1)^2\) and expand:

\[2x^3+4x^2+3x+1=A(x^2+1)^2+(Bx+C)\,x\,(x^2+1)+(Dx+E)\,x .\]

Put \(x=0\): \(1=A\). Now compare coefficients, with \(A=1\), since \(A(x^2+1)^2=x^4+2x^2+1\) and \((Bx+C)x(x^2+1)=Bx^4+Cx^3+Bx^2+Cx\) and \((Dx+E)x=Dx^2+Ex\):

\[x^4:\ 0=1+B;\quad x^3:\ 2=C;\quad x^2:\ 4=2+B+D;\quad x:\ 3=C+E;\quad x^0:\ 1=A.\]

So \(B=-1\), \(C=2\), \(D=4-2-B=3\), \(E=3-C=1\). Thus

\[\frac{2x^3+4x^2+3x+1}{x(x^2+1)^2}=\frac1x-\frac{x-2}{x^2+1}+\frac{3x+1}{(x^2+1)^2}.\]

Integrate each piece. The first is \(\ln\lvert x\rvert\). For the second, \(-\frac{x-2}{x^2+1}=-\frac x{x^2+1}+\frac2{x^2+1}\) gives \(-\frac12\ln(x^2+1)+2\tan^{-1}x\). For the third, here \(b=0\), \(c=1\), \(a=1\), \(u=x\), \(B=3\), \(K=1\), \(n=2\). By Theorem 8.5.9(3), \(\int\frac{3x\,dx}{(x^2+1)^2}=-\frac3{2(x^2+1)}\) and, with the reduction formula for \(n=1\) (\(a=1\)),

\[I_2(x)=\frac{x}{2(x^2+1)}+\frac12\,I_1(x)=\frac x{2(x^2+1)}+\frac12\tan^{-1}x .\]

Adding the pieces,

\[\int\ldots\,dx=\ln\lvert x\rvert-\frac12\ln(x^2+1)+2\tan^{-1}x-\frac3{2(x^2+1)}+\frac x{2(x^2+1)}+\frac12\tan^{-1}x+C ,\]

that is

\[\ln\lvert x\rvert-\frac12\ln\left(x^2+1\right)+\frac52\tan^{-1}x+\frac{x-3}{2(x^2+1)}+C .\]

Check. Differentiate the answer. The quotient rule gives \(\frac{d}{dx}\frac{x-3}{2(x^2+1)}=\frac{(x^2+1)-2x(x-3)}{2(x^2+1)^2}=\frac{-x^2+6x+1}{2(x^2+1)^2}\). The other terms give \(\frac1x-\frac x{x^2+1}+\frac5{2(x^2+1)}\). Over the common denominator \(2(x^2+1)^2\) the last term and the quotient-rule term add to \(\frac{5(x^2+1)-x^2+6x+1}{2(x^2+1)^2}=\frac{2x^2+3x+3}{(x^2+1)^2}\), which equals \(\frac2{x^2+1}+\frac{3x+1}{(x^2+1)^2}\). So the derivative is \(\frac1x-\frac x{x^2+1}+\frac2{x^2+1}+\frac{3x+1}{(x^2+1)^2}\), the three pieces.

Procedure 8.5.12: Integrating a rational function

To evaluate \(\int\frac{N(x)}{D(x)}\,dx\):

  1. If \(\deg N\ge\deg D\), divide (Theorem 8.5.2): \(\frac ND=Q+\frac RD\) with \(\deg R<\deg D\).

  2. Factor \(D\) into linear factors and irreducible quadratics (find a root by trying the divisors of the constant term, then divide it out; a quadratic with \(b^2-4c<0\) stays). If \(D\) is already a derivative-of-the-bottom situation, stop and use a substitution (Example 8.5.16).

  3. Write the form of Theorem 8.5.5: one fraction for each power of each factor, a constant over a linear factor, \(Bx+C\) over a quadratic.

  4. Find the numerators: cover-up and the derivative trick for the linear factors (Theorem 8.5.6), then equate coefficients or substitute for the rest. Check by adding back, or at one more value of \(x\).

  5. Integrate the pieces with Theorem 8.5.9, and integrate \(Q\) term by term.

  6. Differentiate the answer. For a definite integral, check the sign and size.

Example 8.5.13: Equating coefficients and substituting values: three ways, one answer

Decompose \(\dfrac{x^2+3x+7}{(x+1)(x^2+4)}\) and integrate it.

Solution. The form is \(\frac A{x+1}+\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+4}\), so \(x^2+3x+7=A(x^2+4)+(Bx+C)(x+1)\).

Method 1: equate all coefficients. Expanding, \(A(x^2+4)+(Bx+C)(x+1)=(A+B)x^2+(B+C)x+(4A+C)\). So

\[x^2:\ A+B=1,\qquad x:\ B+C=3,\qquad x^0:\ 4A+C=7.\]

From the first, \(B=1-A\). The second gives \(C=3-B=2+A\). The third becomes \(4A+2+A=7\), so \(A=1\), \(B=0\), \(C=3\).

Method 2: substitute values. Put \(x=-1\): \(1-3+7=5=5A\), so \(A=1\). Put \(x=0\): \(7=4A+C=4+C\), so \(C=3\). Put \(x=1\): \(11=5A+2(B+C)=5+2B+6\), so \(B=0\).

Method 3: cover-up and one coefficient. \(A=\frac{(-1)^2+3(-1)+7}{(-1)^2+4}=\frac55=1\) by Theorem 8.5.6; then \(x^2+3x+7-(x^2+4)=3x+3=(Bx+C)(x+1)\), so \(Bx+C=3\).

All three agree: \(\dfrac{x^2+3x+7}{(x+1)(x^2+4)}=\dfrac1{x+1}+\dfrac3{x^2+4}\). Check at \(x=0\): \(\frac74=1+\frac34\). By Theorem 8.5.9(2) with \(B=0\), \(a=2\), \(K=3\):

\[\int\frac{x^2+3x+7}{(x+1)(x^2+4)}\,dx=\ln\lvert x+1\rvert+\frac32\tan^{-1}\frac x2+C .\]

Equating all the coefficients always works, because Theorem 8.5.5 says the system has exactly one solution. Substituting the roots of \(D\) and the cover-up method are shortcuts that usually need less algebra.

Example 8.5.14: Two forms of the same antiderivative

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{3}{(x-1)(2x+1)}\,dx\) on \(x>1\), in two ways, and compare.

Solution. First way. The form is \(\frac A{x-1}+\frac B{2x+1}\). Cover up \(x-1\) at \(x=1\): \(A=\frac3{3}=1\). Cover up \(2x+1\) at \(x=-\frac12\): \(B=\frac3{-3/2}=-2\). Then \(\frac1{x-1}-\frac2{2x+1}\) (check at \(x=2\): \(\frac3{5}\) and \(1-\frac25=\frac35\)), and

\[\int\left(\frac1{x-1}-\frac2{2x+1}\right)dx=\ln(x-1)-\ln(2x+1)+C_1 .\]

(Use \(u=2x+1\) for the second term: \(\int\frac{2\,dx}{2x+1}=\ln\lvert2x+1\rvert\).)

Second way. Factor the \(2\) out of the second factor: \(\frac3{(x-1)(2x+1)}=\frac{3/2}{(x-1)(x+\frac12)}\), and \(\frac1{(x-1)(x+\frac12)}=\frac{2/3}{x-1}-\frac{2/3}{x+\frac12}\) by cover-up. So the integrand is \(\frac1{x-1}-\frac1{x+1/2}\) and

\[\int\left(\frac1{x-1}-\frac1{x+1/2}\right)dx=\ln(x-1)-\ln\left(x+\tfrac12\right)+C_2 .\]

Comparison. The two answers look different. Since \(\ln(2x+1)=\ln2+\ln\left(x+\frac12\right)\), the first answer is \(\ln(x-1)-\ln\left(x+\frac12\right)-\ln2+C_1\). They are both antiderivatives of the same function on an interval, so they differ by a constant, and they do: \(C_2=C_1-\ln2\). Neither is wrong. (For \(x<-\frac12\) or other intervals the absolute values must be restored.)

Example 8.5.15: An application: logistic growth

A population \(P(t)\) (in thousands) grows according to \(\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{P(50-P)}{500}\) with \(P(0)=5\). Find \(P(t)\) and the time at which \(P=25\).

Solution. Separate: \(\dfrac{dP}{P(50-P)}=\dfrac{dt}{500}\) (for \(0<P<50\)). Partial fractions: \(\frac1{P(50-P)}=\frac AP+\frac B{50-P}\) gives \(1=A(50-P)+BP\); at \(P=0\): \(A=\frac1{50}\); at \(P=50\): \(B=\frac1{50}\). So

\[\frac1{50}\int\left(\frac1P+\frac1{50-P}\right)dP=\frac1{50}\Big(\ln P-\ln(50-P)\Big)=\frac1{50}\ln\frac P{50-P}=\frac t{500}+C .\]

(The integral of \(\frac1{50-P}\) is \(-\ln\lvert50-P\rvert\), by the substitution \(w=50-P\).) Multiply by \(50\): \(\ln\frac P{50-P}=\frac t{10}+C_1\). At \(t=0\), \(P=5\): \(\ln\frac5{45}=C_1=-\ln9\). So \(\frac P{50-P}=\frac{e^{t/10}}9\); solving, \(9P=(50-P)e^{t/10}\), \(P\,(9+e^{t/10})=50e^{t/10}\), and

\[P(t)=\frac{50\,e^{t/10}}{9+e^{t/10}}=\frac{50}{1+9e^{-t/10}} .\]

Check the differential equation: with \(P=\frac{50}{1+9e^{-t/10}}\) we get \(50-P=\frac{450e^{-t/10}}{1+9e^{-t/10}}\) and \(\frac{dP}{dt}=\frac{45e^{-t/10}}{(1+9e^{-t/10})^2}=\frac{P(50-P)}{500}\). Now \(P=25\) means \(\frac P{50-P}=1\), so \(e^{t/10}=9\) and \(t=10\ln9\approx21.97\). The population grows slowly at first, fastest when it is half of the limit \(50\), and then levels off at \(50\) thousand (the limit of \(P\) as \(t\to\infty\) is \(50\)). Figure 3 shows the curve.

Figure 3. The solution \(P(t)=\frac{50}{1+9e^{-t/10}}\) starts at \(P(0)=5\), passes through \((10\ln9,\,25)\approx(21.97,\,25)\), where growth is fastest, and approaches the dashed horizontal asymptote \(P=50\).

Example 8.5.16: When partial fractions are not needed

Evaluate (a) \(\displaystyle\int\frac{6x^2}{x^3+5}\,dx\); (b) \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^2+6x+13}\); (c) \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x\,dx}{x^2-9}\) on \(x>3\).

Solution. (a) The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of the denominator: \(\frac d{dx}(x^3+5)=3x^2\). Put \(u=x^3+5\), \(du=3x^2\,dx\), so \(6x^2\,dx=2\,du\) and \(\int\frac{2\,du}u=2\ln\lvert u\rvert=2\ln\lvert x^3+5\rvert+C\). Partial fractions would factor \(x^3+5\) into a linear and a quadratic factor with ugly roots and give the same answer with much more work.

(b) The denominator is irreducible (\(36-52<0\)) and the numerator is constant, so complete the square: \(x^2+6x+13=(x+3)^2+4\), and by Theorem 8.1.13(i) with \(D=13-9=4\), the integral is \(\frac12\tan^{-1}\frac{x+3}2+C\).

(c) Here \(u=x^2-9\), \(du=2x\,dx\) gives \(\frac12\ln(x^2-9)+C\). Partial fractions give the same result in a different form: \(\frac x{(x-3)(x+3)}=\frac{1/2}{x-3}+\frac{1/2}{x+3}\) (cover-up: \(\frac3{6}\) and \(\frac{-3}{-6}\)), so \(\frac12\ln(x-3)+\frac12\ln(x+3)=\frac12\ln\left((x-3)(x+3)\right)=\frac12\ln(x^2-9)\), the same function exactly.

Pause and think 8.5.3: Always decompose?

Before using partial fractions, what two questions can you ask about an integrand \(\frac ND\) that might save you the work? Apply them to \(\dfrac{2x+3}{x^2+3x+5}\) and to \(\dfrac{x}{x^4+1}\).

Answer and discussion

Ask: (1) Is it improper (then divide)? (2) Is the numerator the derivative of the denominator, or can a substitution simplify it, or is the denominator a single irreducible quadratic (then complete the square)? For \(\frac{2x+3}{x^2+3x+5}\) the numerator is exactly the derivative \(2x+3\) of the denominator, so the integral is \(\ln(x^2+3x+5)+C\), with no decomposition. For \(\frac x{x^4+1}\), \(u=x^2\), \(du=2x\,dx\) gives \(\frac12\int\frac{du}{u^2+1}=\frac12\tan^{-1}(x^2)+C\) (factoring \(x^4+1\) into real quadratics would be much harder).

items.title: Making an integrand rational
items.text:
Not every integrand that leads to partial fractions starts as a rational function. A substitution may turn it into one. If \(e^x\) is the only appearance of \(x\), put \(u=e^x\) (\(dx=\frac{du}u\)). If the integrand is a rational function of \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\), the substitution \(t=\tan\frac x2\) makes it a rational function of \(t\) (Example 8.5.32), and so every such integral can in principle be done by partial fractions; it is often not the shortest route, and the section on integration strategies compares the methods. For \(\sqrt[n]{ax+b}\), put \(u=\sqrt[n]{ax+b}\).

Example 8.5.17: A substitution that produces a rational function

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{1+e^x}\).

Solution. Let \(u=e^x\), so \(du=e^x\,dx=u\,dx\) and \(dx=\frac{du}u\). Then

\[\int\frac{dx}{1+e^x}=\int\frac{du}{u(1+u)} .\]

This is rational and proper. Cover-up: \(\frac1{u(1+u)}=\frac Au+\frac B{1+u}\), \(A=\frac11=1\) (at \(u=0\)), \(B=\frac1{-1}=-1\) (at \(u=-1\)). So \(\int\left(\frac1u-\frac1{1+u}\right)du=\ln u-\ln(1+u)=\ln\frac u{1+u}\), since \(u>0\). Back in \(x\): \(\ln\frac{e^x}{1+e^x}=x-\ln(1+e^x)\). Therefore

\[\int\frac{dx}{1+e^x}=x-\ln\left(1+e^x\right)+C .\]

Check. \(\frac d{dx}\left(x-\ln(1+e^x)\right)=1-\frac{e^x}{1+e^x}=\frac1{1+e^x}\).

Example 8.5.18: A challenging example: division, a repeated factor and a quadratic

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x^5+x^4+3x^3+3x^2+10}{x^4-4x+3}\,dx\).

Solution. Divide. The numerator has degree \(5>4\). \(x^5\div x^4=x\) and \(x(x^4-4x+3)=x^5-4x^2+3x\); the difference is \(x^4+3x^3+7x^2-3x+10\). Then \(x^4\div x^4=1\) and \(1\cdot(x^4-4x+3)\); the difference is \(3x^3+7x^2+x+7\). So the quotient is \(x+1\) and the remainder is \(R=3x^3+7x^2+x+7\) (degree \(3<4\)).

Factor the denominator. \(D(1)=1-4+3=0\), so \(x-1\) is a factor; \(D=(x-1)(x^3+x^2+x-3)\) by division. The cubic is again \(0\) at \(x=1\): \(x^3+x^2+x-3=(x-1)(x^2+2x+3)\). So \(D=(x-1)^2(x^2+2x+3)\), and \(x^2+2x+3\) has \(b^2-4c=4-12=-8<0\).

Form. \(\dfrac R D=\dfrac A{x-1}+\dfrac B{(x-1)^2}+\dfrac{Fx+H}{x^2+2x+3}\).

Numerators. With \(E=x^2+2x+3\) and \(G=\frac RE\) (Theorem 8.5.6): \(B=G(1)=\frac{3+7+1+7}{6}=3\), and \(G'(x)=\frac{R'E-RE'}{E^2}\) with \(R'=9x^2+14x+1\), \(E'=2x+2\), so \(G'(1)=\frac{24\cdot6-18\cdot4}{36}=\frac{72}{36}=2=A\). Equate the \(x^3\) coefficients in \(R=A(x-1)E+BE+(Fx+H)(x-1)^2\): \(3=A+F\), so \(F=1\). Equate the constants: \(7=-3A+3B+H=-6+9+H\), so \(H=4\). Check at \(x=0\): \(R(0)=7\) and \(A(-1)(3)+B(3)+H(1)=-6+9+4=7\). So

\[\frac{x^5+x^4+3x^3+3x^2+10}{x^4-4x+3}=x+1+\frac2{x-1}+\frac3{(x-1)^2}+\frac{x+4}{x^2+2x+3}.\]

Integrate. The polynomial part gives \(\frac{x^2}2+x\). The two linear pieces give \(2\ln\lvert x-1\rvert-\frac3{x-1}\). For the quadratic piece, \(u=x+1\), \(a^2=3-1=2\), \(x+4=u+3\), so \(B=1\), \(K=4-\frac12\cdot2=3\), and Theorem 8.5.9(2) gives \(\frac12\ln(x^2+2x+3)+\frac3{\sqrt2}\tan^{-1}\frac{x+1}{\sqrt2}\). So

\[\int\ldots\,dx=\frac{x^2}2+x+2\ln\lvert x-1\rvert-\frac3{x-1}+\frac12\ln\left(x^2+2x+3\right)+\frac3{\sqrt2}\tan^{-1}\frac{x+1}{\sqrt2}+C .\]

Check. The derivative of the quadratic piece’s antiderivative is \(\frac{x+1}{x^2+2x+3}+\frac3{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{1/\sqrt2}{1+(x+1)^2/2}=\frac{x+1}{x^2+2x+3}+\frac{3}{x^2+2x+3}=\frac{x+4}{x^2+2x+3}\), because \(\frac32\cdot\frac{1}{1+(x+1)^2/2}=\frac{3}{2+(x+1)^2}\). The other terms differentiate to \(x+1\), \(\frac2{x-1}\) and \(\frac3{(x-1)^2}\).

items.title: Looking ahead
items.text: Partial fractions complete the toolkit for rational functions: every rational function has an elementary antiderivative made of a polynomial, logarithms, inverse tangents and rational functions. The next section, on integration strategies, asks which method to try first, and the questions of Procedure 8.5.12 (is it already a substitution? is it improper?) are the first on that list. The decomposition is also the tool for improper integrals of rational functions in the section on improper integrals, where the logarithms decide convergence. In the chapters on series, the geometric series is a rational function expanded in powers of \(x\), and the Taylor series of \(\tan^{-1}x\) comes from integrating \(\frac1{1+x^2}\) term by term; partial fractions help to expand rational functions in power series, and they are also the main tool for the Laplace transform in a later course on differential equations. For repeated factors, the cover-up and the derivative trick are the beginning of the theory of residues in complex analysis.

items.title: Example bank
items.text:
What’s in this bank. Fourteen further worked examples, grouped by problem type and ordered from easiest to hardest within each group.

  • Group 1: distinct linear factors.

  • Group 2: repeated linear factors.

  • Group 3: irreducible and repeated irreducible quadratic factors.

  • Group 4: division first.

  • Group 5: definite integrals and applications.

  • Group 6: substitutions that produce rational functions.

  • Group 7: proofs.

items.title: Group 1: Distinct linear factors
items.text:
Example 8.5.19: A quadratic denominator

Find \(\displaystyle\int\frac{7x-7}{x^2+x-12}\,dx\).

Solution. Factor: \(x^2+x-12=(x-3)(x+4)\) (the numbers \(4\) and \(-3\) have product \(-12\) and sum \(1\)). The numerator has degree \(1<2\). Write \(\frac{7x-7}{(x-3)(x+4)}=\frac A{x-3}+\frac B{x+4}\). Cover-up: \(A=\frac{7\cdot3-7}{3+4}=\frac{14}7=2\) and \(B=\frac{7(-4)-7}{-4-3}=\frac{-35}{-7}=5\). Check by adding back: \(2(x+4)+5(x-3)=7x-7\). Then

\[\int\frac{7x-7}{x^2+x-12}\,dx=2\ln\lvert x-3\rvert+5\ln\lvert x+4\rvert+C .\]

Example 8.5.20: Three factors and a definite integral

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_1^3\frac{4x+2}{x(x+1)(x+2)}\,dx\).

Solution. Write \(\frac{4x+2}{x(x+1)(x+2)}=\frac Ax+\frac B{x+1}+\frac C{x+2}\). Cover-up: \(A=\frac{2}{(1)(2)}=1\) at \(x=0\); \(B=\frac{-4+2}{(-1)(1)}=2\) at \(x=-1\); \(C=\frac{-8+2}{(-2)(-1)}=-3\) at \(x=-2\). Check at \(x=1\): \(\frac66=1\) and \(1+\frac22-\frac33=1\). On \([1,3]\) all arguments are positive:

\[\begin{aligned}\Big[\ln x+2\ln(x+1)-3\ln(x+2)\Big]_1^3&=(\ln3+2\ln4-3\ln5)-(0+2\ln2-3\ln3)\\&=4\ln3+2\ln2-3\ln5=\ln\frac{324}{125}\approx0.9524 .\end{aligned}\]

Sign and size. The integrand is positive; it equals \(1\) at \(x=1\) and \(\frac{14}{60}\approx0.23\) at \(x=3\) and decreases, so the integral lies between \(2\cdot0.23=0.47\) and \(2\cdot1=2\); \(0.95\) is plausible.

items.title: Group 2: Repeated linear factors
items.text:
Example 8.5.21: A single repeated factor

Find \(\displaystyle\int\frac{3x-1}{(x-2)^2}\,dx\).

Solution. Form: \(\frac A{x-2}+\frac B{(x-2)^2}\), so \(3x-1=A(x-2)+B\). At \(x=2\): \(5=B\). The coefficient of \(x\): \(3=A\). So \(\frac{3x-1}{(x-2)^2}=\frac3{x-2}+\frac5{(x-2)^2}\). (Equivalently, \(u=x-2\) gives \(3u+5\) in the numerator.) Then

\[\int\frac{3x-1}{(x-2)^2}\,dx=3\ln\lvert x-2\rvert-\frac5{x-2}+C .\]

Example 8.5.22: A double root at \(0\) and a simple root

Find \(\displaystyle\int\frac{4x^2-5x+2}{x^2(x-1)}\,dx\).

Solution. Form: \(\frac Ax+\frac B{x^2}+\frac C{x-1}\). For \(C\) cover up \(x-1\) and put \(x=1\): \(C=\frac{4-5+2}{1}=1\). For the double root \(0\), \(E=x-1\) and \(G=\frac{4x^2-5x+2}{x-1}\) (Theorem 8.5.6): \(B=G(0)=\frac2{-1}=-2\), and \(G'(x)=\frac{(8x-5)(x-1)-(4x^2-5x+2)}{(x-1)^2}\), so \(A=G'(0)=\frac{(-5)(-1)-2}{1}=3\). Check at \(x=2\): left \(\frac{16-10+2}{4}=2\); right \(\frac32-\frac24+1=2\). Then \(\int\left(\frac3x-\frac2{x^2}+\frac1{x-1}\right)dx\):

\[\int\frac{4x^2-5x+2}{x^2(x-1)}\,dx=3\ln\lvert x\rvert+\frac2x+\ln\lvert x-1\rvert+C .\]

items.title: Group 3: Quadratic factors
items.text:
Example 8.5.23: A linear factor and an irreducible quadratic

Find \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2+x+12}{x(x^2+4)}\,dx\).

Solution. Form: \(\frac Ax+\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+4}\). Cover-up at \(x=0\): \(A=\frac{12}4=3\). Then \(x^2+x+12=3(x^2+4)+(Bx+C)x\); compare \(x^2\): \(1=3+B\), so \(B=-2\); compare \(x\): \(1=C\). Check at \(x=1\): left \(\frac{14}5\); right \(3+\frac{-2+1}5=\frac{14}5\). So the integrand is \(\frac3x+\frac{-2x+1}{x^2+4}\). With \(b=0\), \(a=2\), \(B=-2\), \(K=1\), Theorem 8.5.9(2) gives \(-\ln(x^2+4)+\frac12\tan^{-1}\frac x2\) for the second term:

\[\int\frac{x^2+x+12}{x(x^2+4)}\,dx=3\ln\lvert x\rvert-\ln\left(x^2+4\right)+\frac12\tan^{-1}\frac x2+C .\]

Example 8.5.24: A repeated shifted quadratic, no decomposition needed

Find \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x+3}{(x^2+2x+2)^2}\,dx\).

Solution. The integrand is already a single term of the form in Theorem 8.5.5, so no decomposition is needed: \(b=2\), \(c=2\), \(a^2=c-\frac{b^2}4=1\), \(u=x+1\), and \(x+3=u+2\), so \(B=1\), \(K=2\), \(n=2\). By Theorem 8.5.9(3): \(\int\frac{u\,du}{(u^2+1)^2}=-\frac1{2(u^2+1)}\) and, by the reduction formula with \(n=1\), \(a=1\): \(I_2=\frac u{2(u^2+1)}+\frac12\tan^{-1}u\). So the integral is \(-\frac1{2(u^2+1)}+2I_2=-\frac1{2(u^2+1)}+\frac u{u^2+1}+\tan^{-1}u\), and with \(u=x+1\), \(u^2+1=x^2+2x+2\):

\[\int\frac{x+3}{(x^2+2x+2)^2}\,dx=\frac{2x+1}{2\,(x^2+2x+2)}+\tan^{-1}(x+1)+C .\]

Check. Write \(q=x^2+2x+2\), \(q'=2x+2\). By the quotient rule \(\frac d{dx}\frac{2x+1}{2q}=\frac{4q-2(2x+1)q'}{4q^2}=\frac{2q-(2x+1)(2x+2)}{2q^2}=\frac{(2x^2+4x+4)-(4x^2+6x+2)}{2q^2}=\frac{1-x-x^2}{q^2}\). Also \(\frac d{dx}\tan^{-1}(x+1)=\frac1{1+(x+1)^2}=\frac1q=\frac{q}{q^2}=\frac{x^2+2x+2}{q^2}\). The sum is \(\frac{(1-x-x^2)+(x^2+2x+2)}{q^2}=\frac{x+3}{q^2}\).

items.title: Group 4: Division first
items.text:
Example 8.5.25: Equal degrees

Find \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x^4+1}{x^2-1}\,dx\) on each interval not containing \(\pm1\).

Solution. Divide: \(x^4\div x^2=x^2\) and \(x^2(x^2-1)=x^4-x^2\); the difference is \(x^2+1\); then \(x^2\div x^2=1\) and \(1\cdot(x^2-1)\) leaves \(2\). So \(\frac{x^4+1}{x^2-1}=x^2+1+\frac2{x^2-1}\). Cover-up for \(\frac2{(x-1)(x+1)}\): the coefficient of \(\frac1{x-1}\) is \(\frac2{1+1}=1\) (at \(x=1\)) and that of \(\frac1{x+1}\) is \(\frac2{-1-1}=-1\) (at \(x=-1\)), so \(\frac2{x^2-1}=\frac1{x-1}-\frac1{x+1}\). Therefore

\[\int\frac{x^4+1}{x^2-1}\,dx=\frac{x^3}3+x+\ln\left\lvert\frac{x-1}{x+1}\right\rvert+C .\]

Example 8.5.26: Division, then a substitution

Find \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x^3}{x^2+4}\,dx\).

Solution. Divide: \(x^3=x\,(x^2+4)-4x\), so \(\frac{x^3}{x^2+4}=x-\frac{4x}{x^2+4}\). The remainder \(\frac{4x}{x^2+4}\) is already in the form of Theorem 8.5.9(2) with \(B=4\), \(K=0\), so no decomposition is needed (or \(u=x^2+4\), \(du=2x\,dx\)): its integral is \(2\ln(x^2+4)\). Therefore

\[\int\frac{x^3}{x^2+4}\,dx=\frac{x^2}2-2\ln\left(x^2+4\right)+C .\]

items.title: Group 5: Definite integrals and applications
items.text:
Example 8.5.27: A definite integral with a quadratic factor

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{dx}{(x+1)(x^2+1)}\).

Solution. Form: \(\frac A{x+1}+\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+1}\), so \(1=A(x^2+1)+(Bx+C)(x+1)\). At \(x=-1\): \(1=2A\), \(A=\frac12\). Compare \(x^2\): \(0=A+B\), so \(B=-\frac12\). Compare the constants: \(1=A+C\), so \(C=\frac12\). Check at \(x=1\): \(\frac14\) and \(\frac14+\frac{-\frac12+\frac12}{2}=\frac14\). So the integrand is \(\frac{1/2}{x+1}+\frac{-\frac12x+\frac12}{x^2+1}\), with antiderivative \(\frac12\ln(x+1)-\frac14\ln(x^2+1)+\frac12\tan^{-1}x\) (here \(a=1\), \(K=\frac12\)). Then

\[\int_0^1\ldots\,dx=\left(\frac12\ln2-\frac14\ln2+\frac12\cdot\frac\pi4\right)-0=\frac14\ln2+\frac\pi8\approx0.5660 .\]

Sign and size. The integrand is positive, equals \(1\) at \(0\) and \(\frac14\) at \(1\), and is convex-decreasing in between, so the area is less than that of the trapezoid, \(\frac12\left(1+\frac14\right)=0.625\), and more than \(\frac14\). The value \(0.566\) fits.

Example 8.5.28: A second-order reaction

In a reaction \(A+B\to\) product the amount \(x(t)\) of product satisfies \(\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0.02\,(10-x)(5-x)\) with \(x(0)=0\) (units: moles per litre, and \(t\) in minutes). Find the time at which \(x=4\).

Solution. Separate: \(\frac{dx}{(10-x)(5-x)}=0.02\,dt\) for \(0\le x<5\). Partial fractions: \(\frac1{(10-x)(5-x)}=\frac A{10-x}+\frac B{5-x}\), so \(1=A(5-x)+B(10-x)\). At \(x=5\): \(1=5B\), \(B=\frac15\). At \(x=10\): \(1=-5A\), \(A=-\frac15\). Check: \(\frac15\left(\frac1{5-x}-\frac1{10-x}\right)=\frac15\cdot\frac{5}{(5-x)(10-x)}\). The integral over \(0\to4\) is

\[\frac15\Big[-\ln(5-x)+\ln(10-x)\Big]_0^4=\frac15\Big[\ln\frac{10-x}{5-x}\Big]_0^4=\frac15\left(\ln6-\ln2\right)=\frac{\ln3}5 .\]

So \(0.02\,t=\frac{\ln3}5\) and \(t=\frac{\ln3}{5\cdot0.02}=10\ln3\approx10.99\) minutes.

items.title: Group 6: Substitutions that produce a rational function
items.text:
Example 8.5.29: An exponential

Find \(\displaystyle\int rac{e^x}{e^{2x}-3e^x+2}\,dx\).

Solution. Let \(u=e^x\), \(du=e^x\,dx\). Then the integral is \(\int rac{du}{u^2-3u+2}=\int rac{du}{(u-1)(u-2)}\). Cover-up: \( rac1{(u-1)(u-2)}= rac A{u-2}+ rac B{u-1}\) with \(A= rac1{2-1}=1\) and \(B= rac1{1-2}=-1\). So the integral is \(\ln\lvert u-2 vert-\ln\lvert u-1 vert\), and in terms of \(x\),

\[\int rac{e^x}{e^{2x}-3e^x+2}\,dx=\ln\left\lvert rac{e^x-2}{e^x-1} ight vert+C\quad(x e0,\ x e\ln2).\]

Example 8.5.30: A sine and a cosine

Find \(\displaystyle\int rac{\cos x}{\sin^2x+\sin x-2}\,dx\) on an interval where \(\sin x e1\).

Solution. Let \(u=\sin x\), \(du=\cos x\,dx\). Then \(\int rac{du}{u^2+u-2}=\int rac{du}{(u+2)(u-1)}\). Cover-up: \( rac1{(u+2)(u-1)}= rac A{u+2}+ rac B{u-1}\), \(A= rac1{-3}\) at \(u=-2\) and \(B= rac13\) at \(u=1\). So the integral is \( rac13\left(\ln\lvert u-1 vert-\ln\lvert u+2 vert ight)\). Since \(-1\le u\le1\), \(u+2>0\) and \(u-1\le0\), so \(\lvert u-1 vert=1-u\):

\[\int rac{\cos x}{\sin^2x+\sin x-2}\,dx= rac13\ln rac{1-\sin x}{\sin x+2}+C .\]

items.title: Group 7: Proofs
items.text:
Example 8.5.31: Distinct real roots: a formula for every numerator

Let \(D=(x-r_1)\cdots(x-r_n)\) with distinct real \(r_i\) and let \(\deg P<n\). Prove that

\[\frac{P(x)}{D(x)}=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{P(r_i)}{D'(r_i)}\cdot\frac1{x-r_i},\qquad\int\frac PD\,dx=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{P(r_i)}{D'(r_i)}\ln\lvert x-r_i\rvert+C .\]

Then evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2+2}{x^3-x}\,dx\).

Proof. All the factors are linear and distinct, so by Theorem 8.5.5, \(\frac PD=\sum_i\frac{A_i}{x-r_i}\) for unique numbers \(A_i\). By Theorem 8.5.6 with \(m=1\), \(A_i=\frac{P(r_i)}{D'(r_i)}\). This is the first formula; integrating each term with Theorem 8.5.9(1) gives the second. \(\blacksquare\)

Application. \(D=x^3-x=x(x-1)(x+1)\), \(D'=3x^2-1\), \(P=x^2+2\). The roots \(0,1,-1\) give \(\frac{P(0)}{D'(0)}=\frac2{-1}=-2\), \(\frac{P(1)}{D'(1)}=\frac32\), \(\frac{P(-1)}{D'(-1)}=\frac32\). So

\[\int\frac{x^2+2}{x^3-x}\,dx=-2\ln\lvert x\rvert+\frac32\ln\lvert x-1\rvert+\frac32\ln\lvert x+1\rvert+C .\]

Example 8.5.32: The substitution \(t=\tan\frac x2\)

Prove that for \(-\pi<x<\pi\) and \(t=\tan\frac x2\),

\[\cos x=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2},\qquad\sin x=\frac{2t}{1+t^2},\qquad dx=\frac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}.\]

Then evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{2+\cos x}\).

Proof. Since \(\frac x2\in\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)\), \(\cos\frac x2>0\) and \(\sec^2\frac x2=1+t^2\), so \(\cos^2\frac x2=\frac1{1+t^2}\) and \(\sin^2\frac x2=t^2\cos^2\frac x2=\frac{t^2}{1+t^2}\). The double-angle formulas give \(\cos x=\cos^2\frac x2-\sin^2\frac x2=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}\) and \(\sin x=2\sin\frac x2\cos\frac x2=2t\cos^2\frac x2=\frac{2t}{1+t^2}\). Finally \(x=2\tan^{-1}t\) (the inverse of \(t=\tan\frac x2\) on this interval), so \(dx=\frac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}\). \(\blacksquare\)

Application. \(2+\cos x=\frac{2(1+t^2)+1-t^2}{1+t^2}=\frac{t^2+3}{1+t^2}\), so

\[\begin{aligned}\int\frac{dx}{2+\cos x}&=\int\frac{1+t^2}{t^2+3}\cdot\frac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}=\int\frac{2\,dt}{t^2+3}\\&=\frac2{\sqrt3}\tan^{-1}\frac t{\sqrt3}+C=\frac2{\sqrt3}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\tan(x/2)}{\sqrt3}\right)+C\quad(-\pi<x<\pi).\end{aligned}\]

items.title: Answers and discussion
items.text:
Knowledge Check 8.5.1. (a) Yes, the degrees are equal: \(\frac{x^2+1}{x^2-4}=1+\frac5{x^2-4}\) (since \(x^2+1=(x^2-4)+5\)). (b) No: the numerator has degree \(1<2\). (c) Yes: \(x^3=x\,(x^2+1)-x\), so \(\frac{x^3}{x^2+1}=x-\frac x{x^2+1}\).

Knowledge Check 8.5.2. (a) \(\frac Ax+\frac B{x-3}+\frac C{x+5}\). (b) \(\frac Ax+\frac B{x^2}+\frac{Cx+D}{x^2+1}\). (c) \(\frac A{x-1}+\frac B{(x-1)^2}+\frac C{(x-1)^3}+\frac{Dx+E}{x^2+x+1}+\frac{Fx+G}{(x^2+x+1)^2}\). The numbers of unknowns are \(3\), \(4\) and \(7\), equal to the degrees \(3\), \(4\) and \(3+4=7\) of the denominators, as Theorem 8.5.5 says (\(x^2+x+1\) has \(b^2-4c=-3<0\)).

Knowledge Check 8.5.3. Cover up \(x\) at \(x=0\): \(A=\frac{2}{(-1)(2)}=-1\). Cover up \(x-1\) at \(x=1\): \(B=\frac{3+1+2}{(1)(3)}=2\). Cover up \(x+2\) at \(x=-2\): \(C=\frac{12-2+2}{(-2)(-3)}=2\). Check at \(x=2\): left \(\frac{12+2+2}{2\cdot1\cdot4}=2\); right \(-\frac12+2+\frac24=2\).

items.title: 8.6 Integration Strategies
items.text:
Download the PDF version

Guiding question

Sections 8.1 to 8.5 taught one method at a time, so the method was always announced by the title of the section. A real integral does not come with a title. This section is about the question that comes first: which method should I try? Differentiation is mechanical, because the rules of Calculus I always apply. Integration is a craft: the same integral can often be done in several ways, one of them is usually much shorter, and some integrals cannot be done in closed form at all. We give a decision procedure (Procedure 8.6.1), a table of patterns in the integrand, and a collection of examples that need a rewrite, a dead end and a fresh start, or two methods in a row. We prove the facts that make the craft safe: how to check an answer, why two correct answers may look different (Theorem 8.6.2), why a substitution can turn a root or an exponential into a rational function (Theorem 8.6.9), and how to recognize an integral with no elementary antiderivative (Theorems 8.6.16 and 8.6.17).

By the end of this section you should be able to:

  • apply the decision procedure: rewrite, test for a substitution, recognize the pattern, try the first steps of more than one method, and abandon a method that makes the integral worse;

  • combine two or three methods in sequence (a substitution followed by parts, parts followed by partial fractions, a substitution followed by a trigonometric substitution);

  • use a rationalizing substitution for \((ax+b)^{1/n}\) and for \(e^x\);

  • check every antiderivative by differentiating it, and say why a table or a computer algebra result is a claim and not a proof;

  • recognize integrals such as \(\int e^{-x^2}\,dx\) that have no elementary antiderivative, say what that statement means and what it does not mean, and give a numerical value or a bound for the corresponding definite integral.

items.title: A decision procedure
items.text:
An integral is attacked in a fixed order of questions. The order is not a law of nature; it is a list of the cheapest things to try first.

Procedure 8.6.1: Choosing a method

  1. Is it a basic formula? Compare with the table of Section 8.1 (formulas (1)–(17)). If a constant factor or a linear argument \(ax+b\) is the only difference, you are done.

  2. Can it be rewritten? Split a fraction, divide polynomials, use an identity, complete the square, multiply by a conjugate or by \(1\) (Procedure 8.1.9). Rewriting costs nothing and often makes step 3 or 4 obvious.

  3. Is there a substitution? Look for a function \(g(x)\) such that \(g'(x)\), up to a constant factor, is also in the integrand: the inside of a power, a root, an exponential or a trigonometric function; a denominator whose derivative is the numerator (Procedure 8.1.2).

  4. Recognize the pattern (the table below) and use the method of the matching section: parts (8.2), trigonometric integrals (8.3), trigonometric substitutions (8.4), partial fractions (8.5).

  5. Try the first steps of more than one method. Stop as soon as the new integral is no simpler: higher powers, more factors, a return to the start. A dead end is information, not failure.

  6. Combine. After a substitution, parts or a division the new integrand is a new problem: start again at question 1.

  7. If every route fails, ask whether an elementary antiderivative exists at all (Theorems 8.6.16 and 8.6.17); a definite integral can still be computed numerically.

  8. Check. Differentiate an indefinite answer; compare a definite answer with a numerical value or a rough estimate of sign and size.

Pattern in the integrand First method Section \(f(g(x))\,g'(x)\) substitution \(u=g(x)\) 8.1 polynomial \(\times\) \(e^{ax}\), \(\sin ax\), \(\cos ax\) parts, \(u=\) the polynomial (repeat, or tabular) 8.2 \(\ln x\), \(\tan^{-1}x\), \(\sin^{-1}x\), polynomial \(\times\) one of them parts, \(dv=\) the polynomial part 8.2 \(e^{ax}\sin bx\), \(e^{ax}\cos bx\) parts twice and solve (cyclic) 8.2 \(\sin^mx\cos^nx\) odd power: save one factor, substitute; even powers: identities 8.3 \(\tan^mx\sec^nx\), \(\cot^mx\csc^nx\) \(u=\tan x\) or \(u=\sec x\) (or reduction formula) 8.3 \(\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\), \(\sqrt{a^2+x^2}\), \(\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\) trigonometric substitution, unless a plain substitution works 8.4 \(ax^2+bx+c\) in a root or a denominator complete the square 8.1, 8.4 rational function divide if improper; substitution if the numerator is the derivative; else partial fractions 8.5 \((ax+b)^{1/n}\), or \(x\) only inside \(e^x\) rationalizing substitution (Theorem 8.6.9) this section

items.title: Checking an answer, and why two answers can differ
items.text:
Every method in this chapter produces a formula. Whether the formula is correct can be settled in one line, independently of how it was found.

Theorem 8.6.2: Checking and comparing antiderivatives

Let \(f\) be defined on an interval \(I\).

(1) A differentiable function \(F\) is an antiderivative of \(f\) on \(I\) if and only if \(F'(x)=f(x)\) for every \(x\) in \(I\). So any proposed answer, from any source, can be tested by differentiating it.

(2) If \(F\) and \(G\) are antiderivatives of \(f\) on \(I\), then \(F-G\) is constant on \(I\). Two correct answers obtained by different methods can therefore look different, but they differ by a constant.

Proof. (1) This is the definition of an antiderivative. (2) Put \(H=F-G\). Then \(H'=F'-G'=f-f=0\) on \(I\). Let \(p<q\) be two points of \(I\). By the Mean Value Theorem there is a number \(s\) between \(p\) and \(q\) with \(H(q)-H(p)=H'(s)(q-p)=0\). So \(H(q)=H(p)\) for all \(p,q\) in \(I\), and \(H\) is constant. ◻ ∎

Part (2) needs an interval. For \(\frac1x\), the function that equals \(\ln x+5\) for \(x>0\) and \(\ln(-x)-3\) for \(x<0\) is an antiderivative on \(x\ne0\), yet it is not \(\ln\lvert x\rvert\) plus one constant: the constant may change from one interval to the next. The usual “\(+C\)” means one constant for each interval on which the integrand is defined.

A table or a computer result is not a proof

A table of integrals, a computer algebra system or a classmate gives you a claim: “\(F\) is an antiderivative of \(f\)”. It becomes a proven fact only when you differentiate \(F\) and get \(f\) (Theorem 8.6.2(1)). Tables and programs may leave out absolute values, give a formula valid only on part of the domain, or write the answer in a form that differs from yours by a constant (Theorem 8.6.2(2)). In this course every integral in the examples is checked by differentiation, and a table or computer result is used only as a way to guess an \(F\) whose derivative we then compute.

items.title: Rewrite, substitute, recognize
items.text:
Example 8.6.3: Rewrite the integrand

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{1+\cos x}{\sin^2x}\,dx\).

Solution. Split the fraction and use \(\frac1{\sin x}=\csc x\) and \(\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}=\cot x\):

\[\frac{1+\cos x}{\sin^2x}=\frac1{\sin^2x}+\frac1{\sin x}\cdot\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}=\csc^2x+\csc x\cot x .\]

Both terms are in the table of Section 8.1 (formulas (6) and (8) with \(a=1\)), so on each interval on which \(\sin x\ne0\)

\[\int\frac{1+\cos x}{\sin^2x}\,dx=-\cot x-\csc x+C .\]

Check. \(\frac d{dx}(-\cot x-\csc x)=\csc^2x+\csc x\cot x\), which is the integrand by the split above.

Another form. By the half-angle identity \(\cot\frac x2=\frac{1+\cos x}{\sin x}=\csc x+\cot x\), the answer is also \(-\cot\frac x2+C\). The two forms are the same function, so by Theorem 8.6.2(2) the constant is \(0\).

A route that goes in a circle. If instead we write \(\sin^2x=(1-\cos x)(1+\cos x)\) and cancel, the integral becomes \(\int\frac{dx}{1-\cos x}\). This is correct, but it is not in our table. Multiplying top and bottom by \(1+\cos x\) to get rid of the denominator gives \(\frac{1+\cos x}{1-\cos^2x}=\frac{1+\cos x}{\sin^2x}\), the integral we started with. When a rewrite returns to the start, discard it and choose another.

Example 8.6.4: A substitution after a rewrite

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x^3}{\sqrt{25-x^8}}\,dx\) on \(\lvert x\rvert<\sqrt[4]5\).

Solution. The root contains \(25-x^8=25-(x^4)^2\), and the derivative of \(x^4\) is \(4x^3\), which is the numerator up to the factor \(4\). So rewrite the denominator and put \(u=x^4\), \(du=4x^3\,dx\), \(x^3\,dx=\frac14\,du\):

\[\int\frac{x^3\,dx}{\sqrt{25-(x^4)^2}}=\frac14\int\frac{du}{\sqrt{25-u^2}}=\frac14\sin^{-1}\frac u5+C=\frac14\sin^{-1}\frac{x^4}5+C,\]

using formula (12) of Section 8.1 with \(a=5\). (A trigonometric substitution \(x^4=5\sin\theta\) would work too, but the plain substitution does the job in one step, as the table says.)
