Check. \(\frac d{dx}\frac14\sin^{-1}\frac{x^4}5=\frac14\cdot\frac1{\sqrt{1-x^8/25}}\cdot\frac{4x^3}5=\frac{x^3}{5\sqrt{(25-x^8)/25}}=\frac{x^3}{\sqrt{25-x^8}}\), because \(5\sqrt{\frac{25-x^8}{25}}=\sqrt{25-x^8}\).

Example 8.6.5: Identify the method, then finish

For each integral decide on a method from the pattern in the integrand, and evaluate it.

(a) \(\displaystyle\int\frac{5-3x^2}{x^3-5x}\,dx\). (b) \(\displaystyle\int\ln\left(4+x^2\right)dx\). (c) \(\displaystyle\int\sin^3x\cos^2x\,dx\).

Solution. (a) A rational function, but test the substitution first. The derivative of the denominator is \(3x^2-5\), and the numerator is \(5-3x^2=-(3x^2-5)\). Let \(u=x^3-5x\), \(du=(3x^2-5)\,dx\), so \((5-3x^2)\,dx=-du\):

\[\int\frac{5-3x^2}{x^3-5x}\,dx=-\int\frac{du}u=-\ln\lvert u\rvert+C=-\ln\left\lvert x^3-5x\right\rvert+C .\]

Partial fractions (Section 8.5) would give the same function after factoring \(x^3-5x=x(x-\sqrt5)(x+\sqrt5)\): the three covered-up numerators are \(A=\frac5{-5}=-1\) at \(x=0\), and \(-1\) at each of \(x=\pm\sqrt5\) (check: \(\frac{5-15}{\sqrt5\cdot2\sqrt5}=-1\)), and \(-\ln\lvert x\rvert-\ln\lvert x-\sqrt5\rvert-\ln\lvert x+\sqrt5\rvert=-\ln\lvert x^3-5x\rvert\). Same answer, far more work.

(b) A single transcendental function with no polynomial factor: parts with \(dv=dx\) (Section 8.2, as for \(\ln x\)). Let \(u=\ln(4+x^2)\), \(dv=dx\), so \(du=\frac{2x}{4+x^2}\,dx\) and \(v=x\):

\[\int\ln\left(4+x^2\right)dx=x\ln\left(4+x^2\right)-\int\frac{2x^2}{4+x^2}\,dx .\]

The new integrand is improper (equal degrees), so divide: \(2x^2=2(x^2+4)-8\), hence \(\frac{2x^2}{x^2+4}=2-\frac8{x^2+4}\), and \(\int\frac8{x^2+4}\,dx=8\cdot\frac12\tan^{-1}\frac x2=4\tan^{-1}\frac x2\) (formula (11), \(a=2\)). Therefore

\[\int\ln\left(4+x^2\right)dx=x\ln\left(4+x^2\right)-2x+4\tan^{-1}\frac x2+C .\]

(c) Powers of sine and cosine, odd power of sine (Section 8.3): save one factor \(\sin x\) and write \(\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x\). Let \(u=\cos x\), \(du=-\sin x\,dx\):

\[\begin{aligned}\int\sin^3x\cos^2x\,dx&=\int(1-\cos^2x)\cos^2x\,\sin x\,dx=-\int(1-u^2)u^2\,du\\&=-\frac{u^3}3+\frac{u^5}5+C=-\frac{\cos^3x}3+\frac{\cos^5x}5+C .\end{aligned}\]

Check of (b) and (c). \(\frac d{dx}\left(x\ln(4+x^2)-2x+4\tan^{-1}\frac x2\right)=\ln(4+x^2)+\frac{2x^2}{4+x^2}-2+\frac{4\cdot\frac12}{1+x^2/4}=\ln(4+x^2)+\frac{2x^2}{4+x^2}-2+\frac8{4+x^2}=\ln(4+x^2)\), because \(\frac{2x^2+8}{4+x^2}=2\). And \(\frac d{dx}\left(-\frac{\cos^3x}3+\frac{\cos^5x}5\right)=\cos^2x\sin x-\cos^4x\sin x=\sin x\cos^2x(1-\cos^2x)=\sin^3x\cos^2x\).

Knowledge Check 8.6.1: Choose the first move

Name the first technique you would try for each integral (do not evaluate): (a) \(\displaystyle\int x^2e^{x^3}\,dx\); (b) \(\displaystyle\int xe^{3x}\,dx\); (c) \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x+1}{x^2+2x+5}\,dx\); (d) \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^2\sqrt{x^2+9}}\).

Example 8.6.6: A dead end, and a fresh start

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int x^5e^{x^3}\,dx\).

Solution. First attempt: parts. The integrand is a power of \(x\) times an exponential, a pattern that usually calls for parts. We cannot integrate \(e^{x^3}\), so take \(u=e^{x^3}\) and \(dv=x^5\,dx\): \(du=3x^2e^{x^3}dx\), \(v=\frac{x^6}6\). Then

\[\int x^5e^{x^3}\,dx=\frac{x^6e^{x^3}}6-\frac12\int x^8e^{x^3}\,dx .\]

The new integral has the power \(x^8\) in place of \(x^5\): it is worse, so we stop and return to the start.

Second attempt: substitution. The exponent \(x^3\) has derivative \(3x^2\), and \(x^5=x^3\cdot x^2\). Let \(u=x^3\), \(du=3x^2\,dx\), so \(x^2\,dx=\frac13\,du\):

\[\int x^5e^{x^3}\,dx=\int x^3\,e^{x^3}\,x^2\,dx=\frac13\int u\,e^u\,du .\]

Now parts is the right tool (Section 8.2): \(u=u\), \(dv=e^u\,du\) gives \(\int ue^u\,du=ue^u-\int e^u\,du=(u-1)e^u\). Therefore

\[\int x^5e^{x^3}\,dx=\frac13\left(x^3-1\right)e^{x^3}+C .\]

Check. \(\frac d{dx}\left[\frac13(x^3-1)e^{x^3}\right]=\frac13\left[3x^2e^{x^3}+(x^3-1)\cdot3x^2e^{x^3}\right]=x^2e^{x^3}\left(1+x^3-1\right)=x^5e^{x^3}\).

Pause and think 8.6.1: Was the first attempt wrong?

In Example 8.6.6 the first attempt (parts) was not an error: the integral \(\int x^8e^{x^3}\,dx\) can also be done with \(u=x^3\). Why was it still the wrong start, and what could you look at, before integrating, to see this?

Answer and discussion

Parts helps when differentiating \(u\) and integrating \(dv\) make the integrand simpler. Here neither does: the derivative of \(e^{x^3}\) is \(3x^2e^{x^3}\), as complicated as before, and integrating \(x^5\) raises the power from \(x^5\) to \(x^6\), so the new integrand has \(x^8\). Before integrating, look for a function and its derivative: \(x^5e^{x^3}=x^3\,e^{x^3}\cdot x^2\) contains \(g=x^3\) and \(g'=3x^2\), so a substitution comes first, and only afterwards is the product \(ue^u\) handled by parts. The rule of thumb is to try substitution before parts whenever an inside function with its derivative is visible.

Example 8.6.7: Three methods in a row

Find the area under \(y=e^x\sqrt{4+e^{2x}}\) for \(0\le x\le\ln3\), that is, evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\ln3}e^x\sqrt{4+e^{2x}}\,dx\).

Solution. Substitution. The factor \(e^x\) is the derivative of the inside function \(e^x\), and \(e^{2x}=(e^x)^2\). Let \(u=e^x\), \(du=e^x\,dx\). The limits change: \(x=0\) gives \(u=1\) and \(x=\ln3\) gives \(u=3\). So the integral is \(\int_1^3\sqrt{4+u^2}\,du\) (the second picture of Figure 1).

Trigonometric substitution (Section 8.4). The root \(\sqrt{4+u^2}\) has the form \(\sqrt{a^2+u^2}\) with \(a=2\). Let \(u=2\tan\theta\), \(-\frac\pi2<\theta<\frac\pi2\), so \(du=2\sec^2\theta\,d\theta\) and \(\sqrt{4+u^2}=\sqrt{4\sec^2\theta}=2\sec\theta\) (because \(\sec\theta>0\) on this interval). Then

\[\int\sqrt{4+u^2}\,du=\int2\sec\theta\cdot2\sec^2\theta\,d\theta=4\int\sec^3\theta\,d\theta .\]

A reduction formula (Section 8.3). The secant reduction formula with \(n=3\) gives \(\int\sec^3\theta\,d\theta=\frac12\sec\theta\tan\theta+\frac12\int\sec\theta\,d\theta\), and \(\int\sec\theta\,d\theta=\ln\lvert\sec\theta+\tan\theta\rvert\) (Theorem 8.1.7). So

\[4\int\sec^3\theta\,d\theta=2\sec\theta\tan\theta+2\ln\lvert\sec\theta+\tan\theta\rvert+C .\]

Back to \(u\) (Theorem 8.4.2): \(\tan\theta=\frac u2\) and \(\sec\theta=\frac{\sqrt{4+u^2}}2>0\). Then \(2\sec\theta\tan\theta=\frac{u\sqrt{4+u^2}}2\) and \(2\ln(\sec\theta+\tan\theta)=2\ln\frac{u+\sqrt{4+u^2}}2=2\ln\left(u+\sqrt{4+u^2}\right)-2\ln2\); the constant \(-2\ln2\) is absorbed into \(C\). So an antiderivative is

\[F(u)=\frac12\,u\sqrt{4+u^2}+2\ln\left(u+\sqrt{4+u^2}\right).\]

Check. \(\frac{d}{du}\ln\left(u+\sqrt{4+u^2}\right)=\frac{1+u/\sqrt{4+u^2}}{u+\sqrt{4+u^2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4+u^2}}\), so \(F'(u)=\frac12\sqrt{4+u^2}+\frac{u^2}{2\sqrt{4+u^2}}+\frac2{\sqrt{4+u^2}}=\frac{(4+u^2)+u^2+4}{2\sqrt{4+u^2}}=\frac{4+u^2}{\sqrt{4+u^2}}=\sqrt{4+u^2}\).

Evaluate. \(F(3)=\frac{3\sqrt{13}}2+2\ln\left(3+\sqrt{13}\right)\) and \(F(1)=\frac{\sqrt5}2+2\ln\left(1+\sqrt5\right)\), so

\[\text{Area}=F(3)-F(1)=\frac{3\sqrt{13}-\sqrt5}2+2\ln\frac{3+\sqrt{13}}{1+\sqrt5}\approx5.7174 .\]

Check by a numerical value. A numerical evaluation of the original integral gives \(5.71740\), in agreement. The picture shows why the answer is believable: the region has height from \(\sqrt5\approx2.24\) to \(3\sqrt{13}\approx10.8\) over a base of length \(\ln3\approx1.10\), so the area lies between \(2.24\cdot1.10\approx2.5\) and \(10.8\cdot1.10\approx11.9\).

Figure 1. (a) The region under \(y=e^x\sqrt{4+e^{2x}}\) for \(0\le x\le\ln3\). (b) After the substitution \(u=e^x\) the same area is the area under \(y=\sqrt{4+u^2}\) for \(1\le u\le3\). The shapes differ (note the different vertical scales: \(0.3\) cm per unit in (a), \(0.9\) cm per unit in (b)), but both regions have area \(\frac{3\sqrt{13}-\sqrt5}2+2\ln\frac{3+\sqrt{13}}{1+\sqrt5}\approx5.717\).

Example 8.6.8: Parts, then division, then partial fractions

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\ln\left(x^2+x-6\right)dx\) on \(x>2\) (the integrand is defined where \(x^2+x-6=(x-2)(x+3)>0\), that is, for \(x>2\) and for \(x<-3\)).

Solution. Parts (as for \(\ln x\)): \(u=\ln(x^2+x-6)\), \(dv=dx\), so \(du=\frac{2x+1}{x^2+x-6}\,dx\) and \(v=x\):

\[\int\ln\left(x^2+x-6\right)dx=x\ln\left(x^2+x-6\right)-\int\frac{x(2x+1)}{x^2+x-6}\,dx .\]

Division (the numerator \(2x^2+x\) has the same degree as the denominator): \(2x^2+x=2(x^2+x-6)+(12-x)\), so \(\frac{2x^2+x}{x^2+x-6}=2+\frac{12-x}{(x-2)(x+3)}\).

Partial fractions (Section 8.5): \(\frac{12-x}{(x-2)(x+3)}=\frac A{x-2}+\frac B{x+3}\) with \(A=\frac{12-2}{2+3}=2\) (cover up \(x-2\) at \(x=2\)) and \(B=\frac{12+3}{-3-2}=-3\) (at \(x=-3\)). Check at \(x=0\): \(\frac{12}{-6}=-2\) and \(\frac2{-2}+\frac{-3}3=-1-1=-2\). So

\[\int\frac{x(2x+1)}{x^2+x-6}\,dx=\int\left(2+\frac2{x-2}-\frac3{x+3}\right)dx=2x+2\ln\lvert x-2\rvert-3\ln\lvert x+3\rvert,\]

and therefore

\[\int\ln\left(x^2+x-6\right)dx=x\ln\left(x^2+x-6\right)-2x-2\ln(x-2)+3\ln(x+3)+C\qquad(x>2).\]

Check. The derivative is \(\ln(x^2+x-6)+\frac{x(2x+1)}{x^2+x-6}-2-\frac2{x-2}+\frac3{x+3}\), and \(\frac{x(2x+1)}{x^2+x-6}-2=\frac{12-x}{(x-2)(x+3)}=\frac2{x-2}-\frac3{x+3}\) cancels the last two terms. (For \(x<-3\) the same formula holds with \(\ln\lvert x-2\rvert\) and \(\ln\lvert x+3\rvert\).)

items.title: Making an integrand rational
items.text:
A substitution that is not suggested by an inside function can still be the right idea when it removes a root or an exponential. After the substitution the integrand is a rational function, and Section 8.5 finishes the job.

Theorem 8.6.9: Rationalizing substitutions

Let \(R(p,q)\) be a rational function of two variables.

(1) Let \(n\ge2\) be an integer, \(a e0\), and let \(I\) be an open interval on which \(ax+b>0\) (and on which the integrand is continuous). With \(u=(ax+b)^{1/n}\),

\[\int R\left(x,(ax+b)^{1/n} ight)dx=\left[\int R\left( rac{u^n-b}a,\,u ight) rac na\,u^{n-1}\,du ight]_{u=(ax+b)^{1/n}},\]

and the integrand on the right is a rational function of \(u\).

(2) With \(u=e^x\), \(\displaystyle\int R(e^x)\,dx=\left[\int rac{R(u)}u\,du ight]_{u=e^x}\), and the integrand on the right is a rational function of \(u\).

Proof. We use Theorem 8.4.3: if \(g\) is a differentiable one-to-one function from an open interval \(J\) onto an open interval \(I\) with \(g' e0\), and \(f\) is continuous on \(I\), then \(\int f(x)\,dx=\left[\int f(g( heta))g'( heta)\,d heta ight]_{ heta=g^{-1}(x)}\).

(1) Put \(g(u)= rac{u^n-b}a\) on \((0,\infty)\). Then \(g'(u)= rac na\,u^{n-1} e0\) for \(u>0\), so \(g\) is strictly monotone (hence one-to-one) and continuous; its image is the open interval \(\{x:ax+b>0\}\), and \(g^{-1}(x)=(ax+b)^{1/n}\), because \(u^n=ax+b\) and \(u>0\). Take \(J=g^{-1}(I)\). For \(f(x)=R\left(x,(ax+b)^{1/n} ight)\) we get \(f(g(u))=R\left(g(u),(u^n)^{1/n} ight)=R\left( rac{u^n-b}a,u ight)\) since \(u>0\). The theorem gives the formula; the integrand \(R\left( rac{u^n-b}a,u ight) rac na u^{n-1}\) is a rational function of \(u\) because \(R\) is rational and the other factors are polynomials.

(2) Put \(g(u)=\ln u\) on \((0,\infty)\): it is differentiable, one-to-one, onto \((-\infty,\infty)\), with \(g'(u)= rac1u e0\) and \(g^{-1}(x)=e^x\). Here \(f(x)=R(e^x)\), so \(f(g(u))=R(e^{\ln u})=R(u)\), and the theorem gives \(\int R(e^x)\,dx=\left[\int R(u) rac1u\,du ight]_{u=e^x}\). ◻ ∎

Example 8.6.10: A root removed by a substitution

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int rac{x}{2+\sqrt{x+1}}\,dx\) on \(x>-1\).

Solution. The only root is \(\sqrt{x+1}\), so let \(u=\sqrt{x+1}\) (Theorem 8.6.9(1) with \(n=2\), \(a=1\), \(b=1\)). Then \(x=u^2-1\), \(dx=2u\,du\), and

\[\int rac{x}{2+\sqrt{x+1}}\,dx=\int rac{u^2-1}{2+u}\cdot2u\,du=2\int rac{u^3-u}{u+2}\,du .\]

The integrand is an improper rational function, so divide: \(u^3-u=(u+2)(u^2-2u+3)-6\) (check: \((u+2)(u^2-2u+3)=u^3-2u^2+3u+2u^2-4u+6=u^3-u+6\)). Hence \( rac{u^3-u}{u+2}=u^2-2u+3- rac6{u+2}\) and

\[ egin{aligned}2\int\left(u^2-2u+3- rac6{u+2} ight)du&=2\left( rac{u^3}3-u^2+3u-6\ln(u+2) ight)\&= rac23u^3-2u^2+6u-12\ln(u+2).\end{aligned}\]

Return to \(x\) with \(u=\sqrt{x+1}\), \(u^2=x+1\), \(u^3=(x+1)^{3/2}\):

\[\int rac{x}{2+\sqrt{x+1}}\,dx= rac23(x+1)^{3/2}-2(x+1)+6\sqrt{x+1}-12\ln\left(2+\sqrt{x+1} ight)+C .\]

Check. With \(u=\sqrt{x+1}\) we have \( rac{du}{dx}= rac1{2u}\), so by the Chain Rule the derivative of the answer is \( rac1{2u}\left(2u^2-4u+6- rac{12}{u+2} ight)\). Over a common denominator, \(2u^2-4u+6- rac{12}{u+2}= rac{(2u^2-4u+6)(u+2)-12}{u+2}= rac{2u^3-2u}{u+2}\), so the derivative is \( rac1{2u}\cdot rac{2u(u^2-1)}{u+2}= rac{u^2-1}{u+2}= rac{x}{2+\sqrt{x+1}}\), the integrand.

Knowledge Check 8.6.2: Which substitution?

Find a substitution that turns each integral into one of rational type (do not evaluate): (a) \(\displaystyle\int rac{dx}{1+\sqrt{3x+2}}\); (b) \(\displaystyle\int rac{e^{2x}}{e^x+1}\,dx\); (c) \(\displaystyle\int rac{\sqrt x}{1+\sqrt[3]x}\,dx\).

items.title: Patterns: roots, rational functions, definite integrals
items.text:
Example 8.6.11: Do not overlook a simpler solution

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x^3}{\sqrt{4-x^2}}\,dx\) on \(\lvert x\rvert<2\) in two ways.

Solution. Route A: substitution. The root contains \(4-x^2\), whose derivative \(-2x\) shares a factor \(x\) with the numerator. Write \(x^3\,dx=x^2\cdot x\,dx\) and let \(u=4-x^2\), so \(x^2=4-u\) and \(x\,dx=-\frac12\,du\):

\[\begin{aligned}\int\frac{x^3\,dx}{\sqrt{4-x^2}}&=-\frac12\int\frac{4-u}{\sqrt u}\,du=-\frac12\int\left(4u^{-1/2}-u^{1/2}\right)du\\&=-\frac12\left(8u^{1/2}-\frac23u^{3/2}\right)=-4\sqrt u+\frac13u^{3/2}.\end{aligned}\]

So the integral is \(-4\sqrt{4-x^2}+\frac13(4-x^2)^{3/2}+C\).

Route B: trigonometric substitution. The pattern \(\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\) with \(a=2\) suggests \(x=2\sin\theta\), \(dx=2\cos\theta\,d\theta\), \(\sqrt{4-x^2}=2\cos\theta\) (as \(\cos\theta>0\) for \(-\frac\pi2<\theta<\frac\pi2\)). Then \(\frac{x^3\,dx}{\sqrt{4-x^2}}=\frac{8\sin^3\theta\cdot2\cos\theta\,d\theta}{2\cos\theta}=8\sin^3\theta\,d\theta\). This is an odd power of sine (Section 8.3): \(8\int(1-\cos^2\theta)\sin\theta\,d\theta=8\left(-\cos\theta+\frac{\cos^3\theta}3\right)\). With \(\cos\theta=\frac{\sqrt{4-x^2}}2\) (Theorem 8.4.2) this is \(-4\sqrt{4-x^2}+\frac83\cdot\frac{(4-x^2)^{3/2}}8\), which is the same function as in Route A.

Both routes are correct; Route A is shorter because it uses no inverse function and no second technique. The pattern \(\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\) “suggests” a trigonometric substitution, but an odd power of \(x\) outside the root is the signal to look for \(u=a^2-x^2\) first.

Example 8.6.12: A rational function: test, then decompose

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{5x^2-x+7}{(x-1)(x^2+4)}\,dx\).

Solution. Tests first. The fraction is proper (degree \(2<3\)). The derivative of the denominator \(x^3-x^2+4x-4\) is \(3x^2-2x+4\), which is not a constant multiple of the numerator, so a substitution \(u=\) denominator fails. The factor \(x^2+4\) is irreducible (\(0-16<0\)), so partial fractions:

\[\frac{5x^2-x+7}{(x-1)(x^2+4)}=\frac A{x-1}+\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+4},\qquad 5x^2-x+7=A(x^2+4)+(Bx+C)(x-1).\]

Cover up \(x-1\) at \(x=1\): \(A=\frac{5-1+7}{1+4}=\frac{11}5\). Compare the \(x^2\) coefficients: \(5=A+B\), so \(B=\frac{14}5\). Compare the constants: \(7=4A-C=\frac{44}5-C\), so \(C=\frac95\). Check the coefficient of \(x\): \(-1=C-B=\frac95-\frac{14}5=-1\). Now split the quadratic piece into a logarithm part and an inverse tangent part:

\[\frac{14x+9}{5(x^2+4)}=\frac75\cdot\frac{2x}{x^2+4}+\frac95\cdot\frac1{x^2+4},\]

and \(\int\frac{dx}{x^2+4}=\frac12\tan^{-1}\frac x2\) (formula (11) with \(a=2\)). Therefore

\[\int\frac{5x^2-x+7}{(x-1)(x^2+4)}\,dx=\frac{11}5\ln\lvert x-1\rvert+\frac75\ln\left(x^2+4\right)+\frac9{10}\tan^{-1}\frac x2+C .\]

Check. Differentiate term by term. \(\frac d{dx}\frac{11}5\ln\lvert x-1\rvert=\frac{11/5}{x-1}\); \(\frac d{dx}\frac75\ln(x^2+4)=\frac{14x/5}{x^2+4}\); and by the Chain Rule \(\frac d{dx}\frac9{10}\tan^{-1}\frac x2=\frac9{10}\cdot\frac{1/2}{1+x^2/4}=\frac{9/5}{x^2+4}\). The sum is \(\frac{11/5}{x-1}+\frac{14x+9}{5(x^2+4)}\), the decomposition found above, which adds up to the integrand.

Example 8.6.13: A definite integral: substitution, then parts

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi^2/4}\sin\sqrt x\,dx\).

Solution. The only appearance of \(x\) is inside the root, but \(\frac{du}{dx}=\frac1{2\sqrt x}\) is not in the integrand. Instead solve for \(x\): let \(u=\sqrt x\), so \(x=u^2\) and \(dx=2u\,du\) (the idea of Theorem 8.6.9, with an integrand that is not rational). The limits change: \(x=0\) gives \(u=0\) and \(x=\frac{\pi^2}4\) gives \(u=\frac\pi2\). Then

\[\int_0^{\pi^2/4}\sin\sqrt x\,dx=\int_0^{\pi/2}2u\sin u\,du .\]

This is a polynomial times a sine, so use parts: \(p=2u\), \(dv=\sin u\,du\), so \(dp=2\,du\) and \(v=-\cos u\) (the letter \(p\) avoids a clash with the substitution variable):

\[\int_0^{\pi/2}2u\sin u\,du=\Big[-2u\cos u\Big]_0^{\pi/2}+2\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos u\,du=\left(-\pi\cdot0-0\right)+2\Big[\sin u\Big]_0^{\pi/2}=2 .\]

Check. Going back to \(x\) (not to \(u\)): an antiderivative is \(-2\sqrt x\cos\sqrt x+2\sin\sqrt x\). With \(\frac d{dx}\sqrt x=\frac1{2\sqrt x}\) and the Chain Rule, \(\frac d{dx}\left(-2\sqrt x\cos\sqrt x\right)=-\frac{\cos\sqrt x}{\sqrt x}+\sin\sqrt x\) and \(\frac d{dx}\left(2\sin\sqrt x\right)=\frac{\cos\sqrt x}{\sqrt x}\), so the sum is \(\sin\sqrt x\). At the limits: \(-2\cdot\frac\pi2\cdot0+2\cdot1-(0+0)=2\).

![Diagram: $\frac{\pi^2; area \(2\); (a) \(\sin\sqrt x\) on $\left0,\frac{\pi^2; \(\frac\pi2\); area \(2\); (b) \(2u\sin u\) on \(\left[0,\frac\pi2\right]\)

Figure 2. (a) The region under \(y=\sin\sqrt x\) for \(0\le x\le\frac{\pi^2}4\). (b) The region under \(y=2u\sin u\) for \(0\le u\le\frac\pi2\) after the substitution \(x=u^2\). The regions have different shapes and different vertical scales (\(1.9\) cm per unit in (a), \(0.95\) cm per unit in (b)), but the same area, \(2\).

Example 8.6.14: A challenging rewrite

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{\sin x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx\) on an interval where \(\sin x+\cos x\ne0\).

Solution. Nothing in the table fits, no identity simplifies the quotient, and a substitution \(u=\sin x+\cos x\) needs \(du=(\cos x-\sin x)\,dx\), which is not the numerator. But the denominator and its derivative are related to the numerator: with \(s=\sin x\) and \(c=\cos x\) we have \(2s=(s+c)+(s-c)\), so

\[\frac{\sin x}{\sin x+\cos x}=\frac12\cdot\frac{(s+c)+(s-c)}{s+c}=\frac12+\frac12\cdot\frac{\sin x-\cos x}{\sin x+\cos x}.\]

In the last fraction the numerator is minus the derivative of the denominator. Let \(u=\sin x+\cos x\), \(du=(\cos x-\sin x)\,dx\), so \((\sin x-\cos x)\,dx=-du\):

\[\int\frac{\sin x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx=\frac12\int dx-\frac12\int\frac{du}u=\frac x2-\frac12\ln\lvert\sin x+\cos x\rvert+C .\]

Check. \(\frac d{dx}\left[\frac x2-\frac12\ln\lvert\sin x+\cos x\rvert\right]=\frac12-\frac12\cdot\frac{\cos x-\sin x}{\sin x+\cos x}=\frac{(\sin x+\cos x)-(\cos x-\sin x)}{2(\sin x+\cos x)}=\frac{2\sin x}{2(\sin x+\cos x)}=\frac{\sin x}{\sin x+\cos x}\). A definite integral. On \(\left[0,\frac\pi2\right]\) we have \(\sin x+\cos x\ge1>0\), and \(\sin 0+\cos0=1=\sin\frac\pi2+\cos\frac\pi2\), so the logarithm terms cancel and \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx=\frac\pi4\). (Example 8.6.33 explains this value by symmetry.)

Pause and think 8.6.2: Two answers

Evaluate \(\int\sin x\cos x\,dx\) with \(u=\sin x\) and again with \(u=\cos x\). The two answers look different. Are they both right? What exactly is the relation between them?

Answer and discussion

With \(u=\sin x\): \(\int\sin x\cos x\,dx=\frac{\sin^2x}2+C\). With \(u=\cos x\), \(du=-\sin x\,dx\): \(-\int u\,du=-\frac{\cos^2x}2+C\). Both are antiderivatives of \(\sin x\cos x\) on all of \(\mathbb R\), and they are not equal as functions; their difference is \(\frac{\sin^2x}2-\left(-\frac{\cos^2x}2\right)=\frac{\sin^2x+\cos^2x}2=\frac12\), a constant, exactly as Theorem 8.6.2(2) says. (A third form, \(-\frac14\cos2x\), differs from the first by \(\frac14\).)

items.title: Integrals with no elementary antiderivative
items.text:
Some integrals resist every method of this chapter, and that is not because we are not clever enough. First we must be clear about what is claimed.

Definition 8.6.15: Elementary function

A function is elementary if it can be built from constants and the function \(x\) by finitely many sums, differences, products, quotients and compositions, and by taking roots, exponentials, logarithms, sines, cosines and their inverse functions. These are the functions that a scientific calculator can compute from its keys.

Every antiderivative found in Sections 8.1 to 8.5 is elementary. But the statement “\(\int e^{-x^2}\,dx\) is not elementary” does not say that the integral does not exist. The function \(e^{-x^2}\) is continuous, so by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus the function \(F(x)=\int_0^xe^{-t^2}\,dt\) is differentiable with \(F'(x)=e^{-x^2}\): it is an antiderivative. The point is that \(F\) cannot be written with the functions of the definition. It is an honest new function, defined by an area; it is called the error function (up to a constant factor, \(\operatorname{erf}x= rac2{\sqrt\pi}F(x)\)) and it appears in probability and statistics.

How can we know that no combination of elementary functions works? Trying many methods and failing proves nothing. What does prove it is a theorem, which we quote, together with an algebraic fact that we prove in full.

Theorem 8.6.16: Liouville’s criterion for \(f\,e^g\) (quoted)

Let \(f\) and \(g\) be rational functions with \(g\) not constant. If \(\int f(x)\,e^{g(x)}\,dx\) has an elementary antiderivative on an interval, then there is a rational function \(R\) such that \(R(x)e^{g(x)}\) is an antiderivative, that is,

\[R'+g'R=f .\]

We do not prove Theorem 8.6.16. It is a theorem of Liouville (1830s) whose proof uses differential algebra and is beyond this course; it is the one result of this section that is quoted and not proved, and no appendix section supplies it. The converse is easy and we have already used it: if \(R'+g'R=f\) then \( rac d{dx}\left(Re^g ight)=\left(R'+g'R ight)e^g=fe^g\). The next theorem shows that for the integrands of interest the equation \(R'+g'R=f\) has no rational solution. Its proof uses only Euclid’s lemma (Theorem 8.5.4) and the degrees of polynomials.

Theorem 8.6.17: No rational solution

(a) If \(h\) is a nonconstant polynomial, there is no rational function \(R\) with \(R'+hR=1\).

(b) There is no rational function \(R\) with \(R'+R= rac1x\).

Proof. Write \(R= rac PQ\) in lowest terms (\(P\) and \(Q\) polynomials with no common nonconstant factor). In case (a) put \(s=1\) and in case (b) put \(s=x\) and \(h=1\). Multiplying the equation by \(sQ^2\) turns it, in both cases, into

\[s\left(P'Q-PQ'+hPQ ight)=Q^2 . ag{$*$}\]

Step 1: \(Q\) is constant. Suppose not. Let \(p\) be an irreducible factor of \(Q\) and write \(Q=p^mT\) with \(m\ge1\) and \(p\) not dividing \(T\). Then \(Q'=mp^{m-1}p'T+p^mT'\), and

\[P'Q-PQ'+hPQ=p^{m-1}\left[p\,P'T-mPp'T-p\,PT'+p\,hPT ight]=p^{m-1}\,W,\qquad W=p\,U-mPp'T,\]

where \(U=P'T-PT'+hPT\). We claim that \(p\) does not divide \(W\). If it did, \(p\) would divide \(mPp'T\). But \(p\) does not divide \(P\) (otherwise \(P\) and \(Q\) would have the common factor \(p\)), \(p\) does not divide \(T\) (choice of \(m\)), \(p\) does not divide \(m\) (a nonzero constant), and \(p\) does not divide \(p'\) (the polynomial \(p'\) is nonzero with degree less than \(\deg p\)). By Euclid’s lemma (Theorem 8.5.4) applied repeatedly, \(p\) does not divide the product \(mPp'T\), a contradiction. So \(p mid W\).

Now \((*)\) reads \(s\,p^{m-1}W=p^{2m}T^2\), and cancelling \(p^{m-1}\) gives \(sW=p^{m+1}T^2\). Hence \(p\) divides \(sW\). If \(s=1\) then \(p\) divides \(W\), which is false. If \(s=x\), Euclid’s lemma gives \(p\mid x\) or \(p\mid W\); the second is false, so \(p\) divides \(x\), and since \(p\) is not constant, \(p=cx\) for a constant \(c e0\). Then \(x=p/c\), and \(sW=p^{m+1}T^2\) gives \(W=c\,p^mT^2\), which is divisible by \(p\) (because \(m\ge1\)): again a contradiction. So \(Q\) is constant, and \(R\) is a polynomial (absorb the constant into \(P\)): \(Q=1\).

Step 2: \(R=P\) is not a polynomial solution. (a) If \(P=0\) the equation says \(0=1\). If \(P e0\), then \(\deg(hP)=\deg h+\deg P\ge\deg P+1>\deg P'\), so \(\deg\left(P'+hP ight)=\deg h+\deg P\ge1\), but the right side \(1\) has degree \(0\). (b) The equation \(P'+P= rac1x\) gives \(x\left(P'+P ight)=1\); at \(x=0\) the left side is \(0\) and the right side is \(1\). In both cases there is no solution. ◻ ∎

Theorem 8.6.18: Consequences

The functions \(e^{x^2}\), \(e^{-x^2}\), \(e^{x^3}\), \( rac{e^x}x\) and \( rac1{\ln x}\) (for \(x>1\)) have no elementary antiderivative.

Proof. For \(e^{g}\) with \(g=x^2,-x^2,x^3\) take \(f=1\) in Theorem 8.6.16: an elementary antiderivative would give a rational \(R\) with \(R'+g'R=1\), where \(g'=2x,-2x,3x^2\) is a nonconstant polynomial; this contradicts Theorem 8.6.17(a). For \( rac{e^x}x\) take \(g=x\) and \(f= rac1x\): Theorem 8.6.17(b). For \( rac1{\ln x}\): if \(G\) were an elementary antiderivative on \(x>1\), then \(G(e^u)\) (an elementary function of \(u\)) would satisfy \( rac d{du}G(e^u)=G'(e^u)\,e^u= rac{e^u}{\ln e^u}= rac{e^u}u\) for \(u>0\), an elementary antiderivative of \( rac{e^u}u\), which does not exist. ◻ ∎

Procedure 8.6.19: Recognizing a non-elementary integral

  1. Look for the warning sign: a transcendental function (\(e^{(\cdot)}\), \(\sin\), \(\cos\), \(\ln\)) of a non-linear argument (\(x^2\), \(x^3\), \(\ln x\), \( rac1x\)) whose derivative is not present. Compare \(\int xe^{-x^2}\,dx\) (the derivative \(-2x\) is there, so substitution works) with \(\int e^{-x^2}\,dx\) (it is not).

  2. Watch the methods. If parts returns the same kind of integral (or a harder one) and a substitution leaves an \(x\) behind, suspect that no elementary antiderivative exists.

  3. Test with the criterion. For \(\int f\,e^g\,dx\) with \(f,g\) rational, look for a rational \(R\) with \(R'+g'R=f\) (Theorems 8.6.16 and 8.6.17).

  4. Know the standard list (each follows from Liouville’s theorem and its extensions, proofs omitted except those above): \(\int e^{\pm x^2}dx\), \(\int rac{e^x}x\,dx\), \(\int rac{dx}{\ln x}\), \(\int rac{\sin x}x\,dx\), \(\int\sin\left(x^2 ight)dx\), \(\int\cos\left(x^2 ight)dx\), \(\int\sqrt{1+x^3}\,dx\).

  5. A failed search is not a proof, and a computer’s inability to find a formula is not one either. But a proved non-elementary integral is not the end: definite integrals still have values, found numerically or bracketed by inequalities, and \(\int_0^xf(t)\,dt\) is a perfectly good function.

Example 8.6.20: Elementary or not?

Decide whether each integral has an elementary antiderivative; find it, or give the numerical value and a rough bracket.

(a) \(\displaystyle\int xe^{-x^2}\,dx\). (b) \(\displaystyle\int e^{-x^2}\,dx\). (c) \(\displaystyle\int_0^1e^{-x^2}\,dx\).

Solution. (a) The exponent \(-x^2\) has derivative \(-2x\), and \(x\) is present up to the factor \(-2\). Let \(u=-x^2\), \(du=-2x\,dx\), \(x\,dx=- rac12\,du\):

\[\int xe^{-x^2}\,dx=- rac12\int e^u\,du=- rac12e^{-x^2}+C .\]

Check. \( rac d{dx}\left(- rac12e^{-x^2} ight)=- rac12e^{-x^2}\cdot(-2x)=xe^{-x^2}\).

(b) Here the derivative \(-2x\) is missing. Parts with \(u=e^{-x^2}\), \(dv=dx\) gives \(xe^{-x^2}+2\int x^2e^{-x^2}\,dx\), and parts on the new integral (with \(p=x\), \(dv=xe^{-x^2}\,dx\)) brings back exactly \(\int e^{-x^2}\,dx\): the two steps together give the empty identity \(I=I\). This is the warning sign. By Theorem 8.6.18, \(e^{-x^2}\) has no elementary antiderivative. It does have the antiderivative \(F(x)=\int_0^xe^{-t^2}\,dt= rac{\sqrt\pi}2\operatorname{erf}x\) (Figure 3), with \(F'(x)=e^{-x^2}\), \(F(1)\approx0.7468\), and, from a later section on improper integrals, \(F(x) o rac{\sqrt\pi}2\approx0.8862\) as \(x o\infty\).

(c) By the Fundamental Theorem, \(\int_0^1e^{-x^2}\,dx=F(1)\approx0.7468\); no antiderivative formula is needed. We can also bracket it by hand with two inequalities from Calculus I, valid for all \(t\): \(e^{-t}\ge1-t\) (the graph of \(e^{-t}\) lies above its tangent line at \(t=0\)) and \(e^t\ge1+t\) for \(t\ge0\), hence \(e^{-t}\le rac1{1+t}\). With \(t=x^2\), for \(0\le x\le1\),

\[1-x^2\le e^{-x^2}\le rac1{1+x^2},\qquad ext{so}\qquad\int_0^1\left(1-x^2 ight)dx= rac23\le\int_0^1e^{-x^2}\,dx\le\int_0^1 rac{dx}{1+x^2}= rac\pi4 .\]

Numerically \(0.6667\le0.7468\le0.7854\).

Figure 3. (a) The graph of \(e^{-x^2}\); the shaded area from \(0\) to \(1\) is \(F(1)\approx0.7468\). (b) The area function \(F(x)=\int_0^xe^{-t^2}\,dt\): it is an antiderivative of \(e^{-x^2}\), increasing and levelling off at \( rac{\sqrt\pi}2\approx0.886\) (dashed), although no elementary formula for it exists. The vertical scales are \(2.8\) cm and \(3.2\) cm per unit.

Knowledge Check 8.6.3: Elementary or not?

Use the procedure above and the theorems to decide whether each integral has an elementary antiderivative, and say why: (a) \(\displaystyle\int xe^{x^2}\,dx\); (b) \(\displaystyle\int e^{x^2}\,dx\); (c) \(\displaystyle\int\cos x\,e^{\sin x}\,dx\); (d) \(\displaystyle\int rac{e^x}x\,dx\).

Pause and think 8.6.3: Failing is not proving

A student tries parts, three substitutions and a table on \(\int e^{-x^2}\,dx\), fails every time, and writes “so it has no elementary antiderivative”. Why is this not a proof? Which parts of this section do prove the claim, and which part of that proof did we not prove here?

Answer and discussion

A failed search proves only that those methods failed; a cleverer substitution might exist, and mathematicians did not know for a long time. What proves the claim is a theorem: Liouville’s criterion says that if \(e^{-x^2}\) had an elementary antiderivative, there would be a rational \(R\) with \(R'-2xR=1\), and Theorem 8.6.17(a) shows by an algebraic argument (using only Euclid’s lemma and degrees) that no such \(R\) exists. We proved the algebra in full; we did not prove Liouville’s criterion (Theorem 8.6.16), which is quoted.

items.title: Looking ahead
items.text: When an integral cannot be done in closed form, or when the closed form is too long to be useful, the value of a definite integral can still be approximated to any accuracy. The next sections introduce the use of tables and computer algebra (a table entry is a claim to be checked by differentiation, as above), numerical integration with error bounds, and improper integrals, which will give the value \(\int_0^\infty e^{-x^2}\,dx=\frac{\sqrt\pi}2\) quoted in Example 8.6.20. In the chapters on series, a function such as \(\int_0^xe^{-t^2}\,dt\) will be computed by integrating the series of \(e^{-t^2}\) term by term; that is how calculators evaluate it.

items.title: Example bank
items.text:
What’s in this bank. Fourteen further worked examples, grouped by the pattern in the integrand and ordered from easiest to hardest within each group.

  • Group 1: rewrite the integrand first (expand and split, multiply by a conjugate).

  • Group 2: substitution, including a substitution that is not obvious and two substitutions in a row.

  • Group 3: products (a cyclic integral, and a substitution followed by parts).

  • Group 4: trigonometric integrands (odd powers, tangent and secant).

  • Group 5: roots and quadratics (a trigonometric substitution, and a case where a plain substitution is better).

  • Group 6: rational integrands and roots (a substitution that beats partial fractions, a sixth-root substitution).

  • Group 7: proofs (a symmetry trick for definite integrals, a reduction formula).

items.title: Group 1: Rewrite first
items.text:
Example 8.6.21: Expand and split

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{\left(\sqrt x+3\right)^2}x\,dx\) on \(x>0\).

Solution. Expand the square: \(\left(\sqrt x+3\right)^2=x+6\sqrt x+9\). Divide each term by \(x\) (a numerator may be split): \(\frac{x}x+\frac{6\sqrt x}x+\frac9x=1+6x^{-1/2}+\frac9x\). Integrate each term with the power rule and \(\int\frac{dx}x=\ln x\) (for \(x>0\)):

\[\int\left(1+6x^{-1/2}+\frac9x\right)dx=x+6\cdot\frac{x^{1/2}}{1/2}+9\ln x+C=x+12\sqrt x+9\ln x+C .\]

Check. \(\frac d{dx}\left(x+12\sqrt x+9\ln x\right)=1+\frac6{\sqrt x}+\frac9x=\frac{x+6\sqrt x+9}x=\frac{(\sqrt x+3)^2}x\).

Example 8.6.22: Multiply by a conjugate

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{1+\sin x}\) on an interval where \(\cos x\ne0\).

Solution. Nothing in the table fits, but \(1-\sin^2x=\cos^2x\) makes a product of conjugates useful. Multiply the numerator and denominator by \(1-\sin x\):

\[\frac1{1+\sin x}=\frac{1-\sin x}{(1+\sin x)(1-\sin x)}=\frac{1-\sin x}{1-\sin^2x}=\frac{1-\sin x}{\cos^2x}=\sec^2x-\sec x\tan x .\]

Both terms are in the table (formulas (5) and (7)):

\[\int\frac{dx}{1+\sin x}=\tan x-\sec x+C .\]

Check. \(\frac d{dx}(\tan x-\sec x)=\sec^2x-\sec x\tan x=\frac{1-\sin x}{\cos^2x}=\frac{1-\sin x}{(1-\sin x)(1+\sin x)}=\frac1{1+\sin x}\).

items.title: Group 2: Substitution
items.text:
Example 8.6.23: An exponential inside a quadratic

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{e^x}{e^{2x}+4e^x+13}\,dx\).

Solution. All the \(x\) appears in \(e^x\), and \(e^x\,dx\) is there. Let \(u=e^x\), \(du=e^x\,dx\), \(e^{2x}=u^2\):

\[\int\frac{e^x\,dx}{e^{2x}+4e^x+13}=\int\frac{du}{u^2+4u+13} .\]

Complete the square: \(u^2+4u+13=(u+2)^2+9\) (since \(13-4=9>0\), the quadratic has no real root). By formula (11) with \(a=3\) and the shift \(u+2\) (Theorem 8.1.13(i)),

\[\int\frac{du}{(u+2)^2+9}=\frac13\tan^{-1}\frac{u+2}3+C=\frac13\tan^{-1}\frac{e^x+2}3+C .\]

Check. \(\frac d{dx}\frac13\tan^{-1}\frac{e^x+2}3=\frac13\cdot\frac{e^x/3}{1+(e^x+2)^2/9}=\frac{e^x}{9+(e^x+2)^2}=\frac{e^x}{e^{2x}+4e^x+13}\).

Example 8.6.24: Two substitutions in a row

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{\ln(\ln x)}{x\ln x}\,dx\) on \(x>1\).

Solution. The factor \(\frac1x\) is the derivative of \(\ln x\), so let \(u=\ln x\), \(du=\frac{dx}x\) (here \(u>0\)):

\[\int\frac{\ln(\ln x)}{x\ln x}\,dx=\int\frac{\ln u}{u}\,du .\]

Again the derivative of \(\ln u\), which is \(\frac1u\), is present. Let \(w=\ln u\), \(dw=\frac{du}u\):

\[\int\frac{\ln u}u\,du=\int w\,dw=\frac{w^2}2+C=\frac12\left(\ln u\right)^2+C=\frac12\left(\ln\ln x\right)^2+C .\]

Check. \(\frac d{dx}\frac12(\ln\ln x)^2=\ln\ln x\cdot\frac1{\ln x}\cdot\frac1x\).

items.title: Group 3: Products
items.text:
Example 8.6.25: A cyclic integral

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int e^{2x}\cos3x\,dx\).

Solution. Let \(I=\int e^{2x}\cos3x\,dx\) and \(J=\int e^{2x}\sin3x\,dx\). First parts: \(p=\cos3x\), \(dv=e^{2x}dx\), so \(dp=-3\sin3x\,dx\) and \(v=\frac12e^{2x}\):

\[I=\frac12e^{2x}\cos3x+\frac32J .\]

Second parts: \(p=\sin3x\), \(dv=e^{2x}dx\), \(dp=3\cos3x\,dx\), \(v=\frac12e^{2x}\):

\[J=\frac12e^{2x}\sin3x-\frac32I .\]

Substitute \(J\) into the first equation: \(I=\frac12e^{2x}\cos3x+\frac34e^{2x}\sin3x-\frac94I\). Collect the \(I\)’s: \(\frac{13}4I=e^{2x}\left(\frac12\cos3x+\frac34\sin3x\right)\), so

\[\int e^{2x}\cos3x\,dx=\frac{e^{2x}\left(2\cos3x+3\sin3x\right)}{13}+C ,\]

in agreement with Theorem 8.2.12 (\(a=2\), \(b=3\)).

Example 8.6.26: Substitution, then parts

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int x^3e^{-x^2}\,dx\).

Solution. Parts directly would need \(\int x^3\,dx\) times \(e^{-x^2}\) and gets worse. But \(x^3=x^2\cdot x\) and \(x\,dx\) is (up to a factor) the derivative of the exponent. Let \(u=x^2\), \(du=2x\,dx\), \(x^3\,dx=u\cdot\frac{du}2\):

\[\int x^3e^{-x^2}\,dx=\frac12\int ue^{-u}\,du .\]

Now parts with \(p=u\), \(dv=e^{-u}du\), \(dp=du\), \(v=-e^{-u}\): \(\int ue^{-u}\,du=-ue^{-u}+\int e^{-u}\,du=-ue^{-u}-e^{-u}=-(u+1)e^{-u}\). Therefore

\[\int x^3e^{-x^2}\,dx=-\frac12\left(x^2+1\right)e^{-x^2}+C .\]

Check. \(\frac d{dx}\left[-\frac12(x^2+1)e^{-x^2}\right]=-\frac12\left[2xe^{-x^2}-2x(x^2+1)e^{-x^2}\right]=-xe^{-x^2}\left[1-x^2-1\right]=x^3e^{-x^2}\).

items.title: Group 4: Trigonometric integrands
items.text:
Example 8.6.27: An odd power of sine over a power of cosine

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{\sin^3x}{\cos^2x}\,dx\) on an interval where \(\cos x\ne0\).

Solution. The power of sine is odd: save one \(\sin x\) and write \(\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x\). Let \(u=\cos x\), \(du=-\sin x\,dx\):

\[\int\frac{(1-\cos^2x)\sin x}{\cos^2x}\,dx=-\int\frac{1-u^2}{u^2}\,du=-\int\left(u^{-2}-1\right)du=u^{-1}+u+C=\sec x+\cos x+C .\]

Check. \(\frac d{dx}(\sec x+\cos x)=\sec x\tan x-\sin x=\frac{\sin x}{\cos^2x}-\sin x=\frac{\sin x(1-\cos^2x)}{\cos^2x}=\frac{\sin^3x}{\cos^2x}\).

Example 8.6.28: Tangent and secant, odd power of secant

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\tan^3x\sec^3x\,dx\) on an interval where \(\cos x\ne0\).

Solution. The power of tangent is odd, so save \(\sec x\tan x\) (the derivative of \(\sec x\)) and convert the remaining \(\tan^2x=\sec^2x-1\) (Section 8.3):

\[\tan^3x\sec^3x=\left(\sec^2x-1\right)\sec^2x\cdot\sec x\tan x .\]

Let \(u=\sec x\), \(du=\sec x\tan x\,dx\):

\[\int\left(u^2-1\right)u^2\,du=\frac{u^5}5-\frac{u^3}3+C=\frac{\sec^5x}5-\frac{\sec^3x}3+C .\]

Check. \(\frac d{dx}\left(\frac{\sec^5x}5-\frac{\sec^3x}3\right)=\sec^5x\tan x-\sec^3x\tan x=\sec^3x\tan x\left(\sec^2x-1\right)=\sec^3x\tan^3x\).

items.title: Group 5: Roots and quadratics
items.text:
Example 8.6.29: A trigonometric substitution

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^2\sqrt{x^2+9}}\) on \(x\ne0\).

Solution. The root \(\sqrt{x^2+9}\) has the pattern \(\sqrt{a^2+x^2}\) with \(a=3\), and no plain substitution is visible. Let \(x=3\tan\theta\), \(-\frac\pi2<\theta<\frac\pi2\), \(dx=3\sec^2\theta\,d\theta\), \(\sqrt{x^2+9}=3\sec\theta\):

\[\int\frac{3\sec^2\theta\,d\theta}{9\tan^2\theta\cdot3\sec\theta}=\frac19\int\frac{\sec\theta}{\tan^2\theta}\,d\theta=\frac19\int\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta}\,d\theta,\]

since \(\frac{\sec\theta}{\tan^2\theta}=\frac1{\cos\theta}\cdot\frac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta}=\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta}\). With \(w=\sin\theta\), \(dw=\cos\theta\,d\theta\), this is \(\frac19\int w^{-2}\,dw=-\frac1{9\sin\theta}\). By Theorem 8.4.2, \(\sin\theta=\frac x{\sqrt{x^2+9}}\), so

\[\int\frac{dx}{x^2\sqrt{x^2+9}}=-\frac{\sqrt{x^2+9}}{9x}+C\qquad(x\ne0).\]

Check. \(\frac d{dx}\left(-\frac{\sqrt{x^2+9}}{9x}\right)=-\frac19\cdot\frac{\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+9}}\cdot x-\sqrt{x^2+9}}{x^2}=-\frac19\cdot\frac{x^2-(x^2+9)}{x^2\sqrt{x^2+9}}=\frac{1}{x^2\sqrt{x^2+9}}\).

Example 8.6.30: A root, but a plain substitution is better

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int x^3\sqrt{x^2+4}\,dx\).

Solution. The root again has the form \(\sqrt{x^2+a^2}\), but an odd power of \(x\) stands outside, so try \(u=x^2+4\) first: \(du=2x\,dx\), \(x^2=u-4\), \(x^3\,dx=x^2\cdot x\,dx=(u-4)\frac{du}2\):

\[\begin{aligned}\int x^3\sqrt{x^2+4}\,dx&=\frac12\int(u-4)\,u^{1/2}\,du=\frac12\int\left(u^{3/2}-4u^{1/2}\right)du\\&=\frac12\left(\frac25u^{5/2}-\frac83u^{3/2}\right)=\frac{u^{5/2}}5-\frac{4u^{3/2}}3 .\end{aligned}\]

So the integral is \(\frac15\left(x^2+4\right)^{5/2}-\frac43\left(x^2+4\right)^{3/2}+C\). Check. \(\frac d{dx}\left[\frac15u^{5/2}-\frac43u^{3/2}\right]=\left(\frac12u^{3/2}-2u^{1/2}\right)\cdot2x=x\,u^{1/2}(u-4)=x\cdot x^2\sqrt{x^2+4}\).

items.title: Group 6: Rational integrands and roots
items.text:
Example 8.6.31: Substitution beats partial fractions

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{2x^3+3x}{\left(x^2+1\right)^2}\,dx\).

Solution. A repeated irreducible quadratic would need four unknowns. But the numerator is \(x(2x^2+3)\), with a factor \(x\) (an odd power) in front of a function of \(x^2\). Let \(u=x^2+1\), \(du=2x\,dx\), \(x\,dx=\frac{du}2\), \(2x^2+3=2(u-1)+3=2u+1\):

\[\begin{aligned}\int\frac{x(2x^2+3)}{(x^2+1)^2}\,dx&=\int\frac{2u+1}{u^2}\cdot\frac{du}2=\int\left(\frac1u+\frac1{2u^2}\right)du\\&=\ln u-\frac1{2u}+C=\ln\left(x^2+1\right)-\frac1{2(x^2+1)}+C .\end{aligned}\]

Check. \(\frac d{dx}\left[\ln(x^2+1)-\frac1{2(x^2+1)}\right]=\frac{2x}{x^2+1}+\frac{x}{(x^2+1)^2}=\frac{2x(x^2+1)+x}{(x^2+1)^2}=\frac{2x^3+3x}{(x^2+1)^2}\).

Example 8.6.32: Two roots: a sixth-root substitution

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt x+\sqrt[3]x}\) on \(x>0\).

Solution. The roots have indices \(2\) and \(3\), so use the least common multiple \(6\): let \(x=u^6\) with \(u=x^{1/6}>0\). Then \(dx=6u^5\,du\), \(\sqrt x=u^3\) and \(\sqrt[3]x=u^2\):

\[\int\frac{6u^5\,du}{u^3+u^2}=6\int\frac{u^3}{u+1}\,du\qquad\left(\text{cancel }u^2\right).\]

Divide: \(u^3=(u+1)(u^2-u+1)-1\) (check: \((u+1)(u^2-u+1)=u^3+1\)), so \(\frac{u^3}{u+1}=u^2-u+1-\frac1{u+1}\) and

\[6\int\left(u^2-u+1-\frac1{u+1}\right)du=2u^3-3u^2+6u-6\ln(u+1)+C .\]

Back to \(x\): \(u^3=\sqrt x\), \(u^2=\sqrt[3]x\), \(u=x^{1/6}\):

\[\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt x+\sqrt[3]x}=2\sqrt x-3\sqrt[3]x+6\sqrt[6]x-6\ln\left(1+\sqrt[6]x\right)+C .\]

Check at \(x=64\) (\(u=2\)): the integrand is \(\frac1{8+4}=\frac1{12}\). The derivative of the answer is \(\frac{du}{dx}\cdot6\left(u^2-u+1-\frac1{u+1}\right)\) with \(\frac{du}{dx}=\frac1{6u^5}=\frac1{192}\) and \(6\left(4-2+1-\frac13\right)=16\), giving \(\frac{16}{192}=\frac1{12}\).

items.title: Group 7: Proofs
items.text:
Example 8.6.33: A symmetry trick for definite integrals

Prove that if \(f\) is continuous on \([0,a]\), then \(\int_0^af(x)\,dx=\int_0^af(a-x)\,dx\). Use it to evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx\) without finding an antiderivative.

Plan. Substitute \(u=a-x\) in the right-hand integral and use Theorem 8.1.1(2), taking care of the limits and the sign of \(du\).

Proof. Let \(u=g(x)=a-x\); \(g\) has the continuous derivative \(g'(x)=-1\). The function \(u\mapsto f(u)\) is continuous on \([0,a]\), which contains \(g([0,a])\). By Theorem 8.1.1(2),

\[\int_0^af(a-x)\,dx=-\int_0^af(g(x))\,g'(x)\,dx=-\int_{g(0)}^{g(a)}f(u)\,du=-\int_a^0f(u)\,du=\int_0^af(u)\,du .\]

The last step reverses the limits, which changes the sign; the name of the variable does not matter. \(\blacksquare\)

Common mistake: forgetting the minus sign from \(g'(x)=-1\), or keeping the old limits \(0\) and \(a\) after the substitution (they become \(a\) and \(0\)).

Application. Let \(I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx\) and take \(a=\frac\pi2\), \(f(x)=\frac{\sin x}{\sin x+\cos x}\). Since \(\sin\left(\frac\pi2-x\right)=\cos x\) and \(\cos\left(\frac\pi2-x\right)=\sin x\), we have \(f\left(\frac\pi2-x\right)=\frac{\cos x}{\cos x+\sin x}\), so \(I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx\). Add the two expressions for \(I\): \(2I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin x+\cos x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx=\int_0^{\pi/2}1\,dx=\frac\pi2\). Therefore \(I=\frac\pi4\), the value found in Example 8.6.14.

Example 8.6.34: A reduction formula for \(\int(\ln x)^n\,dx\)

Prove that for \(x>0\) and every integer \(n\ge1\), with \(I_n=\int(\ln x)^n\,dx\),

\[I_n=x(\ln x)^n-n\,I_{n-1},\qquad I_0=x+C .\]

Then find \(\displaystyle\int(\ln x)^3\,dx\).

Plan. Parts with \(p=(\ln x)^n\) and \(dv=dx\), as for \(\ln x\) itself in Section 8.2.

Proof. Let \(p=(\ln x)^n\) and \(dv=dx\); then \(dp=n(\ln x)^{n-1}\cdot\frac1x\,dx\) (Chain Rule) and \(v=x\). The parts formula gives

\[I_n=x(\ln x)^n-\int x\cdot n(\ln x)^{n-1}\frac1x\,dx=x(\ln x)^n-n\int(\ln x)^{n-1}\,dx=x(\ln x)^n-nI_{n-1}.\]

\(I_0=\int1\,dx=x+C\). \(\blacksquare\)

Common mistake: the factor \(x\) from \(v\) cancels the \(\frac1x\) in \(dp\); students sometimes lose the factor \(n\) from the Chain Rule.

Application, \(n=3\). \(I_1=x\ln x-I_0=x\ln x-x\). \(I_2=x(\ln x)^2-2I_1=x(\ln x)^2-2x\ln x+2x\). \(I_3=x(\ln x)^3-3I_2\), so

\[\int(\ln x)^3\,dx=x(\ln x)^3-3x(\ln x)^2+6x\ln x-6x+C .\]

items.title: Answers and discussion
items.text:
Knowledge Check 8.6.1. (a) Substitution \(u=x^3\): \(x^2\,dx=\frac13\,du\), giving \(\frac13e^{x^3}+C\) (no parts needed). (b) Parts with \(p=x\), \(dv=e^{3x}dx\): \(\frac x3e^{3x}-\frac13\int e^{3x}dx=\left(\frac x3-\frac19\right)e^{3x}+C\). (c) The numerator is half the derivative of the denominator (\(\frac12(2x+2)=x+1\)), so \(u=x^2+2x+5\) gives \(\frac12\ln\left(x^2+2x+5\right)+C\); no trigonometric substitution or partial fractions. (d) The root \(\sqrt{x^2+9}\) has the form \(\sqrt{a^2+x^2}\) and no plain substitution is visible, so a trigonometric substitution \(x=3\tan\theta\) (Example 8.6.29).

Knowledge Check 8.6.2. (a) \(u=\sqrt{3x+2}\), \(x=\frac{u^2-2}3\), \(dx=\frac{2u}3\,du\), giving \(\int\frac{2u}{3(1+u)}\,du\). (b) \(u=e^x\), \(dx=\frac{du}u\), giving \(\int\frac{u^2}{u+1}\cdot\frac1u\,du=\int\frac u{u+1}\,du\). (c) The roots have indices \(2\) and \(3\); use \(x=u^6\), \(dx=6u^5\,du\), \(\sqrt x=u^3\), \(\sqrt[3]x=u^2\), giving \(\int\frac{u^3}{1+u^2}\cdot6u^5\,du=\int\frac{6u^8}{1+u^2}\,du\), an improper rational function.

Knowledge Check 8.6.3. (a) Yes: \(u=x^2\) gives \(\frac12e^{x^2}+C\) (the derivative of the exponent is present). (b) No: Theorem 8.6.18. (c) Yes: \(u=\sin x\) gives \(e^{\sin x}+C\) (again the derivative of the exponent, \(\cos x\), is present). (d) No: Theorem 8.6.18, which rests on Theorem 8.6.17(b) and the quoted Theorem 8.6.16.

items.title: 8.7 Other Methods of Integration
items.text:
Download the PDF version

Guiding question

In practice an integral is often not done by hand at all: it is looked up in a table of integrals, or typed into a computer algebra system. Both are legitimate and fast, and both can mislead a careless user. A table lists a formula only for a particular form, with conditions on the constants; a computer algebra system prints a formula that may differ from yours by a constant, may omit absolute values, and may be wrong at one point of the interval you care about. This section teaches how to use these tools and how to trust them: how to match an integral to a table entry, how to prepare it by a substitution, by completing the square or by a reduction formula, how to compare two answers that look different, and why a definite integral computed from a formula needs a second look when the formula has a break. Every table entry that we use is proved by differentiation, and every computer result in the examples is checked the same way.

By the end of this section you should be able to:

  • match an integral to the form of a table entry, read off the constants, and check the conditions under which the entry holds;

  • prepare an integral for a table by a substitution, by completing the square, or by one or more steps of a reduction formula;

  • decide whether your answer and the answer of a table or a computer algebra system are the same, and find the constant by which they differ;

  • read the output of a computer algebra system critically: a missing constant, a missing absolute value, a formula valid on only part of the interval, a form that is undefined at a point where the integrand is fine;

  • evaluate a definite integral from a formula whose graph has a jump (Theorem 8.7.14), and recognize a definite integral that cannot be evaluated by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus at all;

  • say plainly that a table entry or a computer result is a claim and not a proof, and check it by differentiating.

items.title: Three families of methods
items.text:
Sections 8.1 to 8.5 were analytical methods: pencil-and-paper manipulations that end in a formula. This section adds two more ways of reaching a formula, and a third kind of answer.

Method What you get What can go wrong by hand (8.1–8.5) a formula an algebra or sign error table of integrals a formula, for a standard form the wrong match of constants; a condition missed; a misprint computer algebra a formula, a special function, or nothing a missing constant or absolute value; a formula with a break; a different form that you do not recognize numerical integration a number (for a definite integral) no formula at all; an error that must be bounded

A table and a computer algebra system are both ways of finding a candidate \(F\). They differ from the methods of the earlier sections only in that someone else did the work. The next section takes up numerical integration; Calculus I and the earlier sections are all that is needed here.

A table or a computer result is not a proof

Looking up an integral, or asking a program, produces a claim: “\(F\) is an antiderivative of \(f\) on this interval”. The claim becomes a fact when you differentiate \(F\) and obtain \(f\) (Theorem 8.6.2(1)). A table is written by people and may contain a misprint, may state its conditions in a footnote, or may be copied with a constant interchanged; a program may print a form valid on only part of the domain. In this section every table entry is proved by differentiation (Theorem 8.7.1), and every integral in an example, whatever its source, is checked by differentiating the answer. Where a definite integral comes from a formula, we also check that the formula is continuous on the interval (Theorem 8.7.14) and that the number has the right sign and size.

items.title: A table of integrals
items.text:
A table of integrals is a list of formulas \(\int f(x)\,dx=F(x)+C\), grouped by the form of \(f\): roots of a linear function, roots of \(x^2\pm a^2\), trigonometric functions of a linear argument, products of a power and an exponential or a sine, and so on. Large tables have hundreds of entries; we use a small one. Together with the basic formulas of Section 8.1 (formulas (1)–(17)), the inverse-trigonometric and logarithmic integrals of Sections 8.2 and 8.4, and the reduction formulas of Sections 8.2, 8.3, 8.4 and 8.6, it is enough for every example here. The letters \(a\) and \(b\) are constants, and each entry holds on every interval on which both sides are defined.

Theorem 8.7.1: A short table of integrals

Write \(s=\sqrt{ax+b}\) in (T1)–(T4) and \(s=\sqrt{x^2+a^2}\) in (T6), (T7). Then

  1. \(\displaystyle\int rac{x}{ax+b}\,dx= rac xa- rac b{a^2}\ln\lvert ax+b vert+C\), where \(a e0\);

  2. \(\displaystyle\int rac{x}{\sqrt{ax+b}}\,dx= rac{2(ax-2b)}{3a^2}\,\sqrt{ax+b}+C\), where \(a e0\) and \(ax+b>0\);

  3. \(\displaystyle\int rac{dx}{x\sqrt{ax+b}}= rac1{\sqrt b}\ln\left\lvert rac{s-\sqrt b}{s+\sqrt b} ight vert+C\), where \(b>0\), \(x e0\) and \(ax+b>0\);

  4. \(\displaystyle\int rac{dx}{x\sqrt{ax+b}}= rac2{\sqrt{-b}} an^{-1} rac{s}{\sqrt{-b}}+C\), where \(b<0\) and \(ax+b>0\);

  5. \(\displaystyle\int rac{dx}{1+\sin ax}=- rac1a an\left( rac\pi4- rac{ax}2 ight)+C\), where \(a e0\), on any interval on which \(\sin ax e-1\);

  6. \(\displaystyle\int\sqrt{x^2+a^2}\,dx= rac x2\sqrt{x^2+a^2}+ rac{a^2}2\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+a^2} ight)+C\), where \(a>0\);

  7. \(\displaystyle\int rac{dx}{x\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}=- rac1a\ln rac{a+\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}{\lvert x vert}+C\), where \(a>0\) and \(x e0\).

Proof. In each case we differentiate the right side and obtain the integrand, which proves the entry (Theorem 8.6.2(1)).

(T1) By the Chain Rule, \( rac d{dx}\ln\lvert ax+b vert= rac a{ax+b}\), so

\[ rac d{dx}\left[ rac xa- rac b{a^2}\ln\lvert ax+b vert ight]= rac1a- rac b{a(ax+b)}= rac{(ax+b)-b}{a(ax+b)}= rac x{ax+b}.\]

(T2) Here \(s=\sqrt{ax+b}\), \(s^2=ax+b\) and \(s'= rac a{2s}\). By the Product Rule,

\[ rac d{dx}\left[ rac{2(ax-2b)}{3a^2}\,s ight]= rac{2a}{3a^2}\,s+ rac{2(ax-2b)}{3a^2}\cdot rac a{2s}= rac{2s^2+(ax-2b)}{3as}= rac{2(ax+b)+ax-2b}{3as}= rac{3ax}{3as}= rac xs.\]

(T3) Let \(b>0\). Since \(s^2=ax+b\), we have \(s^2-b=ax\) and \(x e0\) means \(s e\sqrt b\). Also \(s+\sqrt b>0\). For the logarithm of a quotient, \(\ln\left\lvert rac{s-\sqrt b}{s+\sqrt b} ight vert=\ln\lvert s-\sqrt b vert-\ln(s+\sqrt b)\), and \( rac d{dx}\ln\lvert w vert= rac{w'}w\) for \(w e0\) of either sign (Section 8.1). With \(s'= rac a{2s}\),

\[ rac d{dx}\ln\left\lvert rac{s-\sqrt b}{s+\sqrt b} ight vert= rac{s'}{s-\sqrt b}- rac{s'}{s+\sqrt b}=s'\cdot rac{2\sqrt b}{s^2-b}= rac a{2s}\cdot rac{2\sqrt b}{ax}= rac{\sqrt b}{xs}.\]

Multiplying by \( rac1{\sqrt b}\) gives \( rac1{xs}\).

(T4) Let \(b<0\) and \( eta=\sqrt{-b}>0\), so \(s^2=ax- eta^2\); \(ax+b>0\) gives \(ax> eta^2>0\), so \(x e0\) and \(s^2+ eta^2=ax\). By the Chain Rule and \( rac d{du} an^{-1}u= rac1{1+u^2}\),

\[ rac d{dx} an^{-1} rac s eta= rac1{1+s^2/ eta^2}\cdot rac{s'} eta= rac{ eta^2}{ eta^2+s^2}\cdot rac{a}{2s eta}= rac{ eta a}{2s\cdot ax}= rac eta{2xs}.\]

Multiplying by \( rac2 eta\) gives \( rac1{xs}\).

(T5) The identity \(\cos^2\phi= rac{1+\cos2\phi}2\) (Theorem 8.3.1(3)) with \(2\phi= rac\pi2-ax\) and \(\cos\left( rac\pi2-ax ight)=\sin ax\) gives \(1+\sin ax=2\cos^2\left( rac\pi4- rac{ax}2 ight)\). This is \(0\) exactly when \(\cos\left( rac\pi4- rac{ax}2 ight)=0\), so on an interval where \(\sin ax e-1\) the tangent is defined, and

\[ rac d{dx}\left[- rac1a an\left( rac\pi4- rac{ax}2 ight) ight]=- rac1a\sec^2\left( rac\pi4- rac{ax}2 ight)\cdot\left(- rac a2 ight)= rac1{2\cos^2\left( rac\pi4- rac{ax}2 ight)}= rac1{1+\sin ax}.\]

(T6) Let \(s=\sqrt{x^2+a^2}\), so \(s^2=x^2+a^2\), \(s'= rac xs\) and \(s>\lvert x vert\), hence \(x+s>0\). By the Product Rule \( rac d{dx}\left( rac x2s ight)= rac s2+ rac{x^2}{2s}\), and \( rac d{dx}\ln(x+s)= rac{1+x/s}{x+s}= rac{(s+x)/s}{x+s}= rac1s\). Therefore

\[ rac d{dx}\left[ rac x2s+ rac{a^2}2\ln(x+s) ight]= rac s2+ rac{x^2}{2s}+ rac{a^2}{2s}= rac{s^2+x^2+a^2}{2s}= rac{2s^2}{2s}=s.\]

(T7) With \(s=\sqrt{x^2+a^2}\) again, \(a+s>0\), so \(\ln rac{a+s}{\lvert x vert}=\ln(a+s)-\ln\lvert x vert\) and

\[ rac d{dx}\left[\ln(a+s)-\ln\lvert x vert ight]= rac{x/s}{a+s}- rac1x= rac{x^2-s(a+s)}{xs(a+s)}= rac{x^2-as-s^2}{xs(a+s)}= rac{-a^2-as}{xs(a+s)}=- rac a{xs},\]

because \(x^2-s^2=-a^2\). Multiplying by \(- rac1a\) gives \( rac1{xs}\). ◻ ∎

Pause and think 8.7.1: Why differentiate a table?

A table of integrals is produced by people who evaluated the integrals analytically, so its entries are “exact”. Why, then, do we insist on differentiating an entry before relying on it? What does the check cost, compared with the cost of an error?

Answer and discussion

Analytical evaluation is done by people, and people make slips: a misprint in the table, an interchanged sign, the wrong entry when two entries differ by the sign of a constant (as (T3) and (T4) do), a condition (\(b>0\), \(x>0\), \(a e0\)) that was overlooked, or a mistake in your own copying of the constants. Differentiating takes one line, using rules you already know, and settles the question for this integrand on this interval; an undetected error propagates into every later use of the result, such as a volume, a probability or a bridge load. So the check is cheap and the error is expensive.

The seven entries are typical. (T1) and (T2) are integrals of \(x\) over a linear function or over its square root; (T3) and (T4) are the same integrand \( rac1{x\sqrt{ax+b}}\) but with different answers depending on the sign of \(b\), which is why a table states a condition; (T5) is a trigonometric form; (T6) and (T7) involve a root of \(x^2+a^2\). Notice that (T5) holds only where \(\sin ax e-1\), and that (T3) has a restriction \(x e0\): the conditions are part of the entry.

Procedure 8.7.2: Using a table of integrals

  1. Find the form. Classify the integrand: root of a linear function, root of \(x^2\pm a^2\), trigonometric function of a linear argument, power times exponential, sine or cosine, and so on. Look for that form.

  2. Match the constants literally: write the integrand next to the entry and read off \(a\), \(b\), \(n\). Check the conditions (sign of \(b\), \(a>0\), the interval). If the signs differ from the entry, there may be another entry (for instance (T3) and (T4)) or the entry may not apply.

  3. If no entry matches, prepare the integral: a substitution \(u=g(x)\) so that the integrand becomes \(f(u)\,du\) (Theorem 8.1.1); completing the square when \(ax^2+bx+c\) occurs (Theorem 8.7.5); a rewrite from Procedure 8.1.9; or, for powers, a reduction formula, used repeatedly until the exponent reaches the base case (Theorem 8.7.7 and the reduction formulas of Sections 8.2 to 8.6).

  4. Return to the original variable.

  5. Check by differentiating. For a definite integral, check that the formula is defined and continuous on the whole interval (Theorem 8.7.14) and compare with a rough estimate.

items.title: Fitting an integral to a table entry
items.text:
Example 8.7.3: Matching the constants

Evaluate (a) \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x\sqrt{5x-4}}\) for \(x>\frac45\); (b) \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x\,dx}{\sqrt{4-3x}}\) for \(x<\frac43\), and find \(\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{x\,dx}{\sqrt{4-3x}}\).

Solution. (a) The integrand is \(\frac1{x\sqrt{ax+b}}\) with \(ax+b=5x-4\), so \(a=5\) and \(b=-4\). Because \(b<0\), the matching entry is (T4), not (T3) (which needs \(b>0\) and would require \(\sqrt{-4}\)). With \(\sqrt{-b}=2\),

\[\int\frac{dx}{x\sqrt{5x-4}}=\frac2{2}\tan^{-1}\frac{\sqrt{5x-4}}2+C=\tan^{-1}\frac{\sqrt{5x-4}}2+C .\]

Check. Let \(s=\sqrt{5x-4}\), \(s'=\frac5{2s}\). Then \(\frac d{dx}\tan^{-1}\frac s2=\frac1{1+s^2/4}\cdot\frac{s'}2=\frac4{4+s^2}\cdot\frac5{4s}=\frac5{5x\,s}=\frac1{xs}\), because \(4+s^2=5x\).

(b) The integrand is \(\frac x{\sqrt{ax+b}}\) with \(a=-3\) and \(b=4\), and \(ax+b=4-3x>0\) for \(x<\frac43\): entry (T2). Then \(\frac{2(ax-2b)}{3a^2}=\frac{2(-3x-8)}{27}=-\frac{2(3x+8)}{27}\), so

\[\int\frac{x\,dx}{\sqrt{4-3x}}=-\frac{2(3x+8)}{27}\sqrt{4-3x}+C .\]

Check. With \(s=\sqrt{4-3x}\), \(s'=-\frac3{2s}\) and \(s^2=4-3x\): \(\frac d{dx}\left[-\frac2{27}(3x+8)s\right]=-\frac2{27}\left[3s-\frac{3(3x+8)}{2s}\right]=-\frac2{27}\cdot\frac{6s^2-9x-24}{2s}=-\frac2{27}\cdot\frac{24-18x-9x-24}{2s}=\frac{x}{s}\).

The definite integral. The integrand is defined and continuous on \([0,1]\) (as \(4-3x\ge1\)), and the antiderivative is too, so by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

\[\int_0^1\frac{x\,dx}{\sqrt{4-3x}}=\left[-\frac{2(3x+8)}{27}\sqrt{4-3x}\right]_0^1=-\frac{2\cdot11}{27}\cdot1+\frac{2\cdot8}{27}\cdot2=\frac{-22+32}{27}=\frac{10}{27}\approx0.370 .\]

Rough check. The integrand is \(0\) at \(x=0\), \(\frac{0.5}{\sqrt{2.5}}\approx0.32\) at \(x=\frac12\) and \(1\) at \(x=1\), so an average near \(0.37\) on an interval of length \(1\) is reasonable.

Knowledge Check 8.7.1: Which entry?

For each integral, name the entry of Theorem 8.7.1 that fits and the values of \(a\) and \(b\) (do not integrate): (a) \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x\sqrt{3x+8}}\); (b) \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x\sqrt{3x-8}}\); (c) \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x\,dx}{\sqrt{2-7x}}\).

Example 8.7.4: A substitution to reach the table

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1+e^{2x}}}\).

Solution. No entry contains \(e^{2x}\), but \(x\) appears only through \(e^x\), so put \(u=e^x\) (Section 8.6, Theorem 8.6.9): \(du=e^x\,dx\), so \(dx=\frac{du}u\), and \(e^{2x}=u^2\). Then

\[\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1+e^{2x}}}=\int\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+u^2}}\cdot\frac{du}u=\int\frac{du}{u\sqrt{u^2+1}} .\]

This is entry (T7) with \(a=1\) (and \(u>0\), so \(\lvert u\rvert=u\)):

\[\int\frac{du}{u\sqrt{u^2+1}}=-\ln\frac{1+\sqrt{u^2+1}}{u}+C=-\ln\left(1+\sqrt{u^2+1}\right)+\ln u+C .\]

Replace \(u\) by \(e^x\), so \(\ln u=x\) and \(u^2+1=e^{2x}+1\):

\[\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1+e^{2x}}}=x-\ln\left(1+\sqrt{1+e^{2x}}\right)+C .\]

Check. Let \(s=\sqrt{1+e^{2x}}\), so \(s'=\frac{e^{2x}}s\) and \(s^2-1=e^{2x}\). Then \(\frac d{dx}\ln(1+s)=\frac{s'}{1+s}=\frac{s^2-1}{s(1+s)}=\frac{(s-1)(s+1)}{s(1+s)}=\frac{s-1}s\), so the derivative of the answer is \(1-\frac{s-1}s=\frac1s\), the integrand.

The next entry usually needed is a root of a quadratic. A table lists \(\sqrt{x^2\pm a^2}\) and \(\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\); a general quadratic \(ax^2+bx+c\) is brought to that form by completing the square, which we state once and prove.

Theorem 8.7.5: Completing the square

For constants \(a\ne0\), \(b\), \(c\) and all \(x\),

\[ax^2+bx+c=a\left(x+\frac b{2a}\right)^2+\frac{4ac-b^2}{4a}.\]

Consequently, with \(u=x+\frac b{2a}\) (so \(du=dx\)), an integrand containing \(ax^2+bx+c\) becomes one containing \(au^2+k\), where \(k=\frac{4ac-b^2}{4a}\).

Proof. Expand the right side: \(a\left(x^2+\frac bax+\frac{b^2}{4a^2}\right)+\frac{4ac-b^2}{4a}=ax^2+bx+\frac{b^2}{4a}+c-\frac{b^2}{4a}=ax^2+bx+c\). The substitution \(u=x+\frac b{2a}\) has \(du=dx\) (Theorem 8.1.1). \(\blacksquare\) ◻ ∎

Example 8.7.6: Complete the square, substitute, use the table

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\sqrt{x^2+6x+13}\,dx\).

Solution. No entry has \(x^2+6x+13\) under the root, so complete the square (Theorem 8.7.5 with \(a=1\), \(b=6\), \(c=13\)): \(x^2+6x+13=(x+3)^2+4\). Put \(u=x+3\), \(du=dx\):

\[\int\sqrt{x^2+6x+13}\,dx=\int\sqrt{u^2+2^2}\,du .\]

This is entry (T6) with \(a=2\), so

\[\int\sqrt{u^2+4}\,du=\frac u2\sqrt{u^2+4}+2\ln\left(u+\sqrt{u^2+4}\right)+C .\]

Return to \(x\) with \(u=x+3\) and \(u^2+4=x^2+6x+13\):

\[\int\sqrt{x^2+6x+13}\,dx=\frac{x+3}2\sqrt{x^2+6x+13}+2\ln\left(x+3+\sqrt{x^2+6x+13}\right)+C .\]

Check. The entry (T6) was proved by differentiation, and the Chain Rule with \(\frac{du}{dx}=1\) transfers it to \(x\); numerically at \(x=0\), the derivative of the answer is \(\sqrt{13}\approx3.606\), the value of the integrand.

Another form. A computer algebra system may print \(2\sinh^{-1}\frac{x+3}2\) for the logarithm. Since \(\sinh^{-1}w=\ln\left(w+\sqrt{w^2+1}\right)\) (Example 8.7.27), \(2\sinh^{-1}\frac{x+3}2=2\ln\frac{x+3+\sqrt{x^2+6x+13}}2=2\ln\left(x+3+\sqrt{x^2+6x+13}\right)-2\ln2\): the same answer with a different constant.

A reduction formula does not give the answer in one step; it replaces an integral with a power \(n\) by a similar integral with \(n-1\), and it is used repeatedly until the base case is reached. We met such formulas in Sections 8.2, 8.3, 8.4 and 8.6 (for \(\sin^nx\) and \(\cos^nx\), \(\tan^nx\) and \(\sec^nx\), \((x^2+a^2)^{-n}\) and \((\ln x)^n\)). Tables list many more; here is the one needed for polynomials times sines and cosines.

Theorem 8.7.7: Reduction formulas for \(x^n\sin ax\) and \(x^n\cos ax\)

For \(a\ne0\) and every integer \(n\ge1\),

\[\int x^n\sin ax\,dx=-\frac{x^n\cos ax}a+\frac na\int x^{n-1}\cos ax\,dx,\] \[\int x^n\cos ax\,dx=\frac{x^n\sin ax}a-\frac na\int x^{n-1}\sin ax\,dx .\]

The base cases are \(\int\sin ax\,dx=-\frac{\cos ax}a\) and \(\int\cos ax\,dx=\frac{\sin ax}a\) (formulas (3), (4) of Section 8.1).

Proof. Integrate by parts (Theorem 8.2.1). For the first formula let \(p=x^n\) and \(dv=\sin ax\,dx\), so \(dp=nx^{n-1}\,dx\) and \(v=-\frac{\cos ax}a\):

\[\int x^n\sin ax\,dx=-\frac{x^n\cos ax}a-\int\left(-\frac{\cos ax}a\right)nx^{n-1}\,dx=-\frac{x^n\cos ax}a+\frac na\int x^{n-1}\cos ax\,dx.\]

For the second let \(p=x^n\) and \(dv=\cos ax\,dx\), so \(v=\frac{\sin ax}a\) and the same steps give \(\frac{x^n\sin ax}a-\frac na\int x^{n-1}\sin ax\,dx\). \(\blacksquare\) ◻ ∎

Example 8.7.8: A reduction formula used three times

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int x^3\sin2x\,dx\).

Solution. The formulas alternate between sine and cosine and lower the power of \(x\) by one each time (Theorem 8.7.7 with \(a=2\)). We write \(J_n=\int x^n\sin2x\,dx\) and \(K_n=\int x^n\cos2x\,dx\).

\[\begin{aligned} J_3&=-\frac{x^3\cos2x}2+\frac32K_2, &\text{(first formula, $n=3$)}\\ K_2&=\frac{x^2\sin2x}2-\frac22J_1=\frac{x^2\sin2x}2-J_1, &\text{(second formula, $n=2$)}\\ J_1&=-\frac{x\cos2x}2+\frac12K_0=-\frac{x\cos2x}2+\frac{\sin2x}4. &\text{(first formula, $n=1$)} \end{aligned}\]

Here \(K_0=\int\cos2x\,dx=\frac{\sin2x}2\) is the base case. Substitute from the bottom up. First \(K_2=\frac{x^2\sin2x}2+\frac{x\cos2x}2-\frac{\sin2x}4\). Then

\[\begin{aligned}J_3&=-\frac{x^3\cos2x}2+\frac32\left(\frac{x^2\sin2x}2+\frac{x\cos2x}2-\frac{\sin2x}4\right)\\&=-\frac{x^3\cos2x}2+\frac{3x^2\sin2x}4+\frac{3x\cos2x}4-\frac{3\sin2x}8 .\end{aligned}\]

So \(\displaystyle\int x^3\sin2x\,dx=-\frac{x^3\cos2x}2+\frac{3x^2\sin2x}4+\frac{3x\cos2x}4-\frac{3\sin2x}8+C\). Check by the tabular method (Theorem 8.2.14). Differentiate \(x^3\) repeatedly (\(x^3,3x^2,6x,6,0\)) and integrate \(\sin2x\) repeatedly (\(-\frac{\cos2x}2,-\frac{\sin2x}4,\frac{\cos2x}8,\frac{\sin2x}{16}\)), with alternating signs \(+,-,+,-\):

\[\begin{aligned}&x^3\left(-\frac{\cos2x}2\right)-3x^2\left(-\frac{\sin2x}4\right)+6x\left(\frac{\cos2x}8\right)-6\left(\frac{\sin2x}{16}\right)\\&\quad=-\frac{x^3\cos2x}2+\frac{3x^2\sin2x}4+\frac{3x\cos2x}4-\frac{3\sin2x}8,\end{aligned}\]

the same function. Check by differentiating. Term by term, \(\frac d{dx}\left(-\frac{x^3\cos2x}2\right)=-\frac{3x^2\cos2x}2+x^3\sin2x\); \(\frac d{dx}\frac{3x^2\sin2x}4=\frac{3x\sin2x}2+\frac{3x^2\cos2x}2\); \(\frac d{dx}\frac{3x\cos2x}4=\frac{3\cos2x}4-\frac{3x\sin2x}2\); \(\frac d{dx}\left(-\frac{3\sin2x}8\right)=-\frac{3\cos2x}4\). In the sum, every term cancels except \(x^3\sin2x\).

items.title: When the table’s answer is not your answer
items.text:
Two people who integrate the same function may print different formulas, and so may two tables or two programs. By Theorem 8.6.2(2), if both are antiderivatives on the same interval their difference is constant on that interval. The constant is easy to find (evaluate the difference at one point) and is usually nonzero; it vanishes from every definite integral.

Example 8.7.9: A table form and a computer form that differ by a constant

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{dx}{1+\sin2x}\) with the table, and compare the table’s antiderivative with the one printed by a computer algebra system.

Solution. Entry (T5) with \(a=2\) gives \(F_T(x)=-\frac12\tan\left(\frac\pi4-x\right)\), valid where \(\sin2x\ne-1\). On \([0,\frac\pi2]\) we have \(2x\in[0,\pi]\) and \(\sin2x\ge0\), so \(F_T\) and the integrand are continuous on the whole interval. Then \(F_T\left(\frac\pi2\right)=-\frac12\tan\left(-\frac\pi4\right)=\frac12\) and \(F_T(0)=-\frac12\tan\frac\pi4=-\frac12\), so

\[\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{dx}{1+\sin2x}=\frac12-\left(-\frac12\right)=1 .\]

Rough check. The integrand is \(1\) at \(x=0\) and at \(x=\frac\pi2\) and \(\frac12\) at \(x=\frac\pi4\), so it lies between \(\frac12\) and \(1\) on an interval of length \(\frac\pi2\approx1.57\): the integral lies between \(0.79\) and \(1.57\), and \(1\) does.

The computer’s form. SymPy 1.14 prints \(F_C(x)=-\dfrac1{\tan x+1}\). To check it we differentiate, using \(\frac d{dx}\tan x=\sec^2x\):

\[\begin{aligned}F_C'(x)&=\frac{\sec^2x}{(1+\tan x)^2}=\frac{1/\cos^2x}{(\cos x+\sin x)^2/\cos^2x}\\&=\frac1{(\cos x+\sin x)^2}=\frac1{1+2\sin x\cos x}=\frac1{1+\sin2x}.\end{aligned}\]

So both are antiderivatives. They must differ by a constant, and we can find it exactly. From the angle-subtraction formulas, \(\sin\left(\frac\pi4-x\right)=\frac{\sqrt2}2(\cos x-\sin x)\) and \(\cos\left(\frac\pi4-x\right)=\frac{\sqrt2}2(\cos x+\sin x)\); dividing and then dividing top and bottom by \(\cos x\),

\[\tan\left(\frac\pi4-x\right)=\frac{\cos x-\sin x}{\cos x+\sin x}=\frac{1-\tan x}{1+\tan x},\] \[F_T=-\frac12\cdot\frac{1-\tan x}{1+\tan x}=\frac12\cdot\frac{(\tan x+1)-2}{\tan x+1}=\frac12-\frac1{\tan x+1}=\frac12+F_C .\]

The two forms differ by \(\frac12\) (Figure 1(a)), and the constant cancels in \(F(b)-F(a)\). One more point: \(F_C\) is undefined at \(x=\frac\pi2\) because \(\tan\frac\pi2\) is, although the integrand is perfectly continuous there. As \(x\to\frac\pi2^-\), \(\tan x\to\infty\) and \(F_C\to0\), so the break is removable: with \(F_C\left(\frac\pi2\right):=0\) we get \(F_C\left(\frac\pi2\right)-F_C(0)=0-(-1)=1\) again (Theorem 8.7.14(1) below).

Figure 1. (a) \(F_T=-\frac12\tan\left(\frac\pi4-x\right)\) (blue) and \(F_C=-\frac1{\tan x+1}\) (red): the same shape, a constant vertical distance \(\frac12\) apart. (b) \(\tan^{-1}x\) (blue) and \(-\tan^{-1}\frac1x\) (red, undefined at \(x=0\)): the red curve lies \(\frac\pi2\) below the blue one for \(x>0\) and \(\frac\pi2\) above it for \(x<0\).

Example 8.7.10: A constant that changes from one interval to the next

Find \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{1+x^2}\) in two ways and compare the answers.

Solution. Way 1. Formula (11) of Section 8.1 with \(a=1\) gives \(F_1(x)=\tan^{-1}x\), an antiderivative on all of \(\mathbb R\).

Way 2. For \(x\ne0\) put \(u=\frac1x\), so \(x=\frac1u\) and \(dx=-\frac{du}{u^2}\), and \(1+x^2=1+\frac1{u^2}=\frac{u^2+1}{u^2}\). Then

\[\int\frac{dx}{1+x^2}=\int\frac{u^2}{u^2+1}\cdot\left(-\frac{du}{u^2}\right)=-\int\frac{du}{1+u^2}=-\tan^{-1}u+C=-\tan^{-1}\frac1x+C .\]

So \(F_2(x)=-\tan^{-1}\frac1x\) on \(x>0\) and on \(x<0\). Check: \(\frac d{dx}\left[-\tan^{-1}\frac1x\right]=-\frac1{1+1/x^2}\cdot\left(-\frac1{x^2}\right)=\frac1{x^2+1}\).

Both are right, so how do they differ? By Theorem 8.6.2(2) they differ by a constant on each interval \(x>0\) and \(x<0\). For \(x>0\) let \(\theta=\tan^{-1}x\in\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)\). Then \(\frac\pi2-\theta\in\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)\) and \(\tan\left(\frac\pi2-\theta\right)=\cot\theta=\frac1x\), so \(\tan^{-1}\frac1x=\frac\pi2-\theta\), that is \(\tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}\frac1x=\frac\pi2\) for \(x>0\). Since \(\tan^{-1}\) is an odd function, for \(x<0\) we get \(\tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}\frac1x=-\left[\tan^{-1}(-x)+\tan^{-1}\frac1{-x}\right]=-\frac\pi2\). Hence

\[F_2(x)-F_1(x)=-\left[\tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}\frac1x\right]=\begin{cases}-\frac\pi2,&x>0,\\[2pt]+\frac\pi2,&x<0.\end{cases}\]

The two answers differ by \(-\frac\pi2\) on one side of \(0\) and by \(+\frac\pi2\) on the other (Figure 1(b)). The usual “\(+C\)” stands for one constant per interval on which the integrand is defined, and a formula that is undefined at a point (here \(F_2\) at \(0\)) may carry different constants on the two sides. This is harmless for an indefinite integral on one interval, and dangerous for a definite integral that crosses \(0\): see Example 8.7.15 below.

items.title: Reading computer algebra output
items.text:
Computer algebra systems differ in the form they print, but certain habits recur. They often omit the constant. They may write a logarithm without absolute values, which is correct only for positive arguments. They may print an inverse hyperbolic function, or a special function, where you expect elementary functions. They may produce a formula with a break. Procedure 8.7.11 turns these observations into a routine; the examples that follow use outputs of SymPy 1.14, and other systems differ in form but not in kind.

Procedure 8.7.11: Reading the output of a computer algebra system

  1. Add the constant. An answer to an indefinite integral is \(F(x)+C\), with one constant per interval of the domain (Theorem 8.6.2).

  2. Compare the form. If it differs from yours, subtract, or differentiate both, or evaluate the difference at two points. A nonzero constant difference is fine (Examples 8.7.9 and 8.7.10).

  3. Check the domain. Is each logarithm of a quantity that can be negative? Each root, each \(\tan^{-1}\) of a quotient, each place where a tangent or a denominator is undefined? On which interval is the formula valid? (Example 8.7.12.)

  4. Differentiate. The derivative must be the integrand wherever the formula is defined. This step is the proof.

  5. For a definite integral, test the sign and the size of the answer against the integrand (a positive integrand cannot have a negative integral), look for points of \([a,b]\) where the formula or the integrand is undefined (Theorem 8.7.14, Examples 8.7.13 to 8.7.16), and compare with a numerical value.

  6. If the answer contains a special function or the system returns the integral unevaluated, see Example 8.7.17: the integral may have no elementary antiderivative (Section 8.6), or the system may need a rewrite by hand (Example 8.7.13).

Example 8.7.12: A logarithm without absolute values

A computer algebra system prints \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^2+3x}=\frac13\ln x-\frac13\ln(x+3)\). Is this an antiderivative? On which intervals? Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{-1}\frac{dx}{x^2+3x}\).

Solution. Differentiate (step 4 of Procedure 8.7.11). Wherever the formula is defined, \(\frac d{dx}\left[\frac13\ln x-\frac13\ln(x+3)\right]=\frac13\left(\frac1x-\frac1{x+3}\right)=\frac13\cdot\frac{3}{x(x+3)}=\frac1{x^2+3x}\). So it is an antiderivative, but only where \(\ln x\) and \(\ln(x+3)\) are real numbers, that is for \(x>0\). The integrand is defined on three intervals, \(x<-3\), \(-3<x<0\) and \(x>0\).

The complete answer. The same partial fractions (Section 8.5, \(\frac1{x(x+3)}=\frac13\left(\frac1x-\frac1{x+3}\right)\)) and the rule \(\frac d{dx}\ln\lvert w\rvert=\frac{w'}w\) for \(w\ne0\) of either sign (Section 8.1) give

\[\int\frac{dx}{x^2+3x}=\frac13\ln\lvert x\rvert-\frac13\ln\lvert x+3\rvert+C=\frac13\ln\left\lvert\frac x{x+3}\right\rvert+C,\]

valid on each of the three intervals (with a possibly different \(C\) on each). The definite integral. The interval \([-2,-1]\) lies inside \((-3,0)\), where the integrand \(\frac1{x(x+3)}\) is continuous. The formula with absolute values is continuous there, so

\[\int_{-2}^{-1}\frac{dx}{x^2+3x}=\frac13\left[\ln\left\lvert\frac x{x+3}\right\rvert\right]_{-2}^{-1}=\frac13\left[\ln\frac12-\ln2\right]=-\frac23\ln2\approx-0.462 .\]

Rough check. On \((-3,0)\) the product \(x(x+3)\) is negative, so the integrand and the integral are negative; at \(x=-1.5\) the integrand is \(\frac1{-2.25}\approx-0.44\) and the interval has length \(1\), so about \(-0.46\) is right. The formula without absolute values cannot even be evaluated here: \(\ln(-1)\) and \(\ln(-2)\) are not real numbers.

Example 8.7.13: When the system returns nothing: rewrite by hand

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sqrt{1-\cos x}\,dx\).

Solution. SymPy 1.14 returns this integral unevaluated. A system may fail on a root of a trigonometric expression, so we rewrite by hand (step 6 of Procedure 8.7.11). The power-reducing identity (Theorem 8.3.1(3)) \(\sin^2\frac x2=\frac{1-\cos x}2\) gives \(1-\cos x=2\sin^2\frac x2\), and \(\sqrt{w^2}=\lvert w\rvert\), so

\[\sqrt{1-\cos x}=\sqrt2\,\sqrt{\sin^2\frac x2}=\sqrt2\,\left\lvert\sin\frac x2\right\rvert .\]

The tempting error is \(\sqrt{\sin^2\frac x2}=\sin\frac x2\), which is false when \(\sin\frac x2<0\), that is for \(-\pi\le x<0\). It would give \(\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sqrt2\sin\frac x2\,dx=\left[-2\sqrt2\cos\frac x2\right]_{-\pi}^{\pi}=-2\sqrt2(0-0)=0\), which cannot be right: the integrand is continuous and positive except at \(x=0\), so the integral is positive.

The correct computation. The integrand \(\sqrt2\left\lvert\sin\frac x2\right\rvert\) is an even function, and \(\sin\frac x2\ge0\) on \([0,\pi]\), so

\[\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sqrt{1-\cos x}\,dx=2\int_0^\pi\sqrt2\sin\frac x2\,dx=2\sqrt2\left[-2\cos\frac x2\right]_0^\pi=2\sqrt2\,(0+2)=4\sqrt2\approx5.657 .\]

Rough check. The integrand is \(0\) at \(x=0\), \(1\) at \(x=\pm\frac\pi2\) and \(\sqrt2\approx1.41\) at \(x=\pm\pi\); an average near \(0.9\) over an interval of length \(2\pi\approx6.28\) gives about \(5.7\).

Knowledge Check 8.7.2: Read the output

A program prints \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^2-4}=\frac14\ln(x-2)-\frac14\ln(x+2)\). (a) For which \(x\) is this an antiderivative? (b) What would you write for \(-2<x<2\)?

items.title: Definite integrals and breaks in the formula
items.text:
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says \(\int_a^bf=F(b)-F(a)\) when \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and \(F\) is an antiderivative on all of \([a,b]\). A formula for \(F\) that has a break inside \([a,b]\) is not an antiderivative on \([a,b]\). A break can be removable (the formula is undefined at a point but has a limit, as with \(F_C\) in Example 8.7.9), a jump (the one-sided limits exist but differ), or an infinite one. The theorem says what to do in the first two cases; the third is a different problem (Example 8.7.16).

Theorem 8.7.14: Definite integrals when the formula has breaks

Let \(f\) be continuous on \([a,b]\) and let \(a=c_0<c_1<\dots<c_m<c_{m+1}=b\). Suppose that on each open interval \((c_j,c_{j+1})\) the function \(F\) is differentiable with \(F'=f\), and that the one-sided limits \(F(c_j^+)=\lim_{x\to c_j^+}F(x)\) (for \(j=0,\dots,m\)) and \(F(c_{j+1}^-)=\lim_{x\to c_{j+1}^-}F(x)\) exist as real numbers. Then

\[\int_a^bf(x)\,dx=\sum_{j=0}^{m}\Big[F(c_{j+1}^-)-F(c_j^+)\Big].\]

In particular: (1) if there are no breaks, or each limit \(F(c^-)\) equals \(F(c^+)\) (a removable break), the value is \(F(b^-)-F(a^+)\), that is \(F(b)-F(a)\) with \(F\) defined at the break points by its limits; (2) for a single break at \(c\),

\[\int_a^bf(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a)-\Big[F(c^+)-F(c^-)\Big],\]

so the naive value \(F(b)-F(a)\) is wrong by exactly the jump \(F(c^+)-F(c^-)\).

Proof. Fix \(j\) and numbers \(s<t\) in \((c_j,c_{j+1})\). The function \(f\) is continuous on \([s,t]\) and \(F\) is differentiable on \((s,t)\) and continuous on \([s,t]\) (differentiable at every point of \([s,t]\)), with \(F'=f\), so by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus \(\int_s^tf=F(t)-F(s)\). Let \(M\) be the maximum of \(\lvert f\rvert\) on \([a,b]\) (Extreme Value Theorem). Then \(\left\lvert\int_{c_j}^sf\right\rvert\le M(s-c_j)\to0\) as \(s\to c_j^+\) and \(\left\lvert\int_t^{c_{j+1}}f\right\rvert\le M(c_{j+1}-t)\to0\) as \(t\to c_{j+1}^-\), so \(\int_s^tf\to\int_{c_j}^{c_{j+1}}f\), while \(F(t)-F(s)\to F(c_{j+1}^-)-F(c_j^+)\). Hence \(\int_{c_j}^{c_{j+1}}f=F(c_{j+1}^-)-F(c_j^+)\). Adding over \(j=0,\dots,m\) (additivity of the integral over intervals) gives the formula. For (1), if \(F(c_j^-)=F(c_j^+)\) for \(j=1,\dots,m\) the sum telescopes to \(F(c_{m+1}^-)-F(c_0^+)\). For (2) with \(m=1\), \(c=c_1\): the sum is \(F(c^-)-F(a)+F(b)-F(c^+)=F(b)-F(a)-\big[F(c^+)-F(c^-)\big]\). \(\blacksquare\) ◻ ∎

Example 8.7.15: An antiderivative with a jump

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{dx}{3+\cos x}\).

Solution. The integrand is continuous on \([0,2\pi]\) (\(3+\cos x\ge2\)), so the integral exists. Use the substitution \(t=\tan\frac x2\) of Example 8.5.32 (valid for \(-\pi<x<\pi\); the formulas \(\cos x=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}\) and \(dx=\frac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}\) hold on every interval where \(\tan\frac x2\) is defined). Then \(3+\cos x=\frac{3(1+t^2)+1-t^2}{1+t^2}=\frac{2t^2+4}{1+t^2}\) and

\[\int\frac{dx}{3+\cos x}=\int\frac{1+t^2}{2t^2+4}\cdot\frac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}=\int\frac{dt}{t^2+2}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\tan^{-1}\frac t{\sqrt2}+C .\]

Back to \(x\): \(F(x)=\frac1{\sqrt2}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\tan(x/2)}{\sqrt2}\right)\), an antiderivative on every interval where \(\tan\frac x2\) is defined, that is for \(x\ne\pi\) on \([0,2\pi]\).

The naive evaluation is \(F(2\pi)-F(0)=\frac1{\sqrt2}\tan^{-1}0-\frac1{\sqrt2}\tan^{-1}0=0\). This is impossible: since \(2\le3+\cos x\le4\), the integrand lies between \(\frac14\) and \(\frac12\), so the integral lies between \(\frac{2\pi}4\approx1.57\) and \(\frac{2\pi}2\approx3.14\).

The error. At \(x=\pi\), \(\tan\frac x2\) is undefined. As \(x\to\pi^-\), \(\tan\frac x2\to+\infty\) and \(F\to\frac1{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac\pi2\); as \(x\to\pi^+\), \(\tan\frac x2\to-\infty\) and \(F\to-\frac1{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac\pi2\). So \(F\) has a jump at \(\pi\) (Figure 2): \(F(\pi^+)-F(\pi^-)=-\frac\pi{\sqrt2}\).

The correct evaluation by Theorem 8.7.14(2) with \(c=\pi\):

\[\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{dx}{3+\cos x}=\big[F(\pi^-)-F(0)\big]+\big[F(2\pi)-F(\pi^+)\big]=\frac\pi{2\sqrt2}-0+0+\frac\pi{2\sqrt2}=\frac\pi{\sqrt2}\approx2.221 .\]

This lies between \(1.57\) and \(3.14\), as it must. Equivalently, \(G(x)=F(x)\) for \(x<\pi\) and \(G(x)=F(x)+\frac\pi{\sqrt2}\) for \(x>\pi\) is an antiderivative that is continuous on all of \([0,2\pi]\), with \(G(2\pi)-G(0)=\frac\pi{\sqrt2}\).

Figure 2. \(F(x)=\frac1{\sqrt2}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\tan(x/2)}{\sqrt2}\right)\) (blue) has a jump at \(x=\pi\). Adding \(\frac\pi{\sqrt2}\) to the right branch (red, dashed) gives a continuous antiderivative \(G\); the integral is \(G(2\pi)-G(0)=\frac\pi{\sqrt2}\), not \(F(2\pi)-F(0)=0\).

What a good system does. SymPy 1.14 returns the correct value \(\frac{\sqrt2\,\pi}2=\frac\pi{\sqrt2}\) for this integral, and an antiderivative that contains a term with \(\lfloor\cdot\rfloor\): the term that adds the jump. A program or a hand computation that reports only the formula \(F\) and subtracts \(F(0)\) from \(F(2\pi)\) would give \(0\). The sign and size check is what catches the error.
