Solution. No: at \(x=1\) the series is \(1-1+1-1+\cdots\), whose terms \((-1)^k\) do not tend to \(0\), so it diverges (Divergence Test), and there is no sum for the limit to equal. Numerically, \(f(0.9)=\frac1{1.9}\approx0.526\) and \(f(0.99)=\frac1{1.99}\approx0.5025\) approach \(\frac12\). Abel’s theorem applies only when the series converges at the endpoint; it then says that the limit of \(f\) is the sum.

Example G.3: Abel’s theorem and the alternating harmonic series

Show that \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^{k+1}}k=\ln2\), given that \(\ln(1+x)=\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^{k+1}x^k}k\) for \(\abs x<1\).

Solution. The power series has radius \(1\) and converges at \(x=1\) by the Alternating Series Test (the terms \(\frac1k\) decrease to \(0\)). By Theorem G.1(1), its sum at \(x=1\) equals \(\lim_{x\to1^-}\ln(1+x)=\ln2\), because the logarithm is continuous at \(2\). The convergence is slow: the error after \(n\) terms is at most \(\frac1{n+1}\), and the first ten terms give \(0.6456\) against \(\ln2=0.6931\).

For the second fact, recall that for a real number \(p\) and an integer \(k\ge0\) the binomial coefficient is \(\binom pk=\frac{p(p-1)\cdots(p-k+1)}{k!}\), with \(\binom p0=1\). If \(p\) is a nonnegative integer then \(\binom pk=0\) for \(k>p\) (the factor \(p-p=0\) appears) and \(\sum\binom pkx^k\) is a polynomial. Otherwise no factor is \(0\) and every \(\binom pk\ne0\). Let \(c_k=\binom pk\) and \(u_k=\abs{c_k}\). Multiplying out the definition,

\[(k+1)\,c_{k+1}=(p-k)\,c_k,\qquad\text{so}\qquad(k+1)\,u_{k+1}=\abs{p-k}\,u_k .\tag{$\ast$}\]

We also use \(1-y\le e^{-y}\) for all real \(y\) (the graph of the convex function \(e^{-y}\) lies above its tangent line \(1-y\) at \(y=0\)).

Theorem G.4: The size of the binomial coefficients

Let \(p\) be a real number that is not a nonnegative integer.

  1. If \(p\le-1\) then \(u_k\ge1\) for every \(k\).

  2. If \(-1<p<0\) then \(c_k=(-1)^ku_k\), the numbers \(u_k\) decrease strictly to \(0\), and \(\sum u_k\) diverges.

  3. If \(p>0\), let \(K\) be the smallest integer greater than \(p\). For \(k\ge K\) the signs of \(c_k\) alternate, the numbers \(u_k\) decrease strictly to \(0\), and \(\sum u_k\) converges.

Proof. (1) Here \(\abs{p-k}=k+\abs p\ge k+1\), so \((\ast)\) gives \(u_{k+1}\ge u_k\). Since \(u_0=1\), \(u_k\ge1\) for all \(k\).

(2) Every factor \(p-j\) is negative, so \(c_k\) has the sign \((-1)^k\). Now \(\abs{p-k}=k+\abs p\) with \(0<\abs p<1\), so \((\ast)\) reads \((k+1)u_{k+1}=(k+\abs p)u_k\), which gives three facts. First, \(u_{k+1}<u_k\) because \(k+\abs p<k+1\). Second, \((k+1)u_{k+1}>k\,u_k\), so \(k\,u_k\) increases and \(k\,u_k\ge1\cdot u_1=\abs p\) for \(k\ge1\); that is \(u_k\ge\frac{\abs p}k\), and \(\sum u_k\) diverges by comparison with the harmonic series. Third, \(\frac{u_{k+1}}{u_k}=1-\frac{1-\abs p}{k+1}\le e^{-(1-\abs p)/(k+1)}\), so

\[0<u_n=u_0\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{u_{j+1}}{u_j}\le\exp\left(-(1-\abs p)\sum_{j=1}^n\frac1j\right)\to0,\]

because the harmonic series diverges. So \(u_n\to0\) by the Squeeze Theorem.

(3) For \(k\ge K\) we have \(k>p\), so \(p-k<0\). Then \(\frac{c_{k+1}}{c_k}=\frac{p-k}{k+1}<0\): the signs alternate. By \((\ast)\), \((k+1)u_{k+1}=(k-p)u_k\), so \(u_{k+1}<u_k\). As in (2), \(\frac{u_{k+1}}{u_k}=1-\frac{p+1}{k+1}\le e^{-(p+1)/(k+1)}\), so for \(n>K\), \(0<u_n\le u_K\exp\left(-(p+1)\sum_{j=K+1}^n\frac1j\right)\to0\). Finally \((\ast)\) gives \(k\,u_k-(k+1)u_{k+1}=p\,u_k\) for \(k\ge K\). Adding these equations for \(k=K,\dots,n\), the left sides telescope:

\[p\sum_{k=K}^nu_k=K\,u_K-(n+1)\,u_{n+1}\le K\,u_K .\]

So the partial sums of \(\sum u_k\) are bounded, and since the terms are positive the partial sums increase, so \(\sum u_k\) converges by the Monotone Convergence Theorem (Theorem A.5). ◻ ∎

Theorem G.5: The binomial series at the endpoints

Let \(p\) be a real number that is not a nonnegative integer. The series \(\sum_{k=0}^\infty\binom pkx^k\) has radius of convergence \(1\), and

  1. at \(x=1\) it converges if and only if \(p>-1\);

  2. at \(x=-1\) it converges if and only if \(p>0\).

So its interval of convergence is \((-1,1)\) if \(p\le-1\), \((-1,1]\) if \(-1<p<0\), and \([-1,1]\) if \(p>0\).

Proof. Radius. \(\abs{c_{k+1}/c_k}=\frac{\abs{p-k}}{k+1}\to1\), so \(R=1\) (the Ratio Test applied to the coefficients).

At \(x=1\). If \(p\le-1\) the terms satisfy \(\abs{c_k}\ge1\) (Theorem G.4(1)), so they do not tend to \(0\) and the series diverges (Divergence Test). If \(-1<p<0\) then \(c_k=(-1)^ku_k\) with \(u_k\) decreasing to \(0\) (Theorem G.4(2)), so the series converges by the Alternating Series Test. If \(p>0\), the terms from \(k=K\) on alternate in sign and decrease in absolute value to \(0\) (Theorem G.4(3)); the Alternating Series Test applied to the tail shows that the series converges (the first \(K\) terms are finitely many).

At \(x=-1\). The terms are \((-1)^kc_k\). If \(p\le-1\) their absolute values are \(\ge1\): divergence. If \(-1<p<0\) they are \((-1)^kc_k=u_k>0\), and \(\sum u_k\) diverges (Theorem G.4(2)). If \(p>0\), \(\sum u_k\) converges (Theorem G.4(3); the first \(K\) terms do not matter), so the series converges absolutely. ◻ ∎

Example G.6: The coefficients for \(p=\frac12\)

For \(p=\frac12\) we have \(K=1\) in Theorem G.4(3), and the telescoping identity reads \(\frac12\sum_{k=1}^nu_k=u_1-(n+1)u_{n+1}\), that is

\[\sum_{k=1}^n\abs{\binom{1/2}k}=1-2(n+1)\abs{\binom{1/2}{n+1}} .\]

Check it for \(n=9\) and say what it shows about \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty\abs{\binom{1/2}k}\).

Solution. The absolute values of the coefficients are \(u_1=\frac12\), \(u_2=\frac18\), \(u_3=\frac1{16}\), \(u_4=\frac5{128}\), \(u_5=\frac7{256}\), \(u_6=\frac{21}{1024}\), \(u_7=\frac{33}{2048}\), \(u_8=\frac{429}{32768}\), \(u_9=\frac{715}{65536}\), \(u_{10}=\frac{2431}{262144}\). Their sum for \(k=1,\dots,9\) is \(\frac{53381}{65536}\approx0.81453\), and the right side is \(1-20\cdot\frac{2431}{262144}=\frac{53381}{65536}\): equal. The partial sums increase and are at most \(1\), so they converge to some \(L\le1\), and then \((n+1)u_{n+1}=\frac{1-S_n}2\to\frac{1-L}2\). If this limit were positive, \(u_n\ge\frac cn\) for large \(n\) and \(\sum u_k\) would diverge by comparison with the harmonic series, contradicting Theorem G.4(3). So the limit is \(0\), \(L=1\), and \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty\abs{\binom{1/2}k}=1\). Since \((-1)^k\binom{1/2}k=-u_k\) for \(k\ge1\), this says that \(\sum_{k=0}^\infty\binom{1/2}k(-1)^k=1-1=0=\sqrt{1+(-1)}\).

items.title: Appendix H. Multiplying and Dividing Power Series
items.text:
Section 11.4 multiplies and divides Taylor series to find the first terms of functions such as \(e^x\sin x\) and \( an x\), and uses the product of two series to prove that \(e^xe^y=e^{x+y}\). The product of two sums is not the sum of the products of corresponding terms, so this needs a proof: the rule is the Cauchy product, in which the coefficient of \((x-a)^n\) collects every product \(a_jb_k\) with \(j+k=n\). This section proves that the rule is correct (Theorems H.1 and H.2), that a power series with nonzero constant term has a reciprocal that is again a power series (Theorem H.3), and hence that quotients work too (Theorem H.4). Everything is proved in full. It uses the Monotone Convergence Theorem (Section A), the existence of the radius of convergence (Section F) and the uniqueness of power series coefficients (Theorem F.6).

Theorem H.1: Products of absolutely convergent series

Let \(\sum_{j=0}^\infty u_j\) and \(\sum_{j=0}^\infty v_j\) be absolutely convergent series with sums \(U\) and \(V\), and let \(w_n=\sum_{j=0}^nu_jv_{n-j}\). Then \(\sum_{n=0}^\infty w_n\) converges absolutely and its sum is \(UV\).

Proof. Put \(\mu=\sum\abs{u_j}\), \( u=\sum\abs{v_j}\), \(U_N=\sum_{i=0}^Nu_i\), \(V_N=\sum_{j=0}^Nv_j\) and \(S_N=\sum_{n=0}^Nw_n\). Then \(S_N\) is the sum of \(u_iv_j\) over the pairs of integers \(i,j\ge0\) with \(i+j\le N\), and \(U_NV_N\) is the sum over the pairs with \(i,j\le N\).

Absolute convergence. The pairs with \(i+j\le N\) all have \(i,j\le N\), so

\[\sum_{n=0}^N\abs{w_n}\le\sum_{i+j\le N}\abs{u_i}\abs{v_j}\le\Bigl(\sum_{i=0}^N\abs{u_i}\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{j=0}^N\abs{v_j}\Bigr)\le\mu u .\]

The partial sums of \(\sum\abs{w_n}\) are nondecreasing and bounded above by \(\mu u\), so the series converges (Theorem A.5).

The sum. The difference \(U_NV_N-S_N\) is the sum of \(u_iv_j\) over the pairs with \(i,j\le N\) and \(i+j>N\). If both \(i\le N/2\) and \(j\le N/2\) then \(i+j\le N\), so in each such pair \(i>N/2\) or \(j>N/2\). Let \(M=\lfloor N/2 floor\) and let \(\mu_M=\sum_{i>M}\abs{u_i}\) and \( u_M=\sum_{j>M}\abs{v_j}\) be the tails; they tend to \(0\) as \(N o\infty\) (a tail is \(\mu\) minus a partial sum that tends to \(\mu\)). Splitting the pairs according to which of \(i>M\) and \(j>M\) holds (a pair for which both hold is counted twice, which only enlarges the bound),

\[\abs{U_NV_N-S_N}\le\sum_{i>M}\abs{u_i}\sum_{j\ge0}\abs{v_j}+\sum_{i\ge0}\abs{u_i}\sum_{j>M}\abs{v_j}\le\mu_M\, u+\mu\, u_M\longrightarrow0 .\]

Since \(U_NV_N o UV\) (Theorem B.4), \(S_N=U_NV_N-(U_NV_N-S_N) o UV\). ◻ ∎

Theorem H.2: Products of power series

Let \(f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty a_k(x-a)^k\) and \(g(x)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty b_k(x-a)^k\) for all \(x\) with \(\abs{x-a}<R\), where \(R>0\), and put \(c_n=\sum_{j=0}^na_jb_{n-j}\). Then \(\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n(x-a)^n\) converges to \(f(x)g(x)\) for every \(x\) with \(\abs{x-a}<R\).

Proof. Let \(\abs{x-a}<R\) and choose \(x_1\) with \(\abs{x-a}<\abs{x_1-a}<R\). Both series converge at \(x_1\), so by Theorem F.1 both converge absolutely at \(x\). Apply Theorem H.1 to \(u_j=a_j(x-a)^j\) and \(v_j=b_j(x-a)^j\): then \(w_n=\sum_{j=0}^na_jb_{n-j}(x-a)^{j}(x-a)^{n-j}=c_n(x-a)^n\), and the theorem gives \(\sum c_n(x-a)^n=f(x)g(x)\). ◻ ∎

Theorem H.3: The reciprocal of a power series

Let \(f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty a_k(x-a)^k\) for \(\abs{x-a}<R\), where \(R>0\) and \(a_0 e0\). Define \(b_0= rac1{a_0}\) and \(b_n=- rac1{a_0}\sum_{j=1}^na_jb_{n-j}\) for \(n\ge1\). Then there is \( ho>0\) such that for \(\abs{x-a}< ho\) the series \(\sum b_n(x-a)^n\) converges, \(f(x) e0\) and \(\dfrac1{f(x)}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty b_n(x-a)^n\).

Proof. The coefficients do not grow fast. Choose \(s\) with \(0<s<R\). The series \(\sum a_ks^k\) converges, so its terms tend to \(0\) and are bounded: \(\abs{a_k}s^k\le B\) for every \(k\), where we may take \(B\ge\abs{a_0}\). Put \(L=B/\abs{a_0}\) and \(d_i=s^i\abs{b_i}\), so \(d_0= rac1{\abs{a_0}}\). For \(n\ge1\) the definition of \(b_n\) gives

\[\abs{b_n}\le rac1{\abs{a_0}}\sum_{j=1}^n\abs{a_j}\abs{b_{n-j}}\le L\sum_{j=1}^ns^{-j}\abs{b_{n-j}},\qquad ext{so}\qquad d_n\le L\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}d_i .\]

We claim \(d_n\le d_0(1+L)^n\) for all \(n\). It is true for \(n=0\); if it holds for all indices below \(n\ge1\), then \(d_n\le L\,d_0\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(1+L)^i=d_0 igl((1+L)^n-1 igr)\le d_0(1+L)^n\). Hence \(\abs{b_n}\le d_0\left( rac{1+L}s ight)^n\).

Convergence. Let \( ho= rac s{1+L}\) (so \( ho<s<R\)) and \(\abs{x-a}< ho\). Then \(\abs{b_n(x-a)^n}\le d_0 heta^n\) with \( heta= rac{(1+L)\abs{x-a}}s<1\), so \(\sum b_n(x-a)^n\) converges (comparison with a geometric series); call its sum \(g(x)\).

The product is \(1\). By Theorem H.2 (with \( ho\) in place of \(R\)), \(f(x)g(x)=\sum c_n(x-a)^n\) with \(c_n=\sum_{j=0}^na_jb_{n-j}\). Here \(c_0=a_0b_0=1\), and for \(n\ge1\), \(c_n=a_0b_n+\sum_{j=1}^na_jb_{n-j}=0\) by the definition of \(b_n\). So \(f(x)g(x)=1\) for \(\abs{x-a}< ho\); therefore \(f(x) e0\) and \(g(x)= rac1{f(x)}\). ◻ ∎

Theorem H.4: Quotients of power series

Let \(f(x)=\sum a_k(x-a)^k\) and \(g(x)=\sum b_k(x-a)^k\) for \(\abs{x-a}<R\), with \(R>0\) and \(b_0 e0\). Then there is \( ho>0\) such that \(\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty q_n(x-a)^n\) for \(\abs{x-a}< ho\), where the coefficients are determined one after another by

\[q_n= rac1{b_0}\Bigl(a_n-\sum_{j=1}^nb_jq_{n-j}\Bigr),\qquad ext{equivalently}\qquad a_n=\sum_{j=0}^nb_jq_{n-j}.\]

Proof. By Theorem H.3, \( rac1g=\sum r_n(x-a)^n\) for \(\abs{x-a}< ho_1\), for some \( ho_1>0\) and coefficients \(r_n\). Then \( rac fg=f\cdot rac1g=\sum q_n(x-a)^n\) on \(\abs{x-a}<\min( ho_1,R)=: ho\) by Theorem H.2, where \(q_n=\sum_{j=0}^na_jr_{n-j}\). Apply Theorem H.2 again to \(g\) and \(\sum q_n(x-a)^n\): for \(\abs{x-a}< ho\),

\[f(x)=g(x)\cdot rac{f(x)}{g(x)}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\Bigl(\sum_{j=0}^nb_jq_{n-j}\Bigr)(x-a)^n .\]

Both sides are power series in \((x-a)\) equal on an interval, so their coefficients agree (by Theorem F.6, the coefficient of \((x-a)^n\) in a power series is \( rac{1}{n!}\) times the \(n\)-th derivative of its sum at \(a\)). Hence \(a_n=\sum_{j=0}^nb_jq_{n-j}\); solving for \(q_n\) (the term \(j=0\) is \(b_0q_n\)) gives the formula. ◻ ∎

Example H.5: The product \(e^x\cdot rac1{1-x}\)

Find the first terms of the Maclaurin series of \(\dfrac{e^x}{1-x}\), and the limit of its coefficients.

Solution. With \(a_j= rac1{j!}\) (valid for all \(x\)) and \(b_k=1\) (valid for \(\abs x<1\)), Theorem H.2 with \(R=1\) gives \(c_n=\sum_{j=0}^n rac1{j!}\cdot1\), the partial sums of the series for \(e\):

\[ rac{e^x}{1-x}=1+2x+ rac52x^2+ rac83x^3+ rac{65}{24}x^4+ rac{163}{60}x^5+\cdots\qquad(\abs x<1).\]

The coefficients increase to \(e=2.71828\dots\), because \(c_n=\sum_{j\le n} rac1{j!} o e\).

Example H.6: The first terms of \( an x\)

Use Theorem H.4 with \(f=\sin x\) and \(g=\cos x\) to find the first four nonzero terms of the series of \( an x\).

Solution. \(f\) has \(a_1=1\), \(a_3=- rac16\), \(a_5= rac1{120}\), \(a_7=- rac1{5040}\) and zero for the other indices up to \(7\); \(g\) has \(b_0=1\), \(b_2=- rac12\), \(b_4= rac1{24}\), \(b_6=- rac1{720}\) and zero for odd indices. By the formula \(q_n=a_n-\sum_{j=1}^nb_jq_{n-j}\) (here \(b_0=1\)): \(q_0=0\); \(q_1=a_1=1\); \(q_2=-b_2q_0=0\); \(q_3=a_3-b_2q_1=- rac16+ rac12= rac13\); \(q_4=0\); \(q_5=a_5-b_2q_3-b_4q_1= rac1{120}+ rac16- rac1{24}= rac2{15}\); \(q_7=a_7-b_2q_5-b_4q_3-b_6q_1=- rac1{5040}+ rac1{15}- rac1{72}+ rac1{720}= rac{17}{315}\). So

\[ an x=x+ rac{x^3}3+ rac{2x^5}{15}+ rac{17x^7}{315}+\cdots\]

on some interval about \(0\) (Theorem H.4 guarantees one; its length is not found by this method).

items.title: Appendix I. Parametrizations and Arc Length
items.text:
Section 12.1 computes the length of a curve, the area under it and the area of the surface it generates from a parametrization, and a curve has many parametrizations. Why does the answer not depend on the one we choose? This section proves it, for curves that are traced once. Three things are shown: two such parametrizations of the same set of points are related by a monotone change of parameter (Theorem I.3); the arc length is therefore the same (Theorem I.4); and when the change of parameter is differentiable, the integrals for arc length, surface area and area are unchanged by the substitution rule (Theorem I.5). The facts used from Section 12.1, stated in words only, are: if \(\gamma(t)=(f(t),g(t))\), \(a\le t\le b\), has continuous \(f',g'\), then the length of the inscribed polygon for a partition \(\Pi\) satisfies \(\ell(\Pi)\le L=\int_a^b\abs{\gamma'(t)}\,dt\), and \(\ell(\Pi)\to L\) as the mesh of \(\Pi\) tends to \(0\).

A parametrization \(\gamma:[a,b]\to\R^2\) is a simple arc if it is continuous and one-to-one. (A closed curve traced once, such as a circle, returns to its start; it is handled by cutting it at one point into two simple arcs, and lengths add.)

Theorem I.1: Bolzano–Weierstrass

Every sequence \(\{s_n\}\) in a closed interval \([a,b]\) has a convergent subsequence, with limit in \([a,b]\).

Proof. Call an index \(m\) a peak if \(s_m\ge s_n\) for all \(n>m\). If there are infinitely many peaks \(m_1<m_2<\cdots\), then \(s_{m_1}\ge s_{m_2}\ge\cdots\) is a nonincreasing subsequence. If there are finitely many, let \(n_1\) be larger than all of them. Then \(n_1\) is not a peak, so there is \(n_2>n_1\) with \(s_{n_2}>s_{n_1}\); \(n_2\) is not a peak either, so there is \(n_3>n_2\) with \(s_{n_3}>s_{n_2}\), and so on: an increasing subsequence. In both cases we have a monotone subsequence bounded by \(a\) and \(b\), which converges by the Monotone Convergence Theorem (Theorem A.5); its limit is in \([a,b]\) because the limit respects bounds (Theorem A.6). ◻ ∎

Theorem I.2: The inverse of a simple arc is continuous

Let \(\gamma:[a,b]\to\R^2\) be continuous and one-to-one, with image \(C\). Then the inverse \(\gamma^{-1}:C\to[a,b]\) is continuous: if \(\gamma(s_n)\to\gamma(s)\) then \(s_n\to s\).

Proof. Suppose \(\gamma(s_n)\to\gamma(s)\) but \(s_n\not\to s\). Then there is \(\varepsilon>0\) and a subsequence with \(\abs{s_{n_j}-s}\ge\varepsilon\) for all \(j\). By Theorem I.1 a further subsequence converges to some \(s'\in[a,b]\), and \(\abs{s'-s}\ge\varepsilon\). By continuity of \(\gamma\), \(\gamma(s_{n_{j_i}})\to\gamma(s')\) (limits of points of the plane are taken coordinatewise). But this subsequence also tends to \(\gamma(s)\), so \(\gamma(s')=\gamma(s)\) by uniqueness of limits (Theorem B.1), and \(s'=s\) because \(\gamma\) is one-to-one. This contradicts \(\abs{s'-s}\ge\varepsilon\). ◻ ∎

Theorem I.3: Two simple arcs with the same image

Let \(\gamma:[a,b]\to\R^2\) and \(\tilde\gamma:[c,d]\to\R^2\) be simple arcs with the same image \(C\). Then \(\varphi=\gamma^{-1}\circ\tilde\gamma:[c,d]\to[a,b]\) is a continuous, strictly monotone bijection and \(\tilde\gamma=\gamma\circ\varphi\).

Proof. \(\varphi\) is a bijection because \(\tilde\gamma:[c,d]\to C\) and \(\gamma^{-1}:C\to[a,b]\) are, and it is continuous by Theorem I.2 (if \(s_n\to s\) then \(\tilde\gamma(s_n)\to\tilde\gamma(s)\), hence \(\varphi(s_n)\to\varphi(s)\)). Clearly \(\gamma\circ\varphi=\tilde\gamma\). A continuous one-to-one function on an interval is strictly monotone. To see this, first note that for \(s_1<s_2<s_3\) the value \(\varphi(s_2)\) lies strictly between \(\varphi(s_1)\) and \(\varphi(s_3)\): otherwise, say \(\varphi(s_2)\) is larger than both, choose \(w\) with \(\max(\varphi(s_1),\varphi(s_3))<w<\varphi(s_2)\); the Intermediate Value Theorem gives \(u\in(s_1,s_2)\) and \(u'\in(s_2,s_3)\) with \(\varphi(u)=w=\varphi(u')\), contradicting one-to-one (the case “smaller than both” is the same). Now suppose \(\varphi(c)<\varphi(d)\) (the other case is symmetric). For \(c<s<s'\le d\) we have \(\varphi(c)<\varphi(s)\) by the statement for \(c<s<d\) (or \(s'\)), and \(\varphi(s)\) lies between \(\varphi(c)\) and \(\varphi(s')\), which forces \(\varphi(s)<\varphi(s')\). So \(\varphi\) is strictly increasing. ◻ ∎

Theorem I.4: Arc length does not depend on the parametrization

Let \(\gamma\) and \(\tilde\gamma\) be simple arcs with the same image \(C\) and continuous derivatives. Then they give the same length: \(\int_a^b\abs{\gamma'(t)}\,dt=\int_c^d\abs{\tilde\gamma'(s)}\,ds\). This common value is the supremum of the lengths of all polygons inscribed in \(C\) with vertices in order along \(C\).

Proof. By the facts quoted at the start, \(\ell(\Pi)\le L\) for every partition and \(\ell(\Pi)\to L\) as the mesh tends to \(0\), so \(L=\sup\ell(\Pi)\) (the supremum over all partitions of \([a,b]\)), and the same holds for \(\tilde L\) with partitions of \([c,d]\). Let \(\varphi\) be as in Theorem I.3. A partition \(s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_n\) of \([c,d]\) is carried by the strictly monotone bijection \(\varphi\) to the points \(t_k=\varphi(s_k)\), which, taken in increasing order (this reverses the order if \(\varphi\) is decreasing), form a partition of \([a,b]\), and \(\gamma(t_k)=\tilde\gamma(s_k)\): the two inscribed polygons have the same vertices and the same length. Every partition of \([a,b]\) arises this way, because \(\varphi\) is onto. So the two sets of polygon lengths are equal, hence so are the suprema, \(L=\tilde L\). ◻ ∎

Theorem I.5: Differentiable changes of parameter

Let \(\gamma=(f,g)\) be defined on \([a,b]\) with \(f',g'\) continuous, and let \(\varphi:[c,d]\to[a,b]\) have a continuous derivative that is nonnegative throughout or nonpositive throughout, with \(\varphi\) onto. Put \(\tilde\gamma=\gamma\circ\varphi\). For every continuous function \(h\) on \([a,b]\),

\[\int_c^dh(\varphi(s))\,\abs{\tilde\gamma'(s)}\,ds=\int_a^bh(t)\,\abs{\gamma'(t)}\,dt,\qquad \int_c^dh(\varphi(s))\,\abs{(f\circ\varphi)'(s)}\,ds=\int_a^bh(t)\,\abs{f'(t)}\,dt.\]

In particular the arc length (\(h=1\)), the surface area of revolution (\(h=2\pi g\) or \(2\pi f\)) and the area under a curve (\(h=g\), with \(\abs{f'}\)) are the same for \(\tilde\gamma\) as for \(\gamma\).

Proof. By the Chain Rule \(\tilde\gamma'(s)=\gamma'(\varphi(s))\,\varphi'(s)\), so \(\abs{\tilde\gamma'(s)}=\abs{\gamma'(\varphi(s))}\,\abs{\varphi'(s)}\), and likewise \(\abs{(f\circ\varphi)'(s)}=\abs{f'(\varphi(s))}\,\abs{\varphi'(s)}\). Put \(H(t)=h(t)\abs{\gamma'(t)}\) (or \(h(t)\abs{f'(t)}\)), a continuous function. If \(\varphi'\ge0\), then \(\varphi\) is nondecreasing and onto, so \(\varphi(c)=a\), \(\varphi(d)=b\), and the substitution rule gives \(\int_c^dH(\varphi(s))\varphi'(s)\,ds=\int_a^bH(t)\,dt\), which is the claim because \(\abs{\varphi'}=\varphi'\). If \(\varphi'\le0\), then \(\varphi(c)=b\), \(\varphi(d)=a\), \(\abs{\varphi'}=-\varphi'\), and the substitution rule gives \(\int_c^dH(\varphi(s))(-\varphi'(s))\,ds=-\int_b^aH(t)\,dt=\int_a^bH(t)\,dt\). ◻ ∎

The hypothesis “traced once” cannot be dropped: the formulas measure what is traced, with multiplicity.

Example I.6: The half circle in two ways

The half circle is parametrized by \(\gamma(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)\), \(0\le t\le\pi\), and by \(\tilde\gamma(s)=(\cos s^2,\sin s^2)\), \(0\le s\le\sqrt\pi\), that is, \(\tilde\gamma=\gamma\circ\varphi\) with \(\varphi(s)=s^2\), \(\varphi'(s)=2s\ge0\). The speed of \(\gamma\) is \(1\) and the speed of \(\tilde\gamma\) is \(2s\), so

\[\int_0^\pi1\,dt=\pi=\int_0^{\sqrt\pi}2s\,ds,\]

as Theorem I.4 predicts. If instead the circle is run twice, \(0\le t\le4\pi\), the formula gives \(4\pi\): that parametrization is not one-to-one, and the theorem does not apply.

items.title: Appendix J. Area in Polar Coordinates
items.text:
Section 12.3 finds the area of a region in polar coordinates by cutting it into thin sectors and squeezing its area between sums of sector areas. Two facts are taken from this section: the area of a sector, \(\frac12\rho^2\varphi\) (Theorem J.1), and the fact that a polar curve has no area of its own (Theorem J.2), so that two regions that share only a boundary curve have areas that add. Everything else in the area proofs of Section 12.3 is the definition of the integral.

What is assumed about area. Area is the quantity of Calculus I: the area of the region between the graphs of two continuous functions is \(\int(\text{top}-\text{bottom})\,dx\), and a region that can be cut into finitely many such pieces has the sum of their areas. We use only the following properties, which are not proved here; they are the standard properties of that notion of area.

  1. Monotone. If a region \(R\) is contained in a region \(R'\), then \(\operatorname{area}(R)\le\operatorname{area}(R')\).

  2. Additive. If \(R=R_1\cup R_2\) and \(R_1\cap R_2\) has area zero, then \(\operatorname{area}(R)=\operatorname{area}(R_1)+\operatorname{area}(R_2)\). Here a set has area zero if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), it lies in a region of area less than \(\varepsilon\). A point, a line segment and an arc of a circle have area zero (each is, after a rotation, a graph \(y=g(x)\) of a continuous function over an interval, and the region between two copies of a graph has area \(\int(g-g)\,dx=0\)).

  3. Congruent regions have equal area. Rotations, reflections (in particular the reflection in the origin, which is the rotation through \(\pi\)) and translations do not change area.

  4. A disc of radius \(\rho\) has area \(\pi\rho^2\) (it is \(\int_{-\rho}^{\rho}2\sqrt{\rho^2-x^2}\,dx\)).

Sectors. For \(\rho>0\), \(\alpha\) real and \(0\le\varphi\le2\pi\), the sector \(S(\rho;\alpha,\alpha+\varphi)\) is the set of points \(P(s,\theta)\) with \(0\le s\le\rho\) and \(\alpha\le\theta\le\alpha+\varphi\).

Theorem J.1: Area of a sector

The sector of radius \(\rho\) and angle \(\varphi\), \(0\le\varphi\le2\pi\), has area \(\frac12\rho^2\varphi\).

Proof. Let \(a(\varphi)\) be the area of the sector of angle \(\varphi\). By (A3), \(a(\varphi)\) does not depend on the starting angle \(\alpha\) (rotate the sector). We prove four things.

(i) Additivity. If \(\varphi_1+\varphi_2\le2\pi\), then \(S(\rho;\alpha,\alpha+\varphi_1+\varphi_2)\) is the union of \(S(\rho;\alpha,\alpha+\varphi_1)\) and \(S(\rho;\alpha+\varphi_1,\alpha+\varphi_1+\varphi_2)\), which share only the radius at the angle \(\alpha+\varphi_1\) (and, if \(\varphi_1+\varphi_2=2\pi\), the radius at \(\alpha\)); a segment has area zero. By (A2), \(a(\varphi_1+\varphi_2)=a(\varphi_1)+a(\varphi_2)\).

(ii) Monotone. If \(\varphi\le\varphi'\), the sector of angle \(\varphi\) is contained in the sector of angle \(\varphi'\) with the same \(\alpha\), so \(a(\varphi)\le a(\varphi')\) by (A1).

(iii) The full sector. For \(\varphi=2\pi\) the sector is the disc of radius \(\rho\), so \(a(2\pi)=\pi\rho^2\) by (A4).

(iv) Rational multiples of \(2\pi\). Let \(q\ge1\) be an integer. The full disc is the union of \(q\) sectors of angle \(\frac{2\pi}q\) (one after the other), so by (i) and (iii), \(q\,a\!\left(\frac{2\pi}q\right)=\pi\rho^2\), that is \(a\!\left(\frac{2\pi}q\right)=\frac{\pi\rho^2}q\). For an integer \(p\) with \(0\le p\le q\), (i) gives \(a\!\left(\frac{2\pi p}q\right)=p\cdot\frac{\pi\rho^2}q=\frac12\rho^2\cdot\frac{2\pi p}q\). So the formula holds for every angle that is a rational multiple of \(2\pi\).

(v) Every angle. Let \(0<\varphi<2\pi\). Choose rational multiples \(s<\varphi<s'\) of \(2\pi\) in \([0,2\pi]\). By (ii) and (iv), \(\frac12\rho^2s=a(s)\le a(\varphi)\le a(s')=\frac12\rho^2s'\). Rational multiples of \(2\pi\) come arbitrarily close to \(\varphi\) from both sides, so letting \(s\uparrow\varphi\) and \(s'\downarrow\varphi\) gives \(a(\varphi)=\frac12\rho^2\varphi\). (For \(\varphi=0\) the sector is a segment, of area \(0\); for \(\varphi=2\pi\) see (iii).) ◻ ∎

Theorem J.2: A polar curve has area zero

Let \(f\) be continuous and \(f\ge0\) on \([\alpha,\beta]\), with \(\beta-\alpha\le2\pi\). Then the curve \(C=\{P(f(\theta),\theta):\alpha\le\theta\le\beta\}\) has area zero.

Proof. Let \(\varepsilon>0\). The function \(\frac12f^2\) is continuous on \([\alpha,\beta]\), so the upper and lower sums of a partition \(\Pi\) differ by less than \(\varepsilon\) once the mesh of \(\Pi\) is small enough (Calculus I). Take such a partition \(\alpha=\theta_0<\cdots<\theta_n=\beta\), and let \(m_k\) and \(M_k\) be the minimum and maximum of \(f\) on \([\theta_{k-1},\theta_k]\). The part of \(C\) over \([\theta_{k-1},\theta_k]\) lies in the annular sector \(A_k=\{P(s,\theta):m_k\le s\le M_k,\ \theta_{k-1}\le\theta\le\theta_k\}\). The sector of radius \(M_k\) is the union of the sector of radius \(m_k\) and \(A_k\), which share only an arc of a circle (area zero by (A2)), so by (A2) and Theorem J.1, \(\operatorname{area}(A_k)=\frac12\left(M_k^2-m_k^2\right)\Delta\theta_k\). Neighboring \(A_k\) share only a segment, so the union of the \(A_k\), a region that contains \(C\), has area \(\sum_k\frac12\left(M_k^2-m_k^2\right)\Delta\theta_k=U(\Pi)-L(\Pi)<\varepsilon\), where \(L\) and \(U\) are the lower and upper sums of \(\frac12f^2\) (because \(f\ge0\), \(m_k^2\) and \(M_k^2\) are the least and greatest values of \(f^2\) on the interval). ◻ ∎

Example J.3: The two facts for a circle and a spiral

(a) A sector of radius \(6\) and angle \(\frac\pi3\) has area \(\frac12\cdot36\cdot\frac\pi3=6\pi\), one sixth of the disc (\(36\pi\)), as it should. (b) For the spiral \(r=\theta\), \(0\le\theta\le2\pi\), the annular sector between the radii \(m=\theta_{k-1}\) and \(M=\theta_k\) over \([\theta_{k-1},\theta_k]\) has area \(\frac12\left(\theta_k^2-\theta_{k-1}^2\right)\Delta\theta_k\); for \(n=4\) subintervals of length \(\frac\pi2\) these add to \(\frac12\left((2\pi)^2-0\right)\cdot\frac\pi2=\pi^3\approx31.0\), and the sum \(U-L\) shrinks like \(\frac1n\): for general \(n\) it is \(\frac12(2\pi)^2\cdot\frac{2\pi}n=\frac{4\pi^3}n\).

items.title: Appendix K. Conic Sections: Squaring, Coordinates and the Focus–Directrix Theorem
items.text:
Section 12.4 defines the parabola, the ellipse and the hyperbola by distances, finds their equations by squaring, and unifies the three curves by one number, the eccentricity. Squaring is dangerous: it can add points that do not satisfy the original condition, or hide the fact that a step is not reversible. This section proves four things. (K.1) Exactly when squaring an equation neither gains nor loses solutions. (K.2) An identity for the sum and the difference of the distances from a point to two foci, which turns the two “string” definitions into equations without any loss. (K.3) That the foci and directrix may be placed where we like, because moving the plane rigidly preserves distances. (K.4) The Eccentricity–Directrix Theorem, with every step of the algebra and the reason why the three cases \(e<1\), \(e=1\) and \(e>1\) give the three conics.

Theorem K.1: Squaring without gaining or losing points

Let \(A\) and \(B\) be real numbers. Then \(A=B\) if and only if \(A^2=B^2\) and \(AB\ge0\). In particular, if \(A\ge0\) and \(B\ge0\), then \(A=B\) if and only if \(A^2=B^2\).

Proof. If \(A=B\), then \(A^2=B^2\) and \(AB=A^2\ge0\). Conversely, suppose \(A^2=B^2\) and \(AB\ge0\). Then \((A-B)(A+B)=A^2-B^2=0\), so \(B=A\) or \(B=-A\). If \(B=-A\), then \(AB=-A^2\ge0\) forces \(A=0\), hence \(B=0=A\). In every case \(A=B\). For the last statement: if \(A\ge0\) and \(B\ge0\) then \(AB\ge0\) automatically. ◻ ∎

Example K.2: Squaring adds a point

Solve \(\sqrt{x+2}=x\).

Solution. Put \(A=\sqrt{x+2}\) and \(B=x\). Squaring gives \(x+2=x^2\), that is \(x^2-x-2=(x-2)(x+1)=0\), so \(x=2\) or \(x=-1\). By Theorem K.1 we must also have \(AB\ge0\). For \(x=2\): \(A=2\), \(B=2\), \(AB=4\ge0\), and indeed \(\sqrt4=2\). For \(x=-1\): \(A=\sqrt1=1\), \(B=-1\), \(AB=-1<0\), and indeed \(\sqrt1\ne-1\). So the squared equation has the extra solution \(x=-1\) and the original equation has only \(x=2\).

Theorem K.3: Sum and difference of distances to two foci

Let \(c>0\), \(a>0\), \(F_1=(-c,0)\), \(F_2=(c,0)\), \(P=(x,y)\), \(u=\lvert PF_1\rvert\) and \(v=\lvert PF_2\rvert\). Then \(u^2-v^2=4cx\), and

(i) \(u+v=2a\) if and only if \(u=a+\frac ca\,x\) and \(v=a-\frac ca\,x\);

(ii) \(u-v=2a\) if and only if \(u=\frac ca\,x+a\) and \(v=\frac ca\,x-a\);

(iii) \(v-u=2a\) if and only if \(u=-\frac ca\,x-a\) and \(v=-\frac ca\,x+a\).

Proof. \(u^2=(x+c)^2+y^2\) and \(v^2=(x-c)^2+y^2\), so \(u^2-v^2=(x+c)^2-(x-c)^2=4cx\) (the terms \(y^2\) cancel). Also \(u^2-v^2=(u-v)(u+v)\).

(i) If \(u+v=2a\), then \((u-v)(2a)=4cx\), so \(u-v=\frac{2cx}a\) (we divide by \(2a\ne0\)). Adding and subtracting \(u+v=2a\) and \(u-v=\frac{2cx}a\) gives \(u=a+\frac{cx}a\) and \(v=a-\frac{cx}a\). Conversely, adding the two formulas gives \(u+v=2a\).

(ii) If \(u-v=2a\), then \(2a(u+v)=4cx\), so \(u+v=\frac{2cx}a\). Adding and subtracting \(u-v=2a\) gives \(u=\frac{cx}a+a\) and \(v=\frac{cx}a-a\). Conversely, subtracting the two formulas gives \(u-v=2a\).

(iii) If \(v-u=2a\), then \((u-v)(u+v)=4cx\) gives \(-2a(u+v)=4cx\), so \(u+v=-\frac{2cx}a\). Adding and subtracting \(u-v=-2a\) gives \(u=-\frac{cx}a-a\) and \(v=-\frac{cx}a+a\). Conversely, subtracting the two formulas gives \(v-u=2a\). ◻ ∎

No squaring of a square root appears in this proof: the only squares are \(u^2\) and \(v^2\), which are polynomials in \(x\) and \(y\), so nothing is gained or lost. Section 12.4 uses it to turn \(u+v=2a\) and \(\lvert u-v\rvert=2a\) into equations in \(x\) and \(y\).

Theorem K.4: Placing the coordinates

A rigid motion is a map of the plane that is a composition of translations \((x,y)\mapsto(x+h,y+k)\), rotations about the origin \((x,y)\mapsto(x\cos\varphi-y\sin\varphi,\ x\sin\varphi+y\cos\varphi)\) and the reflection \((x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)\). A rigid motion preserves the distance between any two points, maps lines to lines, and preserves the distance from a point to a line. Given a point \(F\) and a line \(\ell\) not through \(F\), let \(d>0\) be the distance from \(F\) to \(\ell\). There is a rigid motion that carries \(F\) to \((0,0)\) and \(\ell\) to the line \(x=d\).

Proof. For two points with coordinate differences \(\Delta x,\Delta y\), a translation leaves \(\Delta x,\Delta y\) unchanged. A rotation changes them to \(\Delta x\cos\varphi-\Delta y\sin\varphi\) and \(\Delta x\sin\varphi+\Delta y\cos\varphi\), and

\[(\Delta x\cos\varphi-\Delta y\sin\varphi)^2+(\Delta x\sin\varphi+\Delta y\cos\varphi)^2=(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2\,(\cos^2\varphi+\sin^2\varphi)=(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2,\]

because the cross terms \(\mp2\Delta x\Delta y\sin\varphi\cos\varphi\) cancel. A reflection changes the sign of \(\Delta y\) only. So all three preserve distances. Each is given by formulas linear in \(x\) and \(y\) (plus constants), so a line \(\alpha x+\beta y=\gamma\) goes to a line. The distance from a point to a line is the smallest distance from the point to a point of the line; a rigid motion carries the points of the line onto the points of the image line and preserves distances, so it preserves that smallest value.

Now translate \(F\) to the origin. Let \(Q\) be the foot of the perpendicular from the origin to the image of \(\ell\); \(\lvert OQ\rvert=d\). Rotate about the origin so that \(Q\) lies on the positive \(x\)-axis, at \((d,0)\). The image of \(\ell\) is the line through \((d,0)\) perpendicular to \(OQ\), the \(x\)-axis, that is, the line \(x=d\). ◻ ∎

Consequently, if \(\Phi\) is such a rigid motion, a point \(P\) satisfies \(\lvert PF\rvert=e\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell)\) if and only if \(\Phi(P)\) satisfies \(\lvert\Phi(P)\,(0,0)\rvert=e\operatorname{dist}(\Phi(P),\,x=d)\). The conic for \((F,\ell,e)\) is carried onto the conic for \(((0,0),\,x=d,\,e)\), so it is enough to study the second one.

Theorem K.5: The Eccentricity–Directrix Theorem

Let \(d>0\) and \(e>0\), and let \(C\) be the set of points \(P=(x,y)\) with \(\lvert PF\rvert=e\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell)\), where \(F=(0,0)\) and \(\ell\) is the line \(x=d\). Then:

(1) If \(e=1\), \(C\) is the parabola \(y^2=-2d\left(x-\frac d2\right)\) with focus \(F\) and directrix \(\ell\).

(2) If \(0<e<1\), put \(a=\frac{ed}{1-e^2}\), \(c=ae\) and \(b=a\sqrt{1-e^2}\). Then \(a^2=b^2+c^2\) and \(C=\left\{(x,y):\ \frac{(x+c)^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1\right\}\): an ellipse with center \((-c,0)\), foci \((0,0)\) and \((-2c,0)\), and \(\ell\) is at distance \(\frac ae\) from the center.

(3) If \(e>1\), put \(a=\frac{ed}{e^2-1}\), \(c=ae\) and \(b=a\sqrt{e^2-1}\). Then \(b^2=c^2-a^2\) and \(C=\left\{(x,y):\ \frac{(x-c)^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1\right\}\): a hyperbola with center \((c,0)\), foci \((0,0)\) and \((2c,0)\), and \(\ell\) is at distance \(\frac ae\) from the center.

Exactly one of the cases \(e<1\), \(e=1\), \(e>1\) occurs, so every focus–directrix set is a parabola, an ellipse or a hyperbola, and which one is decided by \(e\) alone. By Theorem K.4 the same holds for any focus \(F\) and any line \(\ell\) not through \(F\), with \(d=\operatorname{dist}(F,\ell)\).

Proof. Step 1: the equation. For \(P=(x,y)\), \(\lvert PF\rvert=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\ge0\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell)=\lvert d-x\rvert\), so \(e\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell)\ge0\). By Theorem K.1 the condition is equivalent to \(x^2+y^2=e^2(d-x)^2\), with no point gained or lost. Expanding \(e^2(d-x)^2=e^2d^2-2e^2dx+e^2x^2\) and collecting terms,

\[(1-e^2)\,x^2+2e^2d\,x+y^2=e^2d^2 .\tag{$\star$}\]

Step 2: \(e=1\). Then \((\star)\) reads \(2dx+y^2=d^2\), that is \(y^2=-2dx+d^2=-2d\left(x-\frac d2\right)\).

Step 3: \(e<1\). Then \(1-e^2>0\). Complete the square in \(x\):

\[(1-e^2)\left[x^2+\frac{2e^2d}{1-e^2}\,x\right]=(1-e^2)\left(x+\frac{e^2d}{1-e^2}\right)^2-\frac{e^4d^2}{1-e^2}.\]

With \(c=\frac{e^2d}{1-e^2}\) (this equals \(ae\), because \(a=\frac{ed}{1-e^2}\)), \((\star)\) becomes \((1-e^2)(x+c)^2+y^2=e^2d^2+\frac{e^4d^2}{1-e^2}=\frac{e^2d^2(1-e^2)+e^4d^2}{1-e^2}=\frac{e^2d^2}{1-e^2}\). Divide by this positive number. Since \(a^2=\frac{e^2d^2}{(1-e^2)^2}\) we have \(\frac{1-e^2}{e^2d^2/(1-e^2)}=\frac1{a^2}\), and the second coefficient is \(\frac{1-e^2}{e^2d^2}=\frac1{b^2}\) with \(b^2=\frac{e^2d^2}{1-e^2}=a^2(1-e^2)\). So \((\star)\) is equivalent to \(\frac{(x+c)^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1\). Moreover \(a^2-b^2=a^2e^2=c^2\). By Theorem K.3 and the standard-position equation of the ellipse (translated by \((-c,0)\)), this is the set of points whose distances to \((-c-c,0)=(-2c,0)\) and \((-c+c,0)=(0,0)\) add to \(2a\). The distance from the center \((-c,0)\) to \(\ell\) is \(d+c=d+\frac{e^2d}{1-e^2}=\frac d{1-e^2}=\frac ae\).

Step 4: \(e>1\). Now \(e^2-1>0\). Multiply \((\star)\) by \(-1\): \((e^2-1)x^2-2e^2dx-y^2=-e^2d^2\). Complete the square: \((e^2-1)\left[x^2-\frac{2e^2d}{e^2-1}x\right]=(e^2-1)(x-c)^2-\frac{e^4d^2}{e^2-1}\) with \(c=\frac{e^2d}{e^2-1}=ae\), where \(a=\frac{ed}{e^2-1}\). Then \((e^2-1)(x-c)^2-y^2=\frac{e^4d^2}{e^2-1}-e^2d^2=\frac{e^2d^2\left(e^2-(e^2-1)\right)}{e^2-1}=\frac{e^2d^2}{e^2-1}\). Dividing by this positive number gives \(\frac{(x-c)^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1\), where \(a^2=\frac{e^2d^2}{(e^2-1)^2}\) and \(b^2=\frac{e^2d^2}{e^2-1}=a^2(e^2-1)=c^2-a^2\). This is the hyperbola with center \((c,0)\) and foci \((c\mp c,0)=(0,0),(2c,0)\). The distance from the center to \(\ell\) is \(c-d=\frac{e^2d}{e^2-1}-d=\frac d{e^2-1}=\frac ae\).

Every step was an equivalence (Theorem K.1, an identity for completing the square, division by a nonzero number), so \(C\) is exactly the solution set of the final equation. ◻ ∎

Example K.6: Ellipse from a focus, a directrix and \(e=\frac12\)

Find the conic \(\lvert PF\rvert=\frac12\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell)\) for \(F=(0,0)\) and \(\ell:\ x=4\), and read off its center, foci and directrices.

Solution. Here \(e=\frac12<1\), \(d=4\). Step 1: \(x^2+y^2=\frac14(4-x)^2=\frac14\left(16-8x+x^2\right)\), so \(\frac34x^2+2x+y^2=4\), which is \((\star)\) with \(1-e^2=\frac34\) and \(2e^2d=2\). Complete the square: \(\frac34\left(x^2+\frac83x\right)=\frac34\left(x+\frac43\right)^2-\frac43\), so \(\frac34\left(x+\frac43\right)^2+y^2=\frac{16}3\), and dividing by \(\frac{16}3\),

\[\frac{\left(x+\frac43\right)^2}{64/9}+\frac{y^2}{16/3}=1,\qquad a=\frac83,\ b^2=\frac{16}3,\ c=\frac43 .\]

The center is \(\left(-\frac43,0\right)\), the foci are \((0,0)\) and \(\left(-\frac83,0\right)\), the vertices are \(\left(-\frac43\pm\frac83,0\right)=(4/3,0)\) and \((-4,0)\). The formulas of the theorem agree: \(a=\frac{ed}{1-e^2}=\frac{2}{3/4}=\frac83\), \(c=ae=\frac43\), \(b^2=a^2(1-e^2)=\frac{64}9\cdot\frac34=\frac{16}3\). The second directrix is the mirror image of \(x=4\) in the center: \(x=-\frac43-\frac ae=-\frac43-\frac{16}3=-\frac{20}3\). Check. The vertex \((4/3,0)\) must satisfy the definition: \(\lvert PF\rvert=\frac43\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell)=4-\frac43=\frac83\), and \(\frac12\cdot\frac83=\frac43\).

items.title: Appendix L. Real Polynomials: the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra and Factorization
items.text:
Section 8.5 decomposes a rational function into partial fractions. The decomposition exists because every polynomial with real coefficients factors into real linear factors and real quadratic factors that have no real roots. That factorization rests on the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, which is not proved in a calculus course. This section proves both, from two facts that are named here and not proved. (L.1) A continuous real function on a closed disk in the plane attains a smallest value (the Extreme Value Theorem in two variables). (L.2) Every complex number has a \(k\)-th root, for every positive integer \(k\) (from the polar form of a complex number and de Moivre’s formula). Everything else is proved. Complex numbers are used only here, as a tool; the integrals of Section 8.5 are real.

Theorem L.1: Fundamental Theorem of Algebra (d’Alembert’s proof)

Every polynomial \(p(z)=a_nz^n+\cdots+a_1z+a_0\) with complex coefficients and degree \(n\ge1\) has a complex root.

Proof. Step 1: \(\lvert p vert\) has a smallest value. For \(\lvert z vert\ge1\), \(\lvert p(z) vert\ge\lvert a_n vert\lvert z vert^n-\left(\lvert a_{n-1} vert+\cdots+\lvert a_0 vert ight)\lvert z vert^{n-1}\), by the triangle inequality and \(\lvert z vert^j\le\lvert z vert^{n-1}\) for \(j\le n-1\). The right side is \(\lvert z vert^{n-1}\left(\lvert a_n vert\lvert z vert-S ight)\) with \(S=\lvert a_{n-1} vert+\cdots+\lvert a_0 vert\), and it tends to \(\infty\) as \(\lvert z vert o\infty\). So there is \(R\ge1\) with \(\lvert p(z) vert>\lvert p(0) vert\) whenever \(\lvert z vert>R\). On the closed disk \(\lvert z vert\le R\) the continuous function \(\lvert p vert\) has a smallest value (L.1), attained at some \(z_0\), and \(\lvert p(z_0) vert\le\lvert p(0) vert<\lvert p(z) vert\) outside the disk. Hence \(\lvert p(z_0) vert\le\lvert p(z) vert\) for all \(z\).

Step 2: the smallest value is \(0\). Suppose \(p(z_0) e0\). Put \(q(w)=p(z_0+w)/p(z_0)\). Expanding \(p(z_0+w)\) in powers of \(w\) shows \(q\) is a polynomial of degree \(n\) with \(q(0)=1\), and \(\lvert q(w) vert\ge1\) for all \(w\) by Step 1. Let \(k\ge1\) be the smallest power with a nonzero coefficient, so \(q(w)=1+cw^k+w^{k+1}r(w)\) with \(c e0\) and \(r\) a polynomial (possibly \(0\)). By (L.2) choose \(w_0\) with \(cw_0^k=-1\). For \(0<t<1\),

\[q(tw_0)=1+c\,t^kw_0^k+t^{k+1}w_0^{k+1}r(tw_0)=1-t^k+t^{k+1}w_0^{k+1}r(tw_0).\]

On the closed disk \(\lvert w vert\le\lvert w_0 vert\) the function \(\lvert w_0^{k+1}r(w) vert\) is continuous, so it is bounded by some \(M\) (L.1). Then for \(0<t<1\),

\[\lvert q(tw_0) vert\le\left(1-t^k ight)+Mt^{k+1}=1-t^k\,(1-Mt).\]

For \(0<t<\min\{1,\,1/M\}\) (any \(t\in(0,1)\) if \(M=0\)), the number \(t^k(1-Mt)\) is positive, so \(\lvert q(tw_0) vert<1\). This contradicts \(\lvert q vert\ge1\). So \(p(z_0)=0\). ◻ ∎

Theorem L.2: Real polynomials factor into linear and irreducible quadratic factors

Let \(p\) be a polynomial with real coefficients and degree \(n\ge1\). Then \(p\) is a product of its leading coefficient, factors \(x-r\) with \(r\) real, and factors \(x^2+bx+c\) with \(b,c\) real and \(b^2-4c<0\) (so with no real root). The factors may repeat.

Proof. Induction on \(n\). Let \(a\) be the leading coefficient and divide by it, so assume \(p\) is monic. By Theorem L.1, \(p\) has a complex root \(z\).

Case 1: \(z\) is real. Divide \(p\) by \(x-z\) with the division algorithm (real coefficients): \(p=(x-z)s+ ho\) with \( ho\) a real constant. Putting \(x=z\) gives \( ho=p(z)=0\), so \(p=(x-z)s\) with \(s\) monic, real, of degree \(n-1\). If \(n-1\ge1\), apply the induction hypothesis to \(s\); if \(n=1\) we are done.

Case 2: \(z=u+iv\) with \(v e0\). Because the coefficients are real, \(\overline{p(z)}=p( ar z)\) (conjugation respects sums and products), so \(p( ar z)=\overline0=0\) and \( ar z\) is also a root. Let \(m(x)=(x-z)(x- ar z)=x^2-2ux+\left(u^2+v^2 ight)\). It has real coefficients \(b=-2u\), \(c=u^2+v^2\), and \(b^2-4c=-4v^2<0\). Divide \(p\) by \(m\) with the division algorithm over the reals: \(p=ms+ ho_1x+ ho_0\) with \( ho_1, ho_0\) real. Put \(x=z\) and \(x= ar z\): \( ho_1z+ ho_0=0\) and \( ho_1 ar z+ ho_0=0\). Subtracting gives \( ho_1(z- ar z)=2iv ho_1=0\), so \( ho_1=0\) and then \( ho_0=0\). Thus \(p=ms\) with \(s\) monic and real of degree \(n-2\); apply the induction hypothesis to \(s\) if \(n-2\ge1\) (if \(n=2\), \(s=1\)).

In both cases \(p\) is the leading coefficient times a product of real linear and real irreducible quadratic factors. ◻ ∎

Example L.3: A degree-9 polynomial, factored by the theorem

The polynomial \(p(x)=(x-2)(x+3)^2\left(x^2-2x+10 ight)\left(x^2+x+1 ight)^2\) has degree \(1+2+2+4=9\) and expands to

\[x^9+4x^8+6x^7+34x^6+64x^5-84x^4-287x^3-500x^2-354x-180 .\]

The two quadratics have no real root: \(x^2-2x+10\) has \(b^2-4c=4-40=-36<0\) and \(x^2+x+1\) has \(1-4=-3<0\). The theorem says nothing like this can be avoided: given only the nine-term polynomial, its real factors are exactly these (Section 8.5 proves that the factors are unique). The quartic \(x^4+4\) has no real root either, yet it is not irreducible; it factors as \(\left(x^2+2x+2 ight)\left(x^2-2x+2 ight)\), two quadratics with \(b^2-4c=-4<0\).

items.title: Appendix M. Error Formulas for the Midpoint, Trapezoid and Simpson Rules
items.text:
Section 8.8 bounds the errors of the Midpoint, Trapezoid and Simpson rules. The textbook states those bounds without proof. They are proved here, from the facts of Calculus I only: the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, integration by parts, the substitution rule, the Extreme Value Theorem, the Intermediate Value Theorem, and the fact that the integral respects inequalities (\(g\le h\) on \([p,q]\) implies \(\int_p^qg\le\int_p^qh\)). The method is to write the error of one rule on one panel (a short interval) as an integral of a derivative of \(f\) against an explicit kernel; integration by parts does the work. A Taylor-type estimate (a later chapter treats Taylor polynomials and the Lagrange remainder) would give the same bounds, but the kernel method is shorter here and gives the exact value of the error, so the sign of the error is also decided.

Throughout, a panel is an interval \([c-h,c+h]\) with centre \(c\) and half-width \(h>0\). By the substitution \(u=c+s\) it is enough to work on \([-h,h]\) with \(g(s)=f(c+s)\), because \(g^{(j)}(s)=f^{(j)}(c+s)\) and \(\int_{c-h}^{c+h}f(u)\,du=\int_{-h}^{h}g(s)\,ds\). The three rules on the panel are

\[M=2h\,f(c),\qquad T=h\big(f(c-h)+f(c+h)\big),\qquad S=\frac h3\big(f(c-h)+4f(c)+f(c+h)\big),\]

and \(E_M\), \(E_T\), \(E_S\) denote \(\int_{c-h}^{c+h}f\) minus \(M\), \(T\), \(S\). (Simpson’s rule on a panel of half-width \(h\) uses three nodes at distance \(h\) apart.)

Theorem M.1: Mean Value Theorem for integrals, weighted form

Let \(w\) and \(g\) be continuous on \([p,q]\) with \(p<q\), and let \(w\ge0\) with \(W=\int_p^qw>0\). Then there is a number \(\xi\in[p,q]\) with

\[\int_p^qw(s)\,g(s)\,ds=g(\xi)\int_p^qw(s)\,ds.\]

If \(w\le0\) and \(\int_p^qw<0\) the same conclusion holds.

Proof. By the Extreme Value Theorem \(g\) has a smallest value \(m\) and a largest value \(\mu\) on \([p,q]\). Since \(w\ge0\), \(m\,w(s)\le w(s)g(s)\le\mu\,w(s)\) for every \(s\). Integrating, \(mW\le\int_p^qwg\le\mu W\), so the number \(\frac1W\int_p^qwg\) lies between \(m\) and \(\mu\). By the Intermediate Value Theorem \(g\) takes every value between \(m\) and \(\mu\), so \(g(\xi)=\frac1W\int_p^qwg\) for some \(\xi\in[p,q]\). If \(w\le0\) apply the result to \(-w\). \(\blacksquare\) ◻ ∎

Theorem M.2: One panel: Midpoint and Trapezoid

Let \(g\) have a continuous second derivative on \([-h,h]\), and put

\[K_M(s)=\frac{(h-\lvert s\rvert)^2}2,\qquad K_T(s)=\frac{h^2-s^2}2\qquad(\lvert s\rvert\le h).\]

Then \(K_M\ge0\), \(K_T\ge0\), \(\int_{-h}^hK_M=\frac{h^3}3\), \(\int_{-h}^hK_T=\frac{2h^3}3\), and

\[\int_{-h}^hg-2h\,g(0)=\int_{-h}^hK_M(s)\,g''(s)\,ds,\qquad \int_{-h}^hg-h\big(g(-h)+g(h)\big)=-\int_{-h}^hK_T(s)\,g''(s)\,ds.\]

Proof. The kernels. Both are nonnegative on \([-h,h]\), and

\[\int_{-h}^hK_M=2\int_0^h\frac{(h-s)^2}2\,ds=\left[-\frac{(h-s)^3}3\right]_0^h=\frac{h^3}3,\qquad \int_{-h}^hK_T=\frac12\left[h^2s-\frac{s^3}3\right]_{-h}^{h}=\frac12\left(2h^3-\frac{2h^3}3\right)=\frac{2h^3}3.\]

Midpoint. Integrate by parts on each half, with the antiderivative of \(1\) that vanishes at the far end of that half: on \([-h,0]\) use \(s+h\) and on \([0,h]\) use \(s-h\). Then

\[\int_{-h}^0g=\Big[(s+h)g(s)\Big]_{-h}^0-\int_{-h}^0(s+h)g'(s)\,ds=h\,g(0)-\int_{-h}^0(s+h)g'(s)\,ds,\] \[\int_0^hg=\Big[(s-h)g(s)\Big]_0^h-\int_0^h(s-h)g'(s)\,ds=h\,g(0)-\int_0^h(s-h)g'(s)\,ds.\]

Adding, \(\int_{-h}^hg-2hg(0)=-\int_{-h}^0(s+h)g'\,ds-\int_0^h(s-h)g'\,ds\). Now \(K_M\) is an antiderivative of \(s+h\) on \([-h,0]\) (there \(K_M=\frac{(s+h)^2}2\)) and of \(s-h\) on \([0,h]\) (there \(K_M=\frac{(s-h)^2}2\)). Integrate by parts again; \(K_M(-h)=K_M(h)=0\) and \(K_M(0)=\frac{h^2}2\) from both sides:

\[-\int_{-h}^0(s+h)g'=-\Big[K_Mg'\Big]_{-h}^0+\int_{-h}^0K_Mg''=-\frac{h^2}2g'(0)+\int_{-h}^0K_Mg'',\] \[-\int_0^h(s-h)g'=-\Big[K_Mg'\Big]_0^h+\int_0^hK_Mg''=\frac{h^2}2g'(0)+\int_0^hK_Mg''.\]

The boundary terms cancel, and the sum is \(\int_{-h}^hK_Mg''\).

Trapezoid. Integrate by parts with the antiderivative \(s\) of \(1\): \(\int_{-h}^hg=\big[sg(s)\big]_{-h}^h-\int_{-h}^hs\,g'(s)\,ds=h\big(g(h)+g(-h)\big)-\int_{-h}^hsg'\). The function \(-K_T(s)=\frac{s^2-h^2}2\) has derivative \(s\) and vanishes at \(\pm h\), so integrating by parts again,

\[\int_{-h}^hs\,g'(s)\,ds=\Big[-K_T(s)\,g'(s)\Big]_{-h}^h-\int_{-h}^h\big(-K_T(s)\big)\,g''(s)\,ds=\int_{-h}^hK_T\,g'',\]

because the boundary term is \(0\). Hence \(\int_{-h}^hg-h\big(g(-h)+g(h)\big)=-\int_{-h}^hs\,g'=-\int_{-h}^hK_Tg''\). \(\blacksquare\) ◻ ∎

Theorem M.3: One panel: Simpson

Let \(g\) have a continuous fourth derivative on \([-h,h]\), and put

\[K_S(s)=\frac{(h-\lvert s\rvert)^3\,(h+3\lvert s\rvert)}{72}\qquad(\lvert s\rvert\le h).\]

Then \(K_S\ge0\), \(\displaystyle\int_{-h}^hK_S=\frac{h^5}{90}\), and

\[\int_{-h}^hg-\frac h3\big(g(-h)+4g(0)+g(h)\big)=-\int_{-h}^hK_S(s)\,g^{(4)}(s)\,ds.\]

Proof. The kernel. \(K_S\ge0\) because \(h-\lvert s\rvert\ge0\). Expanding, \((h-s)^3(h+3s)=h^4-6h^2s^2+8hs^3-3s^4\), so

\[\int_{-h}^hK_S=\frac2{72}\int_0^h\big(h^4-6h^2s^2+8hs^3-3s^4\big)ds=\frac1{36}\left(h^5-2h^5+2h^5-\frac35h^5\right)=\frac1{36}\cdot\frac25h^5=\frac{h^5}{90}.\]

The error. On a panel, \(\frac13(2M+T)=\frac13\big(4hg(0)+h(g(-h)+g(h))\big)=S\), so \(E_S=\frac13(2E_M+E_T)\). By Theorem M.2, \(2E_M+E_T=\int_{-h}^hq\,g''\) with

\[q(s)=2K_M(s)-K_T(s)=(h-\lvert s\rvert)^2-\frac{(h-\lvert s\rvert)(h+\lvert s\rvert)}2=\frac{(h-\lvert s\rvert)(h-3\lvert s\rvert)}2.\]

The function \(q\) changes sign (at \(\lvert s\rvert=\frac h3\)), so we integrate by parts twice more, each time with an antiderivative that vanishes at \(\pm h\). Let

\[Q(s)=\frac{s\,(h-\lvert s\rvert)^2}2,\qquad R(s)=-\frac{(h-\lvert s\rvert)^3(h+3\lvert s\rvert)}{24}=-3K_S(s).\]

Both are continuous, and both vanish at \(s=\pm h\). For \(s>0\), \(Q'(s)=\frac{(h-s)^2}2-s(h-s)=\frac{(h-s)(h-3s)}2=q(s)\), and \(R'(s)=-\frac{-3(h-s)^2(h+3s)+3(h-s)^3}{24}=\frac{(h-s)^2\,s}2=Q(s)\). For \(s<0\) the same computations, with \(\lvert s\rvert=-s\), give \(Q'(s)=\frac{(h+s)(h+3s)}2=q(s)\) and \(R'(s)=\frac{s(h+s)^2}2=Q(s)\). Now integrate by parts on \([-h,0]\) and on \([0,h]\) separately. The boundary terms at \(s=\pm h\) vanish, and those at \(s=0\) cancel because \(Q\) and \(R\) are continuous there. Hence

\[\int_{-h}^hq\,g''=-\int_{-h}^hQ\,g'''=\int_{-h}^hR\,g^{(4)}=-3\int_{-h}^hK_S\,g^{(4)},\]

and \(E_S=\frac13(2E_M+E_T)=-\int_{-h}^hK_S\,g^{(4)}\). \(\blacksquare\) ◻ ∎

Theorem M.4: One panel: the error as a value of a derivative

Let \(f\) be defined on the panel \([c-h,c+h]\).

(1) If \(f''\) is continuous, there are points \(\xi_1,\xi_2\) in the panel with \(E_M=\dfrac{h^3}3f''(\xi_1)\) and \(E_T=-\dfrac{2h^3}3f''(\xi_2)\).

(2) If \(f^{(4)}\) is continuous, there is a point \(\xi_3\) in the panel with \(E_S=-\dfrac{h^5}{90}f^{(4)}(\xi_3)\).

In particular, if \(\lvert f''\rvert\le M_2\) on the panel then \(\lvert E_M\rvert\le\frac{h^3}3M_2\) and \(\lvert E_T\rvert\le\frac{2h^3}3M_2\), and if \(\lvert f^{(4)}\rvert\le M_4\) then \(\lvert E_S\rvert\le\frac{h^5}{90}M_4\).

Proof. Apply Theorem M.1 with \(g(s)=f''(c+s)\) and \(w=K_M\) (continuous, \(\ge0\), with integral \(\frac{h^3}3>0\)): \(E_M=\int K_Mg''=g''(\xi)\frac{h^3}3\), that is, \(E_M=\frac{h^3}3f''(c+\xi)\). The same argument with \(w=K_T\) gives \(E_T=-\frac{2h^3}3f''(c+\xi')\), and with \(w=K_S\) and \(g^{(4)}\) it gives \(E_S=-\frac{h^5}{90}f^{(4)}(c+\xi'')\). The bounds follow by taking absolute values. \(\blacksquare\) ◻ ∎

Example M.5: The three kernel identities for \(f(x)=x^4\) on \([-1,1]\)

Take \(c=0\), \(h=1\), \(f(x)=x^4\), so \(f''(x)=12x^2\) and \(f^{(4)}=24\). The integral is \(\int_{-1}^1x^4\,dx=\frac25\).

Midpoint: \(M=2f(0)=0\), so \(E_M=\frac25\); the kernel side is \(\int_{-1}^1\frac{(1-\lvert s\rvert)^2}2\cdot12s^2\,ds=12\int_0^1(1-s)^2s^2\,ds=12\cdot\frac1{30}=\frac25\).

Trapezoid: \(T=f(-1)+f(1)=2\), so \(E_T=\frac25-2=-\frac85\); the kernel side is \(-\int_{-1}^1\frac{1-s^2}2\cdot12s^2\,ds=-12\cdot\frac2{15}=-\frac85\).

Simpson: \(S=\frac13(1+0+1)=\frac23\), so \(E_S=\frac25-\frac23=-\frac4{15}\); the kernel side is \(-24\int_{-1}^1K_S=-24\cdot\frac1{90}=-\frac4{15}\).

All three identities hold, and the signs agree with the theorem: \(E_M>0\) and \(E_T<0\) because \(f''\ge0\), and \(E_S<0\) because \(f^{(4)}>0\).

items.title: Appendix N. Monotone Functions and Nonnegative Integrals at a Finite Endpoint
items.text:
Appendix C proved that a nondecreasing function on \([a,\infty)\) has a limit at \(\infty\) (Theorem C.3) and used it for improper integrals of nonnegative functions over an infinite interval (Theorem C.4). The Comparison Test of Section 8.9 is also used at a finite endpoint where the integrand is unbounded, and the same argument works there. We prove the two facts that this needs. Both rest on the completeness of the real numbers (Appendix A), through the supremum and Theorem A.3.

Theorem N.1: A monotone function has a limit at a finite endpoint

Let \(g\) be defined on \([a,b)\) and nondecreasing.

(a) If \(g\) is bounded above, then \(\lim_{x\to b^-}g(x)\) exists and equals \(\sup\{g(x):a\le x<b\}\).

(b) If \(g\) is not bounded above, then \(g(x)\to\infty\) as \(x\to b^-\).

Proof. (a) The set \(\{g(x):a\le x<b\}\) is nonempty and bounded above, so \(M=\sup\{g(x):a\le x<b\}\) exists (Completeness Axiom). Let \(\varepsilon>0\). By Theorem A.3 there is \(x_0\in[a,b)\) with \(M-\varepsilon<g(x_0)\le M\). For every \(x\) with \(x_0<x<b\), monotonicity gives \(M-\varepsilon<g(x_0)\le g(x)\le M\), so \(\abs{g(x)-M}<\varepsilon\). This holds for all \(x\) in the interval \((x_0,b)\), which is the statement \(g(x)\to M\) as \(x\to b^-\) (take \(\delta=b-x_0>0\)).

(b) Let \(K\) be a number. Since \(K\) is not an upper bound, there is \(x_0\in[a,b)\) with \(g(x_0)>K\), and then \(g(x)\ge g(x_0)>K\) for all \(x\in(x_0,b)\). \(\blacksquare\) ◻ ∎

Theorem N.2: Improper integrals of nonnegative functions at a finite endpoint

Let \(f\) be continuous on \([a,b)\) with \(f(x)\ge0\), and let \(F(t)=\int_a^tf(x)\,dx\) for \(a\le t<b\). Then \(F\) is nondecreasing, and

(a) the improper integral \(\int_a^bf(x)\,dx=\lim_{t\to b^-}F(t)\) converges if and only if \(F\) is bounded above, and then \(F(t)\le\int_a^bf(x)\,dx\) for every \(t\);

(b) if \(F\) is not bounded above, then \(\int_a^bf(x)\,dx=\infty\).

The same statements hold for \(\int_a^bf\) with a singularity at the left-hand end \(a\), using \(F(t)=\int_t^bf\) for \(a<t\le b\).

Proof. If \(a\le s<t<b\) then \(F(t)-F(s)=\int_s^tf\ge0\), so \(F\) is nondecreasing. By Theorem N.1, if \(F\) is bounded above then \(\lim_{t\to b^-}F(t)=\sup F\) exists and is at least every \(F(t)\); if \(F\) is not bounded above then \(F(t)\to\infty\), so the integral does not converge. This proves (a) and (b), since a convergent integral has a finite limit and therefore forces \(F\) to be bounded above. For the left-hand end, apply the result to \(\tilde f(x)=f(a+b-x)\) on \([a,b)\) (the graph of \(f\) reflected in the line \(x=\frac{a+b}2\)): the substitution \(u=a+b-x\) turns \(\int_t^bf\) into \(\int_a^{a+b-t}\tilde f\). \(\blacksquare\) ◻ ∎

Example N.3: Bounded and unbounded partial integrals

Decide whether \(\int_0^1\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x}}\) and \(\int_0^1\frac{dx}{1-x}\) converge, using Theorem N.2.

Solution. Both integrands are continuous and positive on \([0,1)\) and tend to \(\infty\) at \(x=1\). For the first, \(F(t)=\int_0^t\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x}}=2-2\sqrt{1-t}\), and \(F(t)<2\) for every \(t\) in \([0,1)\), so \(F\) is bounded above and the integral converges, to \(2\). For the second, \(F(t)=\int_0^t\frac{dx}{1-x}=-\ln(1-t)\), which exceeds any number \(K\) once \(t>1-e^{-K}\). So \(F\) is not bounded above and the integral diverges to \(\infty\). (The bounded criterion is exactly the dichotomy of the \(p\)-integrals at \(p=\frac12\) and \(p=1\).)
